items.title: Why AI Makes Identity Security Urgent
items.summary: With contributions from Scott Whitehouse and Maor Franco. Helping Customers Move from Urgency to Action As organizations put AI agents to work, they’re giving more identities access to sensitive information, critical systems and the ability to take action across the business. Each new agent deployment involves decisions about how much access the agent needs — and how to control that access. AI adds a new layer of security complexity for customers already working to manage the permissions employees and machines hold. Excessive privileges, exposed credentials and forgotten accounts create opportunities for malicious actors both inside and outside the organization, and AI can help them exploit those weaknesses faster. In a recent Unit 42 investigation , an attacker used AI agents to breach an enterprise network in less than 10 hours — an intrusion that would typically take human operators about two weeks. Along the way, the agents exploited exposed credentials to gain privileged access and steal cloud keys. Customers need to bring existing access under control while establishing guardrails for AI initiatives. When separate tools and teams manage different parts of identity security, it becomes harder to see the full picture and act on it consistently. That makes a unified approach to identity security increasingly essential — one enabled by Idira , the Palo Alto Networks next-generation identity security platform. In a previous post , I highlighted the opportunity for Palo Alto Networks and our partners to seize a defining moment in identity security and help customers rethink identity as a foundation of security for the AI enterprise. (You can explore that connection further in this video and blog post .) Our challenge, and opportunity, is to help customers understand where their current approach leaves them exposed and take practical steps to close those gaps. For partners, this creates a full services lifecycle: assessing identity risk, implementing modern privilege controls and managing governance over time. Each stage is a natural engagement, and together they give partners a path to grow with customers as their AI use expands. Recognizing Why Identity Security Can’t Wait When organizations adopt AI, they’re introducing agents into environments where employees may already have more access than they need, and machine accounts may still hold permissions from projects that ended months ago. Adding agents without addressing those gaps can compound the risk. Partners can help customers connect their AI plans with the access decisions those initiatives require. A customer may be focused on what a new agent can accomplish, but they also need to understand what they’re authorizing it to do. An agent acting for an employee should stay within the access appropriate to that person and task. Establishing those boundaries at the outset puts customers in a better position to expand AI use securely. Those access decisions also matter when something goes wrong. If an identity is compromised, the permissions attached to it can determine how far an attacker gets and what damage they can cause. Reducing unnecessary access — and limiting how long elevated permissions remain available — removes some of the fuel that allows an attack to spread. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report reinforces that point: Privilege management could help mitigate roughly 65% of the privilege escalation and credential access techniques examined in its analysis. Controlling permissions can make a meaningful difference in how far an attacker gets. Network, cloud and endpoint defenses remain essential, of course. But identity security reinforces those protections by limiting what an attacker can do with a compromised account or credential. The 2026 Global Incident Response Report from Unit 42 underscores its importance, finding that identity weaknesses played a material role in nearly 90% of investigations over the past year. Strong identity security can help stop an initial intrusion from escalating into data theft, disrupted operations or lasting damage to customer trust. Rethinking Who and What Holds Privilege Ask customers who their privileged users are and, for many, IT administrators will likely come to mind first. But access to sensitive information and important business systems extends to users across the organization. Think about the access people need to do their jobs. Someone in marketing may manage the company’s social accounts, while a colleague in sales can download customer records and confidential pricing agreements. Neither may be considered a privileged user, yet a compromised account could damage the company’s reputation or expose sensitive customer information, confidential business plans or intellectual property. Now consider a developer giving an AI agent access to code repositories. That agent is taking on access that carries its own risks and needs appropriate controls. Examining privileged access in these everyday activities can bring more people into the identity security discussion. Application owners, development teams and business leaders can help identify which permissions are necessary and where tighter controls could interfere with day-to-day work. For example, cumbersome access processes can encourage developers to find workarounds. Making appropriate access easier to obtain while ensuring elevated permissions expire when no longer needed can reduce exposure without slowing development. Keeping Access Aligned with Business Needs Access is often granted to meet an immediate business need. But without continuous oversight, permissions, credentials and connections can persist long after that need has passed. This accumulated “identity debt” can leave organizations exposed in ways they no longer recognize or fully understand. Consider a partner implementing a new application for a customer. The project may require temporary access and connections between systems. Before the project ends, the partner should work with the customer to determine which permissions remain necessary, who will own the associated identities and how access will be reviewed and revoked over time. According to our 2026 Identity Security Landscape report , machine identities, including AI agents, now outnumber human identities 109 to 1. These identities often retain access they no longer need. Securing them requires different controls than securing human users, but a unified approach helps customers manage permissions across all identities and adjust them as business needs change. Enabling Continuous Discovery, Control and Governance of Identities Through Platformization Partners can help customers get started with implementing identity security by focusing on three priorities: Discover identity risk. Help customers see which human, machine and AI agent identities have access, what privileges they hold and where credentials may be exposed. AI-driven discovery and analytics can surface risks that are difficult to find manually. Identifying excessive privileges and standing access gives partners a practical starting point for a customer assessment. Control every privilege. Partners can help customers rethink how much access they leave in place between tasks. Modern privileged access management (PAM) from Idira supports a move toward zero standing privilege for every identity, with elevated permissions granted just in time to perform authorized work. Organizations can give people the access they need while reducing the risk that comes with leaving those permissions always on. Automate governance. Keep permissions aligned with changing roles, projects and business needs. CORA AI, built into Idira, helps automate how access is granted, reviewed and removed across the identity lifecycle. That helps businesses keep pace with change, reduce administrative work and support compliance. These activities need to work together. Once a customer identifies excessive access, they need to adjust permissions and keep them aligned with evolving business needs. Continuous discovery helps them spot new risks along the way. Idira simplifies this process by bringing discovery, privilege controls and governance together across human, machine and agentic identities. Bringing Identity Security into Customer Transformation Plans Partners are well-positioned to connect identity security to the transformations customers already have underway. A cloud migration, application modernization project or AI deployment is a chance to help customers evaluate who and what needs access and how to manage that access from the start. Some customers will need an assessment and a road map. Others will seek implementation expertise, privilege modernization or ongoing operational support. Understanding those needs gives partners a starting point to expand their services and help customers make identity security part of their broader security strategy. For managed security service providers (MSSPs) , Idira offers an opportunity to build managed identity security services on a unified platform, with native identity posture management and threat detection capabilities, rather than stitching together separate tools. Our customers are making many critical decisions about AI and access now. We can help them ask the right questions before granting permissions, put processes in place to revisit those decisions as their business changes and make identity security part of how they operate, with access that serves a clear purpose and is removed when that purpose ends. Ready to Lead the Identity Security Conversation? Through the NextWave program, partner teams can build their knowledge of Idira and its role in Palo Alto Networks broader platformization strategy . I encourage sales, technical and services teams to explore the latest resources and enablement in the NextWave Partner Portal and bring identity security into the next discussion about a customer’s cloud, application or AI plans. Key Takeaways AI makes identity security more urgent by expanding access and accelerating attacks. A unified platform connects discovery, privilege controls and governance to secure every identity - human, machine and AI agent. Through the newly reimagined NextWave program, partners can build Idira expertise and deliver services that can help customers strengthen identity security.

items.title: How Agentic Engineering Puts AppSec Teams Under Pressure
items.summary: On 16 November, I gave a guest lecture to the Software Engineering course at Humboldt University Berlin (HU). It is an updated version of my HTW Berlin lecture from June, and this time I built the storyline around a single observation: agentic engineering puts application security (AppSec) teams under pressure from two sides. They drown in findings, and the reactive gates they rely on to help engineering teams build secure software are too slow and too detached for agent loops. The slide deck has all 47 slides, including a glossary and backup material. The dedicated talk page has the reading list with every source for the numbers, quotes and examples on the slides. AppSec Teams Drown in Findings # Throughout 2026, finding vulnerabilities became much less expensive, and the bucket of findings and verified vulnerabilities grows faster than anyone can empty it. Of the 26,153 findings that Anthropic claims for Project Glasswing, VulnCheck counted 202 as fixed in September 2026. Maintainers see the same: Axios reports , with numbers from the OpenSSL Foundation, that the security reports and inquiries to OpenSSL went from 9 per month in May to July 2025 to 71 per month in the same months of 2026. At the same time, triaging also became more complicated, because nearly all of the new findings come at least with a high rating. Claude rated 91.5% of the Glasswing findings “critical” or “high”, while the maintainers still rated 51.3% that way after review. The severity rating doesn’t really help people with prioritising which finding to fix first. On top of that, agentic use cases create yet another class of problems and attack vectors. I used an actual incident as the stage-setting opener for the talk: Clinejection allowed arbitrary actors to inject instructions to the AI triage agent in the GitHub repository of the coding agent Cline. It was discovered and disclosed by the security researcher Adnan Khan, who also showed how an attacker could get from there to the artifact publishing tokens, impersonating the actual maintainers. Established scanning gates, manual triaging and ticketing are not sufficient anymore for this amount of findings. My idea for an SRE error budget inspired security risk budget also made into this talk: a limit on how long a high-risk, reachable vulnerability may stay in production, so people and agents fix the findings that use the budget and defer the rest. Reactive Gates Are Too Slow for Agent Loops # AppSec is also under pressure when it comes to supporting engineering teams in building secure software. A coding agent writes, tests, reads the failure and rewrites many times per session. A gate that reports a finding after the code exists, as part of PR checks or CI/CD pipelines, is too slow for that loop and too detached from it. One of the obvious levers to improve the situation is the agent harness. Google’s New SDLC whitepaper estimates an agent at roughly 10% model and 90% harness. AppSec teams don’t control the model, but they can improve the harness by shifting security left into it. Leveraging agent loop hook, to run static application security testing (SAST) tool in the session, and nudging the agent to correct itself while the task is still in its context is one of the approaches I outline. The other is classic security knowledge skills. Both approaches might not yield the expected outcome though. The CoSAI CodeGuard evaluation that I shared with the students, shows that a single sentence prompt that asks for secure code did as well as the fully fledged CodeGuard security skill. One possible explanaition: The underlying benchmark uses generic tasks, and general security knowledge is likely already part of the modern frontier models. It seems fair to assume that the same holds for scanner feedback that only tests for general security issues. I’d expect hooks and skills to pay off where they carry the proprietary knowledge of an organization, and no public benchmark measures that (yet). The Agent Itself Needs a Sandbox # At the same time, the agent itself can become dangerous, as it runs commands and reads untrusted content such as the issue title in Clinejection. Sandboxing the agent is therefore an AppSec topic too. A sandbox limits which files and network hosts the agent’s commands can reach. However, like the rest of the harness improvements, also the sandbox stays a local decision that each developer configures on their own machine if there is no centrally enforced sandbox. Shift Security Down into the Platform # An orthogonal and potentially better option than improving individual harnesses is to shift security down into a platform and to create golden paths that are secure by default. Shift-left asks whether a team implemented authentication correctly, while shift-down asks why the team implements authentication at all. When the platform provides authentication, neither the team nor its agent writes authentication code that someone has to scan and fix afterwards. In case you want to learn more about this platform role, read Shift Down: Why Agentic Engineering Demands Platform-Level Security . Cline’s own fixes point in the same direction: they removed the triage workflow, took the build cache out of the publish workflows and moved npm releases to OIDC publishing with short-lived tokens. None of them is a better prompt, and each one limits what the agent or its pipeline can reach. Agent Substrate, which Google donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) in November, is one step in this direction for agents, as it keeps credentials out of the agent’s sandbox altogether. What I Left Open for the Students # For the students, and for research, the open problems from the talk are the important part. I closed with three of them and suggested each one as a thesis topic: How to model delegation and secure the actor chain when an headless agent acts on behalf of a machine, without a person in the loop. How to evaluate a skill that is specific to one organization, when public benchmarks measure generic knowledge (and without leaking the approach into training data). How to triage the flood of vulnerabilities that AI finds and how to support maintainers of critical open source projects.

items.title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: New Sentinel Connectors Announcement
items.summary: Microsoft Sentinel helps organizations detect, investigate, and respond to threats across increasingly complex environments. As AI transforms security operations, bringing together the right data and context is more important than ever, giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete view of the environment to reason over and act on. These integrations bring signals from Microsoft and third-party technologies together across the security environment, unlocking richer context for investigations and helping power the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender , where human defenders and AI agents can reason across the environment with shared context. The connector ecosystem isn’t the only area seeing rapid growth. Microsoft Sentinel continues to add new capabilities, including Nested API support, Azure Blob support, and multi-account support, while AI-powered tools like the connector builder agent are making it easier than ever for developers to build integrations and bring more of their security data into Sentinel. At the same time, Unified Data Management , now in public preview, makes it easier for customers to manage their Microsoft Sentinel data, connectors, tables, and ingestion health in one place. For Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re excited to showcase recent additions to this growing ecosystem and the partners making them possible. These new and enhanced connectors continue to broaden the security data available to customers, helping human defenders and AI agents gain the context they need across the technology estate. Airlock Digital for Microsoft Sentinel Airlock Digital helps prevent malware, ransomware, and unauthorized software with deny by default application control, allowing only trusted applications, scripts, and processes to run. Its Microsoft Sentinel push integration ingests execution history, browser extension control events, server administrative activity, and policy changes for monitoring and investigation. Included parsers map execution and audit events to Microsoft’s ASIM for analysis alongside other security signals. A customizable workbook supports investigation and monitoring, and teams can create analytics rules using the ingested data. NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentinel NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentin el from archTIS brings user activity and protection logs from NC Protect into Sentinel for centralized security analysis. The connector captures user activities and access-related events, while built-in workbooks support investigation and visualization of user behavior. By correlating NC Protect audit data with other security telemetry, the integration helps teams identify suspicious user activity, trigger alerts and response workflows, strengthen auditing, and monitor guest activity across SharePoint and Teams. blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel brings external and internal attack-surface data, risk-prioritized vulnerabilities, darknet intelligence, and supply-chain risks into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests exposed assets, compromised identities, stolen credentials and session cookies, typosquatting domains, and supplier activity on ransomware leak sites. The solution includes a data connector and analytics rule for creating Sentinel incidents, with configurable notification rules for alert severity and type. Findings are available in Log Analytics for correlation with existing Sentinel signals and can support custom analytics rules, workbooks, automation, and threat investigations. BloodHound Enterprise BloodHound Enterprise (BHE) helps organizations protect critical assets across modern hybrid environments by continuously uncovering identity attack paths and providing actionable remediation guidance. By integrating with Microsoft Sentinel, BHE delivers attack path data and identity security posture insights directly into Sentinel workflows. This helps security teams prioritize remediation efforts based on exposure to critical assets while enriching investigations into identity-based threats, including lateral movement and privilege escalation. Together, BHE and Microsoft Sentinel help security teams connect threat detection to underlying identity risk, speed investigations, and reduce opportunities for attackers. BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance brings compliance activity from the Anthropic Claude Compliance API into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests Claude compliance events into Sentinel, giving security, risk, and audit teams centralized visibility into AI usage and related activity. By correlating these compliance signals with identity, endpoint, and other security telemetry, the integration supports threat hunting, investigation of policy violations and anomalous behavior, compliance monitoring, and repeatable audit workflows. Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel brings security and network events from the Cato SASE Platform into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) Push pattern. The connector pushes events into a dedicated Log Analytics table, making Cato activity available alongside other Sentinel data. By centralizing this telemetry in Sentinel, the integration enables security teams to incorporate Cato events into threat hunting, detection, and visualization workflows alongside broader security signals. Check Point EM ThreatCloud Intelligence Feed Connector for Microsoft Sentinel The Check Point EM ThreatCloud Intelligence Feed Connector brings threat intelligence from Check Point Exposure Management into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests indicators of compromise (IoCs), including malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with threat context such as confidence, severity, kill-chain stage, and campaign associations. An included playbook further enriches incident IoCs through ThreatCloud, helping security teams correlate intelligence with existing telemetry, accelerate triage and investigation, and reduce the manual effort required to maintain threat intelligence. Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel brings threat intelligence from Check Point Infinity External Risk Management into Sentinel. The connector ingests malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with context such as severity, confidence, and detected activity. By correlating these indicators of compromise (IoCs) with existing logs through analytics rules, hunting queries, and watchlists, the integration helps security teams reduce manual intelligence management, identify matches with external threats, and accelerate threat detection and investigation. Citrix SPA Sentinel App Citrix SPA Sentinel App brings Citrix Secure Private Access and Device Posture service events into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector imports critical logs, policy outcomes, and user activity data, giving security teams greater visibility into application access and device posture activity. An included workbook supports visualization and analysis of Citrix data, helping SOC teams correlate activity with broader security telemetry, investigate security risks, support compliance monitoring, and strengthen threat hunting across their environment. ContraForce Events for Microsoft Sentinel ContraForce Events for Microsoft Sentinel brings security delivery and administrative activity from ContraForce workspaces into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). ContraForce is an Agentic Security Delivery Platform for service providers and security teams running triage, investigation, and response across Microsoft Defender XDR and Sentinel. Microsoft Sentinel helps organizations detect, investigate, and respond to threats across increasingly complex environments. As AI transforms security operations, bringing together the right data and context is more important than ever, giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete view of the environment to reason over and act on. 

These integrations bring signals from Microsoft and third-party technologies together across the security environment, unlocking richer context for investigations and helping power the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, where human defenders and AI agents can reason across the environment with shared context. 

The connector ecosystem isn’t the only area seeing rapid growth. Microsoft Sentinel continues to add new capabilities, including Nested API support, Azure Blob support, and multi-account support, while AI-powered tools like the connector builder agent are making it easier than ever for developers to build integrations and bring more of their security data into Sentinel. At the same time, Unified Data Management, now in public preview, makes it easier for customers to manage their Microsoft Sentinel data, connectors, tables, and ingestion health in one place. 

For Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re excited to showcase recent additions to this growing ecosystem and the partners making them possible. These new and enhanced connectors continue to broaden the security data available to customers, helping human defenders and AI agents gain the context they need across the technology estate.

Its Microsoft Sentinel push integration ingests execution history, browser extension control events, server administrative activity, and policy changes for monitoring and investigation. Included parsers map execution and audit events to Microsoft’s ASIM for analysis alongside other security signals. The solution includes a data connector and analytics rule for creating Sentinel incidents, with configurable notification rules for alert severity and type. By making validated exposures available in Sentinel, security teams can correlate external risks with endpoint and network telemetry, track remediation progress, and build analytics rules, workbooks, and hunting queries on top of FireCompass findings. 

Gambit Security Sentinel Solution

Gambit brings resilience context into Microsoft Sentinel. It finds the resilience issues in your environment and syncs them to your Sentinel workspace daily, to help analysts see recovery risk before anything goes wrong. Sentinel correlates those issues with its detections. Your team can then prioritize the attacks most likely to disrupt critical operations: the ones hitting resources that aren’t ready to recover. Sentinel tells you what’s happening. Gambit tells you whether you can recover from it. 

Holm Security for Microsoft Sentinel 

Holm Security for Microsoft Sentinel brings asset data from the Holm Security platform into Sentinel via the Holm Security REST API. The connector ingests web and network assets into Microsoft Sentinel, including metadata such as IP addresses, hostnames, operating systems, tags, and vulnerability counts per asset. By incorporating this asset inventory alongside other security telemetry, the integration enables security teams to build dashboards, create custom alerts, and correlate asset information with other data in Microsoft Sentinel. 

 

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager for Microsoft Sentinel 

The Idira® Endpoint Privilege Manager by Palo Alto Networks integration for Microsoft Sentinel pulls application events and policy audit activity into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework and the Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager REST API. Events land in a dedicated Log Analytics table, so security teams can analyze privilege activity alongside their other telemetry and build detections. 

 

IPinfo: IP geolocation & intelligence database

IPinfo: IP geolocation & intelligence database brings contextual IP intelligence into Microsoft Sentinel to enrich security logs and investigations. The solution provides data such as IP geolocation, network ownership and routing, proxy and residential proxy detection, ASN information, and other IP classifications. By adding this context to IP addresses observed in Sentinel, the integration helps security teams better understand indicators of compromise, prioritize security events, strengthen threat detection and investigation, and inform network and access management decisions. 

 

Island Solution for Microsoft Sentinel

Island Solution for Microsoft Sentinel brings user activity and administrative audit events from the Island Enterprise Browser into Microsoft Sentinel for centralized security monitoring. The solution automatically shares events from the Island Management Console with Sentinel and includes data connectors and workbooks for user activity and admin audit logs. By adding browser activity context to existing security telemetry, the integration helps security teams monitor and analyze user and administrative activity and investigate potential security issues.

 

NetApp Ransomware Resilience for Microsoft Sentinel

NetApp Ransomware Resilience detects and contains ransomware attacks on NetApp ONTAP workloads in real time, then enables fast, clean recovery. Its Microsoft Sentinel integration enriches alerts with data-layer context, including attack type, severity, user and IP, and affected cluster, volume, and SVM. The NetApp SOAR playbook can take actions on ONTAP such as trigger immutable snapshots, block suspicious users or IPs, and take compromised volumes offline. Together, these integrations extend the NetApp Platform’s ability to help security teams triage and respond to ransomware attacks, limit data loss, protect recovery points, and coordinate response across storage and security teams. 

 

NordStellar for Microsoft Sentinel

NordLayer Intelligence by NordStellar for Microsoft Sentinel brings external threat and exposure findings into Sentinel through the Azure Monitor Logs Ingestion API. The integration provides findings including leaked credentials, breach exposures, malware and info-stealer infections, dark web activity, domain impersonation risks, and external attack surface vulnerabilities. By correlating these findings with other security telemetry in Sentinel, the solution helps teams investigate external threats, identify exposures affecting their organization, and automate triage and response through analytics rules and SOAR playbooks.

 

Panorays for Microsoft Sentinel

Panorays for Microsoft Sentinel brings third-party security findings from the Panorays platform into Sentinel through the Panorays API. The connector provides security teams with visibility into the security posture of vendors and supply-chain organizations, making third-party risk and vulnerability findings available alongside other security telemetry. By incorporating Panorays findings into Sentinel workflows, the integration helps SOC teams centrally monitor and investigate third-party risks and correlate them with internal security signals.

 

USTA Account Takeover Prevention Sentinel Connector

USTA Account Takeover Prevention Sentinel Connector brings compromised credential intelligence from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Intelligence platform into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests alerts for exposed corporate credentials, enabling security teams to investigate potential account takeover risks within existing Sentinel workflows. Included analytics can identify newly compromised credentials and successful Microsoft Entra ID sign-ins involving known-compromised accounts, helping SOC teams operationalize external credential intelligence and prioritize investigation and response.

 

USTA IoC Threat Stream for Sentinel

USTA IoC Threat Stream for Sentinel brings curated indicators of compromise (IoCs) from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Stream into Microsoft Sentinel Threat Intelligence. The integration provides indicators including malicious URLs, phishing sites, and malware hashes derived from PRODAFT investigations. By making these indicators available for correlation with existing telemetry, hunting queries, and detection rules, the solution helps security teams identify connections to malicious infrastructure, investigate phishing and malware activity, and incorporate external threat intelligence into existing triage and response workflows.

 

USTA Payment Card Fraud Intelligence Sentinel Connector

USTA Payment Card Fraud Intelligence Sentinel Connector brings compromised payment card intelligence from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Intelligence platform into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector retrieves alerts associated with an organization’s payment card BIN ranges and makes them available within Sentinel for investigation. Included analytics identify newly exposed and non-expired compromised cards, helping security teams centralize payment fraud intelligence, prioritize potentially actionable exposures, and incorporate them into existing investigation and response workflows.

 

Pulumi Cloud Audit Logs for Microsoft Sentinel 

Pulumi Cloud Audit Logs for Microsoft Sentinel brings audit logs from Pulumi, the infrastructure platform for humans and agents, into Microsoft Sentinel through the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests authentication events, organization membership changes, stack lifecycle operations, policy changes, and access token usage. It also includes three analytics rules that detect failed login attempts, stack deletions, and organization membership changes. Your security team can see what a human or agent did, when, and where across infrastructure as code, secrets, configuration, and policies, which helps speed up security and governance investigations.  

 

QCrypton PQC Scanner for Microsoft Sentinel 

QCrypton PQC Scanner for Microsoft Sentinel brings post-quantum cryptography readiness findings from Azure environments into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector provides visibility into cryptographic assets including Key Vault keys, TLS certificates and configurations, and Entra ID app registration certificates, with quantum posture ratings and risk scores. Included are six analytics rules, a workbook, and a notification playbook to help security teams identify vulnerable cryptographic assets and prioritize post-quantum migration planning. 

 

SailPoint for Microsoft Sentinel 

SailPoint for Microsoft Sentinel brings identity security telemetry from SailPoint Identity Security Cloud into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The solution streams audit and search events into Sentinel tables, where analysts can correlate identity activity with other security signals and query SailPoint APIs for additional identity and account context during incident triage. Automated playbooks can also remediate threats by revoking access or disabling compromised accounts, helping teams connect identity insight with investigation and response.

 

SAP LogServ (RISE), S/4HANA Cloud private edition

SAP LogServ (RISE), S/4HANA Cloud private edition extends Microsoft Sentinel security monitoring for SAP RISE environments with infrastructure, database, operating system, and network security logs managed by SAP Enterprise Cloud Services. Deployed alongside the Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP applications, it complements application-layer monitoring to provide visibility across the SAP stack and enable cross-layer threat detection and correlation. The solution supports near real-time log collection, built-in analytics and workbooks, ASIM-based security content, and correlation with signals from endpoints, Microsoft Entra ID, and other sources in Microsoft Sentinel.   

 

MailRisk data connector for Microsoft Sentinel

MailRisk data connector for Microsoft Sentinel brings suspicious email data analyzed by users through Secure Practice MailRisk into Sentinel. The connector ingests enriched email metadata and risk assessment updates from the Secure Practice API, providing potential indicators of compromise identified from reported emails. By incorporating MailRisk data alongside other security telemetry, the integration helps security teams correlate suspicious email activity, search and investigate potential threats, and incorporate user-reported email intelligence into alerting and incident response workflows. 

SecurityScorecard Ratings for Microsoft Sentinel 

SecurityScorecard Ratings for Microsoft Sentinel provides cybersecurity posture ratings based on continuously monitored risk factors and threat intelligence. SecurityScorecard evaluates organizations using an A-F rating, helping security teams identify and track cybersecurity risks. The solution supports use cases including enterprise cyber risk management, third-party risk monitoring, executive reporting, and cyber due diligence. 

 

SIGNL4 - Mobile Alerting & Response for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud

SIGNL4 bridges the gap between security detection and human response with mobile-first alerting and incident management for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud. Its two-way integrations allow security teams to acknowledge, escalate, and resolve incidents directly from their mobile devices, with updates automatically synchronized back to Sentinel. Critical Defender for Cloud findings trigger actionable response workflows, while persistent mobile notifications, automated escalations, and on-call scheduling ensure the right people are reached when it matters most. The result is faster incident response, clear accountability, and a fully auditable process - wherever responders are.


SOC Prime Audit CCP

SOC Prime Audit CCP brings SOC Prime Platform audit logs into Microsoft Sentinel for centralized security monitoring and analysis. The connector ingests platform activity including user actions, API calls, and administrative events, providing an audit trail across detection engineering processes. By correlating SOC Prime activity with other security signals in Sentinel, the integration helps security teams investigate platform activity, support compliance monitoring, and incorporate audit telemetry into broader threat detection and response workflows. 

 

SOCRadar Alerts Azure Sentinel Directional Solution

SOCRadar Threat Intelligence for Microsoft Sentinel enriches security operations by bringing prioritized, context-rich alerts directly into Microsoft Sentinel. Covering SOCRadar’s Extended Threat Intelligence capabilities, including Brand Protection, External Attack Surface Management (ASM), Third-Party Findings, and other security modules, the integration helps organizations monitor external threats and manage investigations within their existing SOC workflows. Bidirectional synchronization also helps keep incident status, severity, and comments aligned between Microsoft Sentinel and SOCRadar.

SpyCloud Enterprise Protection for Microsoft Sentinel  

SpyCloud Enterprise Protection for Microsoft Sentinel brings stolen identity data from infostealer malware, phishing attacks, and third-party breaches into Microsoft Sentinel, helping security teams uncover compromised identities, prioritize high-risk exposures, and accelerate remediation to prevent session hijacking and other targeted identity-based attacks. The solution includes a custom API connector, a Logic Apps playbook for ingesting data into Log Analytics, analytic rules that generate Sentinel incidents from breach and malware data, and additional Logic Apps playbooks for incident automation and enrichment. 

 

Tenable App for Microsoft Sentinel

Tenable App for Microsoft Sentinel brings asset and vulnerability data from Tenable One Vulnerability Management into Sentinel for centralized security analysis. The integration combines Tenable cyber exposure insights with Sentinel’s collection, detection, and investigation capabilities, making vulnerability context available alongside other security telemetry. By incorporating asset and vulnerability findings into Sentinel workflows, the solution helps security teams correlate exposure data with security signals, investigate risks affecting vulnerable assets, and better prioritize remediation efforts.

Uniqkey Security Events for Microsoft Sentinel

Uniqkey Security Events for Microsoft Sentinel brings authentication, credential access and management, sharing, administrative activity, and platform threat detections into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). Included analytics rules identify scenarios such as sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses, excessive credential access, data exports, and security policy or privilege changes. A workbook visualizes activity and threat detections, helping security teams monitor password-management activity, investigate potential credential risks, and correlate findings with broader security telemetry. 

 

Utimaco Enterprise Secure Key Manager

Utimaco Enterprise Secure Key Manager (ESKM) integrates with Microsoft Sentinel to provide centralized security monitoring and visibility into cryptographic key management activities through KMIP server logs. The solution enables organizations to monitor key operations, KMIP client activity, and authentication events, helping security teams identify suspicious behavior and investigate potential threats. Built-in analytics rules help detect brute-force authentication attempts, repeated permission-denied events, and key-destruction activity, while hunting queries and a dedicated workbook support deeper investigation of unusual users, source IPs, key retrieval patterns, and after-hours activity. 

 

valimail-sentinel-enforce

Valimail enables organizations to see who sends email using your domain, protects against domain impersonation, and displays a verified logo in inboxes to increase brand trust. Our Microsoft Sentinel Connector brings Valimail Enforce event data directly into Sentinel, allowing security teams to incorporate our telemetry into unified SIEM workflows, monitor authentication and enforcement trends in real time, and build custom alerts and visualizations based on DMARC events. Once configured, Sentinel continuously ingests Valimail event logs, enriching your broader security intelligence and helping to improve your ability to detect and respond to threats across your environment. 

Varonis for Sentinel Solutions

Varonis for Sentinel Solutions brings enriched, data-centric Varonis alerts into Microsoft Sentinel for triage, investigation, and remediation. Varonis insights are contextualized alongside other security events to provide a unified view of data risk. This allows security teams to view and close Varonis alerts directly within Sentinel, reducing the need to switch interfaces and supporting incident resolution with less manual effort

Whisper for Sentinel

Whisper for Sentinel enriches Microsoft Sentinel incidents and alerts with threat and infrastructure intelligence for IPs, domains, ASNs, and networks. The solution provides threat scores, supporting evidence, infrastructure relationships, and historical context directly within Sentinel. Included enrichment playbooks, analytics rules, hunting queries, and workbooks support investigation of threats including C2 communications, malicious infrastructure, suspicious domains, and BGP anomalies, while retained enrichment data can be queried and correlated with existing logs.

WhoisFreaks Threat Intelligence for Microsoft Sentinel  

The WhoisFreaks solution for Microsoft Sentinel brings domain threat intelligence and newly registered domain (NRD) data into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). Customers can connect malware, phishing, and spam threat feeds, along with gTLD and ccTLD NRD feeds with or without WHOIS data. Included analytics rule templates help identify high-confidence malicious domains, newly registered domains appearing in threat feeds, threat-listed parked domains, and unusual NRD volumes that may indicate bulk registration activity. 

Wiz for Microsoft Sentinel  

Wiz for Microsoft Sentinel brings Wiz Issues, Vulnerability Findings, and Audit logs into Microsoft Sentinel. Wiz identifies and prioritizes cloud security risks across areas including vulnerabilities, malware, internet exposure, identity, and data security in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, OCI, Alibaba, and Kubernetes environments. 

 

In addition to the solutions from our third-party partners, we are also excited to announce the following connectors published by the Microsoft Sentinel team:

Building a more connected foundation for security operations 

The strength of the connector ecosystem reflects the work of Microsoft and our technology partners to support our shared customers. Together, we are helping organizations connect the technologies they rely on and bring more of their security data into a unified operational experience. 

For customers 

If you are a Microsoft Sentinel or ISOC customer, or considering adopting it, we want you to have the security connectors and integrations you need to get value from the platform. If an integration with an independent software vendor (ISV) is not yet available, or you have an issue with an existing solution, we have a dedicated team that may be able to assist by working with ISVs to build new or update existing connectors.

items.title: Frida 17.27.5 Released
items.summary: A bug-fix release, with @kkuehl behind most of it: a leak of thread handles in every Windows process we attach to, an attach that never returned, a crash on Android when opening a second local session, and a rare hang on teardown. Windows 11 26H1 on ARM64 works with our mapper, our mapped dbghelp can reach symbol servers thanks to @mochaaP , and @mrmacete fixed iOS devices that stayed unreachable after booting. Windows Since 17.25.0 our agent is mapped into the target rather than loaded by the system’s loader. Kirby found that every attach then left seven to eight thread handles open in the target, each to a thread that had already exited. GLib only cleaned up a thread on the thread-detach notification, which the loader never sends to an image it doesn’t know about. A thread GLib started now cleans up on its own way out. Threads GLib didn’t start had the same problem with their private data, which stayed allocated and fragmented the heap of a long-lived agent in a process that keeps creating threads. Those are now cleaned up through a fiber-local storage slot, which is how the POSIX backend has always done it with a pthread key. Kirby also fixed two issues around attaching: When the mapper couldn’t map the agent, attach() never returned. The error arrived in a domain that wasn’t propagated, so the task was dropped without being completed. A process that has exited can still be opened by PID for as long as anyone holds a handle to it. Attaching to one failed with “Unable to allocate target memory”. It is now reported the same way as a PID that no longer exists, with and without the mapper. On ARM64, mapping an image with static TLS aborted on Windows 11 26H1, as @januwA reported. The heuristics for finding the loader’s TLS routines expected fixed registers and a flags check, and the compiler had laid them out differently. They are now recognized by what they do, as on x86 since 17.26.0, with the same decoder used for native and emulated processes. This was validated against ntdll from Windows 10 19041 and Windows 11 22000, 22621, 26100, 26200 and 28000, in their native, ARM64EC and CHPE flavors. And @mochaaP noticed that our mapped dbghelp never got as far as loading symsrv.dll. Being unknown to the loader, it failed to look up its own path. We now answer with the main executable’s path, so the path it derives still hits our redirects. Thanks, all three! macOS Gadget and frida-inject can watch scripts and reload them when they change. In a watched directory on macOS, a write to an existing file went unnoticed, as GLib’s kqueue backend only diffs directory listings. Our FileMonitor , which both now use, watches directories through FSEvents there. iOS Francesco fixed devices staying unreachable until idund was restarted. When a device didn’t reveal its IPv6 address within two seconds, as while still booting after an erase or after enabling developer mode, the NCM driver was left running. Every retry opened another one, and with several of them consuming frames from the device, the datagram carrying the address almost always ended up in an abandoned one. Abandoned drivers are now closed. Thanks! Android Kirby found that closing the local session and opening another crashed. The local backend runs its helper in a Java VM that it creates inside the host process, and destroyed it when the session closed, but ART can’t create a second VM in the same process. frida-server never sees this, as it keeps one session for its whole life, but an embedder does. The helper is now started once per process and shared between sessions. Process enumeration also failed altogether when a process ran as a uid without a passwd entry. The user is now left out for such a process, and the uid is always provided, as on Linux. Teardown Kirby also tracked down a rare hang when closing a DeviceManager , seen on macOS. A reply queued just before the peer vanished could pass through the agent’s message filter after the connection had closed, wrapping its count of pending calls below zero. Unload then waited forever for calls that would never complete. Thanks for all of these, Kirby! CModule With the external toolchain, compile errors read “Linking failed: Compilation failed: …”, as that toolchain compiles while linking. Each backend now picks its own prefix. Enjoy! Changelog glib: Clean up threads without relying on thread-detach on Windows, fixing leaked thread handles and private data in mapped agents. Thanks @kkuehl ! glib: Don’t wait forever when a D-Bus client rejects the server’s authentication data. Thanks @DJm00n ! windows: Fix attach() hanging when mapping fails. Thanks @kkuehl ! windows: Report exited processes as not found, with and without the mapper. Thanks @kkuehl ! pe-mapper: Find the ARM64 loader TLS routines robustly, fixing Windows 11 26H1. Thanks @januwA ! dbghelp: Redirect GetModuleFileNameW() , so symsrv.dll gets loaded. Thanks @mochaaP ! file-monitor: Use FSEvents for macOS directories. gadget: Watch scripts with FileMonitor . inject: Watch the script with FileMonitor . agent: Fix a pending-call underflow on disconnect, which could hang teardown. Thanks @kkuehl ! idun: Close abandoned NCM drivers. Thanks @mrmacete ! android: Share the in-process helper between sessions. Thanks @kkuehl ! android: Omit the user when a uid has no passwd entry. Thanks @kkuehl ! cmodule: Don’t wrap compile errors as link errors.
items.summary_html:
A bug-fix release, with @kkuehl behind most of it: a leak of thread handles in every Windows process we attach to, an attach that never returned, a crash on Android when opening a second local session, and a rare hang on teardown. Windows 11 26H1 on ARM64 works with our mapper, our mapped dbghelp can reach symbol servers thanks to @mochaaP, and @mrmacete fixed iOS devices that stayed unreachable after booting.

Windows

Since 17.25.0 our agent is mapped into the target rather than loaded by the system’s loader. Kirby found that every attach then left seven to eight thread handles open in the target, each to a thread that had already exited. GLib only cleaned up a thread on the thread-detach notification, which the loader never sends to an image it doesn’t know about. A thread GLib started now cleans up on its own way out. Threads GLib didn’t start had the same problem with their private data, which stayed allocated and fragmented the heap of a long-lived agent in a process that keeps creating threads. Those are now cleaned up through a fiber-local storage slot, which is how the POSIX backend has always done it with a pthread key.

Kirby also fixed two issues around attaching:

  • When the mapper couldn’t map the agent, attach() never returned. The error arrived in a domain that wasn’t propagated, so the task was dropped without being completed.
  • A process that has exited can still be opened by PID for as long as anyone holds a handle to it. Attaching to one failed with “Unable to allocate target memory”. It is now reported the same way as a PID that no longer exists, with and without the mapper.

On ARM64, mapping an image with static TLS aborted on Windows 11 26H1, as @januwA reported. The heuristics for finding the loader’s TLS routines expected fixed registers and a flags check, and the compiler had laid them out differently. They are now recognized by what they do, as on x86 since 17.26.0, with the same decoder used for native and emulated processes. This was validated against ntdll from Windows 10 19041 and Windows 11 22000, 22621, 26100, 26200 and 28000, in their native, ARM64EC and CHPE flavors.

And @mochaaP noticed that our mapped dbghelp never got as far as loading symsrv.dll. Being unknown to the loader, it failed to look up its own path. We now answer with the main executable’s path, so the path it derives still hits our redirects. Thanks, all three!

macOS

Gadget and frida-inject can watch scripts and reload them when they change. In a watched directory on macOS, a write to an existing file went unnoticed, as GLib’s kqueue backend only diffs directory listings. Our FileMonitor, which both now use, watches directories through FSEvents there.

iOS

Francesco fixed devices staying unreachable until idund was restarted. When a device didn’t reveal its IPv6 address within two seconds, as while still booting after an erase or after enabling developer mode, the NCM driver was left running. Every retry opened another one, and with several of them consuming frames from the device, the datagram carrying the address almost always ended up in an abandoned one. Abandoned drivers are now closed. Thanks!

Android

Kirby found that closing the local session and opening another crashed. The local backend runs its helper in a Java VM that it creates inside the host process, and destroyed it when the session closed, but ART can’t create a second VM in the same process. frida-server never sees this, as it keeps one session for its whole life, but an embedder does. The helper is now started once per process and shared between sessions.

Process enumeration also failed altogether when a process ran as a uid without a passwd entry. The user is now left out for such a process, and the uid is always provided, as on Linux.

Teardown

Kirby also tracked down a rare hang when closing a DeviceManager, seen on macOS. A reply queued just before the peer vanished could pass through the agent’s message filter after the connection had closed, wrapping its count of pending calls below zero. Unload then waited forever for calls that would never complete. Thanks for all of these, Kirby!

CModule

With the external toolchain, compile errors read “Linking failed: Compilation failed: …”, as that toolchain compiles while linking. Each backend now picks its own prefix.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • glib: Clean up threads without relying on thread-detach on Windows, fixing leaked thread handles and private data in mapped agents. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • glib: Don’t wait forever when a D-Bus client rejects the server’s authentication data. Thanks @DJm00n!
  • windows: Fix attach() hanging when mapping fails. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • windows: Report exited processes as not found, with and without the mapper. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • pe-mapper: Find the ARM64 loader TLS routines robustly, fixing Windows 11 26H1. Thanks @januwA!
  • dbghelp: Redirect GetModuleFileNameW(), so symsrv.dll gets loaded. Thanks @mochaaP!
  • file-monitor: Use FSEvents for macOS directories.
  • gadget: Watch scripts with FileMonitor.
  • inject: Watch the script with FileMonitor.
  • agent: Fix a pending-call underflow on disconnect, which could hang teardown. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • idun: Close abandoned NCM drivers. Thanks @mrmacete!
  • android: Share the in-process helper between sessions. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • android: Omit the user when a uid has no passwd entry. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • cmodule: Don’t wrap compile errors as link errors.

items.title: Duo thoughts
items.summary: I consider myself a technology enthusiast, and have for a long time also called myself an “Apple Fanboy”. In recent years that fandom has waned a bit, but I’m still quite entrenched in the larger Apple ecosystem. So it is of litte surprise to those that know me that I got myself an iPhone Duo . Despite preordering it the second it became available, I only recently had mine delivered and have had the device for about 5 days now. Enough time to have gotten it completely set up and to have taken it through a number of normal days of use. Here’s a quick list of thoughts, covering some negatives and positives from my time with the phone thus far. Negatives In no particular order, here’s some things I haven’t liked about the iPhone Duo thus far (non-exhuastive). The way keyboards manifest on this device is a bit all over the place. Sometimes you have keys cut off. When the phone is folded out it’s a big ungainly. It slows me down a bit , but it’s a pretty minor inconvenience overall so far. My previous phone, the iPhone Pro Max was a lot taller than this one, and had a thinner overall profile (compared to the Duo when closed). This made sticking it into my back pocket, and then retrieving it from that same pocket a lot easier. Generally, this phone is a bit harder to put into and get out of any pocket due to it being a bit thicker and more stout. That said, it still does fit into all the pockets I’ve tried thus far. Unlocking the device is not as good. Before I got the phone, I watched a ton of reviews and most folks thought the lack of FaceID was going to be a huge problem. I brushed off that complaint because I knew this device would support “unlock with Apple Watch”, and I always wear an Apple Watch. In theory, that should have solved the no-FaceID situation and would have actually been arguably better and more seamless. The problem is, it doesn’t work all the time. In the 5 days I’ve had this device, I think it works like 70% of the time maybe. Not great . Reaching over and tapping one of the many fingers I’ve enrolled in TouchID is very easy. But it’s just annoying to try to swipe up, the Apple Watch doesn’t do it’s thing, and then I’m confused for a sec before I realize I need to touch my finger on the biometric sensor. I have the original Apple Watch Ultra, so one theory is that the watch unlock just doesn’t work well with an older watch? But I’m just not sure. It’s something I think I can live with long term, but a year+ is a lot longer than 5 days. Time will tell… This one took me until today I think to get used to, but the placement of the volume control buttons is a little hard to use. items.summary_html:
I consider myself a technology enthusiast, and have for a long time also called myself an “Apple Fanboy”. In recent years that fandom has waned a bit, but I’m still quite entrenched in the larger Apple ecosystem. So it is of litte surprise to those that know me that I got myself an iPhone Duo. Despite preordering it the second it became available, I only recently had mine delivered and have had the device for about 5 days now. Enough time to have gotten it completely set up and to have taken it through a number of normal days of use. Here’s a quick list of thoughts, covering some negatives and positives from my time with the phone thus far.

Negatives

In no particular order, here’s some things I haven’t liked about the iPhone Duo thus far (non-exhuastive).

  • The way keyboards manifest on this device is a bit all over the place. Sometimes you have keys cut off. When the phone is folded out it’s a big ungainly. It slows me down a bit, but it’s a pretty minor inconvenience overall so far.

  • My previous phone, the iPhone Pro Max was a lot taller than this one, and had a thinner overall profile (compared to the Duo when closed). This made sticking it into my back pocket, and then retrieving it from that same pocket a lot easier. Generally, this phone is a bit harder to put into and get out of any pocket due to it being a bit thicker and more stout. That said, it still does fit into all the pockets I’ve tried thus far.

  • Unlocking the device is not as good. Before I got the phone, I watched a ton of reviews and most folks thought the lack of FaceID was going to be a huge problem. I brushed off that complaint because I knew this device would support “unlock with Apple Watch”, and I always wear an Apple Watch. In theory, that should have solved the no-FaceID situation and would have actually been arguably better and more seamless. The problem is, it doesn’t work all the time. In the 5 days I’ve had this device, I think it works like 70% of the time maybe. Not great. Reaching over and tapping one of the many fingers I’ve enrolled in TouchID is very easy. But it’s just annoying to try to swipe up, the Apple Watch doesn’t do it’s thing, and then I’m confused for a sec before I realize I need to touch my finger on the biometric sensor. I have the original Apple Watch Ultra, so one theory is that the watch unlock just doesn’t work well with an older watch? But I’m just not sure. It’s something I think I can live with long term, but a year+ is a lot longer than 5 days. Time will tell…

  • This one took me until today I think to get used to, but the placement of the volume control buttons is a little hard to use. I think they did the best they could in terms of where they actually placed the buttons, but that doesn’t mean it isn’t a little awkward to use them in practice. As of today though, I think I’ve got the hang of it. So not a big deal.

  • The duo has VERY small bezels. And opening and closing the phone often means fingers sliding a bit off the bezel onto the screen itself. This has resulted in a ton of cases where I am triggering the app wiggle thing without meaning to. I haven’t actually deleted any of my apps or moved them accidentally yet, but triggering that wiggle is kinda annoying.

  • One thing I’ve clicked by accident a ton of times is the power button. When I’m opening/closing the device, or getting a grip on the phone to reach up and engage the volume buttons, I find myself sending the phone into its locked state by accident more than I care for. This might be another thing that I just get used to with more hands-on time.

  • Everyone has complained about this one, and I will too. The apps. More developers need to get their apps updated for the Duo screen! A petty complaint, but I can’t wait to see what the experience will be like when apps have been optimized or re-engineered with the Duo’s screen in mind.

  • It’s heavy. In closed mode there’s only so long I can hold it resting on my finger and scrolling. This was true of the max as well, but something I’ve definitely clocked in longer scrolling sessions.

  • Due to the shorter profile of the Duo, Apple’s design language now pushes menu bar elements to the right side of the device (rather than the top). This has been one of the hardest things to get used to so far — just remembering that that’s where things are. In some cases, this has also resulted in me just not being able to find certain elements I am looking for. One example was me trying to figure out how to trigger the share sheet in Safari. I just couldn’t find how to do it. Eventually, I realized it was buried in another UI element’s menu. Which is ok, I guess. Just one of those things I have to reteach myself.

  • Battery life is notably worse than the Max so far. But still gets me through a day no problem.

Positives

Here’s some notably good things I’ve experienced while using the Duo thus far.

  • The smaller form factor (while closed) makes it really easy for me to reach just about the entire screen, despite the added chunk. This was impossible to do with the Max, and in some situations was quite precarious when I attempted to perform hand gymnastics to reach things one hand on the larger phone.

  • It’s really satisfying to open and close the device. The animation is perfection and the hinge-feel is perfectly confident. Sure, maybe that will get old or w/e in a few weeks, but thus far it’s just super fun.

  • Having the ability to use two apps side-by-side in the open state is super useful for a bunch of workflows I have. Here’s some examples…

    • I watch a fair bit of TV when I’m doing other things around the house. Now, I can easily watch TV on one side of the phone and do w/e else I want on the other. Sure it’s a landscape orientation on a vertical half-screen layout, but it’s good enough for when I’m just a few inches from the device.

    • I often need to have my budget/expense app open at the same time as a browser window when I am categorizing transactions. Easy!

    • I can have my workout tracking app open at the same time as my notes app.

    • I can have my calorie/food tracking app open on one side with Hello Fresh app or recipe open on the other side.

    • I can take notes and have research/blog post open in Safari.

    • These are just a handful of things I do day-to-day. I encounter more situations like this every day it seems!

  • Not really a “pro”, but I am noticing that I use the device way more in the closed state than the open state. Y’know most of the time I’m just scrolling Mastodon or something so really don’t need the big ‘ol screen for that.

Overall, I really like the device. I think a lot of my gripes will be overcome either through practice or with Apple/Developer updates. There’s very few things if any that I think are pure downsides of the devices form-factor. But! It’s only been 5 days, so this may all just be a honeymoon phase. I’ll need to check back in with this review in a few months probably.

items.title: Who signs the AI permission slip?
items.summary: By Brandon Epstein Originally published in the November 2026 issue of Magnet Unlocked. Want to be the first to see new content? Sign up for our monthly newsletter, Magnet Unlocked. AI is a revolutionary tool in digital forensics. Let’s prove it. Last week I asked ChatGPT to turn a photo of my daughter’s handwritten middle school basketball schedule into calendar entries. Great use of a tool. Also, a use where a wrong answer costs me twenty minutes in a gym parking lot. Now raise the stakes. In our world, a misread timestamp isn’t twenty minutes. It can be the difference between an alibi and a charge, and sometimes decades of somebody’s life. That gap between “looks right” and “is demonstrably right” is the entire conversation about AI in digital forensics, and it’s the one I’ve been thinking about after reading Magnet Forensics’ new public sector report, Clearing the path to justice . The appetite is real. The trust isn’t. 300+ public sector professionals who work with digital evidence shared their opinions to form our new report, roughly half of them examiners. On the topic of AI , appetite is not the problem: 41% already use it in their investigations, mostly for analyzing text and images, summarizing long documents, translating, transcribing, and finding matching images across devices. Among those users, 73% expect AI-assisted capabilities to be very helpful or essential to future investigations. Only 27% say the current state of AI meets their needs. So, what’s holding people back? The top concerns tell the story: accuracy and false positives, privacy and compliance, lack of validation or testing, difficulty defending results in court, and a lack of standards or accepted methods. Read that list like an examiner. Three of the five aren’t about what the tool can do. They’re about whether you can prove what it did. Trust cuts both ways The same report shows why this can’t wait. 56% of respondents have encountered manipulated , synthetic, or AI-generated media, most often in ICAC cases . More than a third have had someone claim a piece of evidence isn’t real. Only 17% are confident their agency can identify synthetic media, and only about a quarter are confident they could prove a genuine file hasn’t been altered. Meanwhile, a vast majority shared that authenticity challenges are becoming more important in court . A convincing fake sends you in the wrong direction. A real video gets dismissed when nobody can show otherwise. Either way, the examiner who can’t show their work loses. AI is part of the problem and part of the answer, but only if we can trust it. Anyone can build a demo Here’s the uncomfortable part. Anybody with $20 of Claude tokens and a free weekend can now build something that looks impressive on a conference-room screen. Capability is no longer the differentiator. Evidence that the capability holds up is. And, if I’m honest, our profession’s existing answer to “how do we prove it” hasn’t been great. A few years ago, I had a small part in a study on what builds a quality culture in digital forensics. We interviewed practitioners, lab managers, attorneys , everyone with a stake. Ask what contributes most to quality in a lab and nearly everyone says tool testing and validation. Then we asked a follow-up; can you give me one example where tool validation found a shortcoming or changed your workflow? Zero. Not “rarely.” Zero. Either the testing wasn’t designed to catch errors, or there wasn’t time to do it, or it simply confirmed what the examiner already believed. Everybody agrees validation matters. Almost nobody’s validation is doing the work we say it does. Why it takes a village There are something like 15,000 organizations in the US that meet the definition of a digital forensics lab. I don’t expect each of them to build a ground-truth dataset and stress-test an AI platform. They don’t have the time, and frankly, I wouldn’t ask. When I started out, whatever validation I could have done alone would have scratched the surface. That’s one of the core ideas behind the new Magnet AI Research Lab . Its purpose is to conduct empirical research into how AI performs in digital forensics. Working with practitioners and academic partners, the Lab examines real-world questions, measures outcomes, and publishes findings through peer-reviewed research. I think of it as an AI permission slip. Everyone I talk to is looking for someone to say, with receipts, “yes, you can use this.” Where it matters: The witness stand Picture the cross-examination. Why did you use this tool, and how do you know it works? Under Daubert in the US or Mohan in Canada, the questions are predictable: Has the method been tested? Has it been peer reviewed? Is there a known error rate? Are there standards? A published study answers several of those on the spot. I’d argue we can finally give an honest answer on error rates, for the first time across much of digital forensics tooling. That’s actually easier with AI than with humans . I can’t get 2,000 examiners to complete a survey on a Tuesday. I can run a model tens of thousands of times across a pile of datasets. It also exposes the double standard we’ve written about before; no one asks an expert witness how often they slip up in a typical week . Come build it with us A permission slip isn’t a green light to stop thinking. It’s a receipt; here’s what was tested, here’s how it performed, here’s where it falls short, and here’s the journal that checked the work. That’s what lets you say yes to AI and still defend every conclusion you sign your name to. We’re also working with universities, because so much useful research never reaches the people doing casework. It sits in a journal somewhere, or in a master’s thesis on a university server. I’d love to close that loop. Students get real-world projects, and examiners get research they can actually use. If you have a research question you’d like answered, or a study you’d like to partner on, reach out to the AI Research Lab . And if you want the full numbers behind everything above, the report is there for you to read . If you’ve been waiting for your permission slip, consider this the nudge. We’ll show our work. You tell us if it falls short.
items.summary_html:
By Brandon Epstein

Originally published in the November 2026 issue of Magnet Unlocked. Want to be the first to see new content? Sign up for our monthly newsletter, Magnet Unlocked.

AI is a revolutionary tool in digital forensics. Let’s prove it.

Last week I asked ChatGPT to turn a photo of my daughter’s handwritten middle school basketball schedule into calendar entries. Great use of a tool. Also, a use where a wrong answer costs me twenty minutes in a gym parking lot.

Now raise the stakes. In our world, a misread timestamp isn’t twenty minutes. It can be the difference between an alibi and a charge, and sometimes decades of somebody’s life. That gap between “looks right” and “is demonstrably right” is the entire conversation about AI in digital forensics, and it’s the one I’ve been thinking about after reading Magnet Forensics’ new public sector report, Clearing the path to justice.

The appetite is real. The trust isn’t.

300+ public sector professionals who work with digital evidence shared their opinions to form our new report, roughly half of them examiners. On the topic of AI, appetite is not the problem:

  • 41% already use it in their investigations, mostly for analyzing text and images, summarizing long documents, translating, transcribing, and finding matching images across devices.
  • Among those users, 73% expect AI-assisted capabilities to be very helpful or essential to future investigations.
  • Only 27% say the current state of AI meets their needs.

So, what’s holding people back?

The top concerns tell the story: accuracy and false positives, privacy and compliance, lack of validation or testing, difficulty defending results in court, and a lack of standards or accepted methods.

Read that list like an examiner. Three of the five aren’t about what the tool can do. They’re about whether you can prove what it did.

Trust cuts both ways

The same report shows why this can’t wait. 56% of respondents have encountered manipulated, synthetic, or AI-generated media, most often in ICAC cases. More than a third have had someone claim a piece of evidence isn’t real. Only 17% are confident their agency can identify synthetic media, and only about a quarter are confident they could prove a genuine file hasn’t been altered. Meanwhile, a vast majority shared that authenticity challenges are becoming more important in court.

A convincing fake sends you in the wrong direction. A real video gets dismissed when nobody can show otherwise. Either way, the examiner who can’t show their work loses. AI is part of the problem and part of the answer, but only if we can trust it.

Anyone can build a demo

Here’s the uncomfortable part. Anybody with $20 of Claude tokens and a free weekend can now build something that looks impressive on a conference-room screen. Capability is no longer the differentiator. Evidence that the capability holds up is.

And, if I’m honest, our profession’s existing answer to “how do we prove it” hasn’t been great. A few years ago, I had a small part in a study on what builds a quality culture in digital forensics. We interviewed practitioners, lab managers, attorneys, everyone with a stake. Ask what contributes most to quality in a lab and nearly everyone says tool testing and validation.

Then we asked a follow-up; can you give me one example where tool validation found a shortcoming or changed your workflow?

Zero.

Not “rarely.” Zero. Either the testing wasn’t designed to catch errors, or there wasn’t time to do it, or it simply confirmed what the examiner already believed. Everybody agrees validation matters. Almost nobody’s validation is doing the work we say it does.

Why it takes a village

There are something like 15,000 organizations in the US that meet the definition of a digital forensics lab. I don’t expect each of them to build a ground-truth dataset and stress-test an AI platform. They don’t have the time, and frankly, I wouldn’t ask. When I started out, whatever validation I could have done alone would have scratched the surface.

That’s one of the core ideas behind the new Magnet AI Research Lab. Its purpose is to conduct empirical research into how AI performs in digital forensics. Working with practitioners and academic partners, the Lab examines real-world questions, measures outcomes, and publishes findings through peer-reviewed research.

I think of it as an AI permission slip. Everyone I talk to is looking for someone to say, with receipts, “yes, you can use this.”

Where it matters: The witness stand

Picture the cross-examination. Why did you use this tool, and how do you know it works? Under Daubert in the US or Mohan in Canada, the questions are predictable: Has the method been tested? Has it been peer reviewed? Is there a known error rate? Are there standards?

A published study answers several of those on the spot. I’d argue we can finally give an honest answer on error rates, for the first time across much of digital forensics tooling. That’s actually easier with AI than with humans. I can’t get 2,000 examiners to complete a survey on a Tuesday. I can run a model tens of thousands of times across a pile of datasets.

It also exposes the double standard we’ve written about before; no one asks an expert witness how often they slip up in a typical week.

Come build it with us

A permission slip isn’t a green light to stop thinking. It’s a receipt; here’s what was tested, here’s how it performed, here’s where it falls short, and here’s the journal that checked the work. That’s what lets you say yes to AI and still defend every conclusion you sign your name to.

We’re also working with universities, because so much useful research never reaches the people doing casework. It sits in a journal somewhere, or in a master’s thesis on a university server. I’d love to close that loop. Students get real-world projects, and examiners get research they can actually use.

If you have a research question you’d like answered, or a study you’d like to partner on, reach out to the AI Research Lab. And if you want the full numbers behind everything above, the report is there for you to read.

If you’ve been waiting for your permission slip, consider this the nudge. We’ll show our work. You tell us if it falls short.
