    | project-keep AlertName, raw
    | evaluate bag_unpack(raw, columnsConflict="replace_source")
    | extend SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue = column_ifexists(SuppressionField, "SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue")
    | extend SecurityAlertSuppressionSuppressionFieldValueDynamic = parse_json(SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue)
    | extend SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldColumn = iff(
        gettype(SecurityAlertSuppressionSuppressionFieldValueDynamic) == "array",
        tostring(array_sort_asc(SecurityAlertSuppressionSuppressionFieldValueDynamic)),
        tostring(SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue)
    );
  T
  | extend TableSuppressionFieldValue = column_ifexists(SuppressionField, "SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue")
  | extend TableSuppressionFieldValueDynamic = parse_json(TableSuppressionFieldValue)
  | extend TableSuppressionFieldColumn = iff(
      gettype(TableSuppressionFieldValueDynamic) == "array",
      tostring(array_sort_asc(TableSuppressionFieldValueDynamic)),
      tostring(TableSuppressionFieldValue)
  )
  | join kind=leftanti ExistingAlerts on $left.TableSuppressionFieldColumn == $right.SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldColumn
  | project-away TableSuppressionFieldValue, TableSuppressionFieldValueDynamic, TableSuppressionFieldColumn
};
SuppressAlerts(T=T, SuppressionAlertName=SuppressionAlertName, SuppressionWindow=SuppressionWindow, SuppressionField=SuppressionField)

We’ll break down the query and provide some explanation on it.

The function takes four input parameters that determine how suppression will be applied. T represents the results table of the calling analytics rule query, SuppressionAlertName identifies the alert name used to retrieve previously generated alerts, SuppressionWindow defines the lookback period during which existing alerts are considered, and SuppressionField specifies the entity field used to determine whether a new result should be suppressed.

let SuppressAlerts = (
  T: (*),
  SuppressionAlertName: string,
  SuppressionWindow: timespan,
  SuppressionField: string
  )

The function first queries the SecurityAlert table to retrieve existing alerts matching the specified alert name, with a status of New, generated within the configured suppression window.

let ExistingAlerts = SecurityAlert
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(SuppressionWindow)
    | where Status == "New"
    | where AlertName == SuppressionAlertName

For each matching alert, the function extracts the Query property from the ExtendedProperties field. It then uses a regular expression to retrieve the Base64-encoded payload and decompresses it using zlib_decompress_from_base64_string(). This reconstructs the original log entries that triggered the alert, making their associated entities accessible for further processing.

| extend Query = parse_json(ExtendedProperties).Query
| extend b64 = extract(@".*?\[\'([A-Za-z0-9+/=]+)\'\].*", 1, tostring(Query))
| extend raw = todynamic(zlib_decompress_from_base64_string(b64))

The decompressed payload is a dynamic object containing the original query results. Using bag_unpack(), the function expands this object into individual columns, allowing us to access the original fields. It then dynamically extracts the field specified through the SuppressionField parameter using column_ifexists() which acts as a fail safe to prevent the analytics rule query from failing if for any reason the decoding fails.

| project-keep AlertName, raw
| evaluate bag_unpack(raw, columnsConflict="replace_source")
| extend SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue = column_ifexists(SuppressionField, "SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue")

Since the suppression field may contain either a single value or an array of values, we need to normalize its representation before performing the comparison. The function first attempts to parse the value as JSON and checks whether it represents an array. If it does, the elements are sorted and converted into a string. Otherwise, the original value is converted directly into a string. This ensures that arrays containing identical elements are treated as equivalent, regardless of the order in which those elements appear. Therefore, an existing alert containing an array of two IP addresses will not suppress a subsequent alert containing an array of three IP addresses, even if the latter includes both previously observed IP addresses.

| extend SecurityAlertSuppressionSuppressionFieldValueDynamic = parse_json(SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue)
| extend SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldColumn = iff(
    gettype(SecurityAlertSuppressionSuppressionFieldValueDynamic) == "array",
    tostring(array_sort_asc(SecurityAlertSuppressionSuppressionFieldValueDynamic)),
    tostring(SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldValue)
);

The function then uses a leftanti join to compare the normalized suppression field values from the current query results against those extracted from previously generated alerts. The leftanti join returns only records from the current results that do not have a matching entity in the reference dataset. Consequently, records associated with entities that have already triggered an alert within the configured suppression window are excluded, while records associated with different entities remain eligible to generate new alerts.

| join kind=leftanti ExistingAlerts
    on $left.TableSuppressionFieldColumn ==
       $right.SecurityAlertSuppressionFieldColumn

Finally, the last line of the query invokes the function logic.

SuppressAlerts(T=T, SuppressionAlertName=SuppressionAlertName, SuppressionWindow=SuppressionWindow, SuppressionField=SuppressionField)

To save the function, copy the query above in the KQL editor and click on Save as function.

Save as function option.

In the side panel that opens, make sure to populate the function parameters with the correct values and data types.

Function parameter options.Using the Function in Log Analytic Rule Queries

Once saved, the function can be reused across multiple analytics rules without having to duplicate the suppression logic. To test this, we’ll use a sample dataset that simulates security events and apply our newly created function to its results.

let SecurityEvents = datatable(
    SourceIP:string,
    Threat:string,
    Signature: string,
)
[
    "192.168.10.25", "Malware", "Trojan.Generic",
    "192.168.10.25", "Malware", "Trojan.Generic",
    "192.168.10.25", "CredentialTheft", "Mimikatz.Detect"
];
let frequency = 1h;
let suppression_window = 1h;
SecurityEvents
| extend TimeGenerated = now() + (rand(300) * 1s)
| where TimeGenerated > ago(frequency)
| summarize
    minTimeGenerated = min(TimeGenerated),
    maxTimeGenerated = max(TimeGenerated),
    Threat = make_set(Threat),
    Signature = make_set(Signature)
by SourceIP
| invoke SuppressAlertsRawOneField(SuppressionAlertName="Suppression Test Rule", SuppressionWindow=suppression_window, SuppressionField="SourceIP")

To use the function correctly within our analytics rules, we need to pay particular attention to the rule’s execution frequency and lookback times.

Since our suppression function queries the SecurityAlert table to identify previously generated alerts, the rule's lookback period must be aligned with the suppression window configured in the function. For example, if we want to suppress alerts for one hour, the lookback period specified in the analytics rule settings should also be set to one hour.

Analytic rule configuration to work with the Suppression Function

Now that we are retrieving data for the entire one-hour lookback period, we also need to account for the analytics rule’s execution frequency within the query itself. We must filter the results to include only events that occurred within the rule’s execution interval. For example, if the rule is configured to run every 15 minutes, we need to add a time filter to the query that returns only events from the last 15 minutes. This ensures that we can use the extended one-hour lookback period to identify previously generated alerts for suppression without repeatedly processing the same events across consecutive rule executions.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(frequency)

With these settings, we can use the suppression function as intended, with the extended lookback period needed to identify previously generated alerts while ensuring that only newly occurring events are processed during each rule execution.

Indeed, after allowing our test analytic rule to run for a few hours, we can confirm that Sentinel alerts are being suppressed for one hour, while Sentinel incidents are generated every 1 hour and 15 minutes, as intended based on our suppression function settings and rule scheduling.

Sentinel incidents of our test suppression ruleLimitations and Considerations

Some limitations and considerations worth taking into account as these may affect the reliability of the suppression function and should be taken into consideration if you decide to adopt this method:

  • The function relies on the ExtendedProperties.Query field, which is subject to a 10 KB size limitation (source). If the compressed query payload exceeds this limit, a warning is typically displayed, preventing the function from extracting the entities required for suppression. Analytics rules producing particularly verbose or large result sets may therefore be unsuitable for this approach.
  • An alternative implementation would be to leverage the Alert Entities or Custom Details available in Sentinel rather than relying on the original query output. This would allow us to perform suppression field matching using the entity information or explicitly defined custom details associated with each alert, potentially avoiding the dependency on the compressed query payload. It should be noted though that this method also comes with its own limitations (source).
  • Another important consideration is the delay between the execution of the analytics rule query and the actual generation and ingestion of the corresponding alert into the SecurityAlert table. If the rule execution frequency is too short or the suppression window is too small, a subsequent execution may occur before the previously generated alert becomes available in SecurityAlert. As a result, the suppression function may fail to identify an existing alert, allowing duplicate alerts to be generated. Based on my tests a frequency of 15m and a suppression windows of 1h should be the minimum reliable values for this method to work effectively but these values may vary per environment.
  • Finally, an additional point worth noting is that the function can be extended to use multiple entity fields for suppression, rather than relying on a single field. This would allow suppression to be based on a combination of entities, such as a source IP address and signature, providing greater flexibility over which alerts are suppressed.
Closing Thoughts

As detection engineers, we need to be creative in finding ways to work around the limitations of the tools we use. The approach in this blog post demonstrates how we can leverage the capabilities provided by SIEM query language and correlation engine to implement an entity-based suppression method without compromising the execution of our analytics rules.

Of course, as most solutions this one also comes with its own limitations and trade-offs, and it is important to understand them before adopting it in production. Nevertheless, it provides a practical alternative and a good example of how a little creativity can help bridge gaps in native SIEM capabilities.

If you faced the same issue in Microsoft Sentinel I would be more than intrested to discussing the solution you came up with.

Implementing an Alert Suppression Function in Microsoft Sentinel was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.summary: Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, microservices, and AI agents in minutes. Many of you rely on it for some of the most critical data you operate: the identities and attributes your applications use to authenticate and authorize every request. Recently, we launched point-in-time recovery (PITR) for Amazon Cognito user pools, which lets you restore a user pool to an earlier point in time if an accidental deletion, a faulty migration, or an erroneous bulk operation changes data you need. It’s turned on automatically for user pools on the eligible feature plans. Before this launch, protecting user pool data meant building your own solution, such as exporting user attributes and group data on a schedule. That approach was time-consuming to build and operate, versioning the exports to find a clean point in time was another challenge, and reconstructing a pool from them was complicated. Users also got new sub identifiers as part of the restore process, which might break any downstream reference to the originals. Passwords, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys might not be recovered, so every affected user had to reset. In this post, we show you how to recover a user pool after an erroneous bulk operation, using the preview to review changes before you approve them. How PITR works On eligible user pools (see Prerequisites), Amazon Cognito now tracks changes so you can recover the pool to any point within the recovery window. The length of that window depends on your user pool feature plan. The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed. One behavior to understand is what happens to passwords during a recovery. A recovery restores passwords for users it recreates. A user who still exists and changed their password after the target time keeps the same password. The recovery doesn’t revert password changes, so users who legitimately changed their credentials don’t lose them. A recovery is preview-based and has three steps: Initiate a recovery to a target point in time ( InitiatePointInTimeRecovery ). Amazon Cognito pauses write operations to the user pool and generates a preview for your review before any changes are applied. Read operations and sign-in continue to work normally. The call returns a RestoreId . Review the recovery preview ( DescribePointInTimeRecovery ). Amazon Cognito reports how many users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys the recovery would create, update, or delete to return the pool to its state at the target time. Approve or cancel . If the preview looks right, you approve the recovery with StartPointInTimeRecovery , and Amazon Cognito restores the pool to its state at the target time. If it doesn’t look right, you cancel it with CancelPointInTimeRecovery ; no changes are applied, and write operations resume. Prerequisites To follow along with this post, you need: An AWS account with an Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus feature plan. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. The examples use a pool named anycompany-prod-user-pool in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region ( us-east-1 ). The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with permissions for the Amazon Cognito user pools PITR operations. Before you run a recovery, keep these limits in mind: You can run one recovery at a time per user pool, and one successful recovery per 24 hours per pool. The target time must be at least 15 minutes in the past and no earlier than the pool’s creation time. Recovery is initiated from the pool’s primary Region and can’t start while a multi-Region replication (MRR) operation, such as replica creation or deletion, is in progress on the pool. Recovering a user pool after an unintentional change AnyCompany runs its user sign-in on an Amazon Cognito user pool, anycompany-prod-user-pool . At 15:45 PDT, an operator runs a bulk change that’s supposed to set an attribute on a subset of users. A defect in the script instead deletes and modifies users. By 15:54 PDT, support receives cases of failed sign-ins and the operator halts the script. The team needs the pool as it was at 15:39 PDT. They decide to use PITR and preview the recovery before approving it. Step 1: Start the recovery The team initiates a recovery with a target time of 15:39 PDT by running the command in the preceding example. Figure 1 shows the same step in the console, where the team enters the target time and starts the recovery. The response includes a RestoreId that identifies this recovery throughout the workflow, along with a RestoreStatus and the RestoreTimestamp that you targeted. aws cognito-idp initiate-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-timestamp 2026-10-28T22:39:00Z Figure 1: Initiating a recovery to a target point in time Step 2: Review the recovery preview DescribePointInTimeRecovery returns the Restoration for this RestoreId , including a RestorePreview that summarizes how many entities will be affected if the pool is returned to the target time. The team reviews the preview and confirms the number of affected users matches the scope. aws cognito-idp describe-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a69b8c1e-9866-441d-EXAMPLE11111 In this case, the preview reports 16 users to create and 5 users to update, as the following sample response shows. Figure 2 shows the same preview in the console, with the create, update, and delete counts for users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys. These numbers match the scope of the bulk operation, so the team continues. If the preview had shown unexpected changes, the team could cancel the recovery with no changes applied. { "Restoration": { "RestoreId": "a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111", "RestorePreview": [ { "Entity": "Users", "CreateCount": 16, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 5 }, { "Entity": "Groups", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "User MFAs", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "Passkeys", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 } ], "RestoreStatus": "PREVIEW_GENERATED", "RestoreTimestamp": 1793227140, "TriggerTimestamp": 1793228700 } } Figure 2: Reviewing the recovery preview before applying Step 3: Approve the recovery If the preview is correct, the team approves the recovery with the command in the following example, and Amazon Cognito restores anycompany-prod-user-pool to its 15:39 PDT state. Figure 3 shows the approval step in the console, and Figure 4 shows the confirmation that appears after the recovery starts. Writes to the user pool resume automatically after the recovery completes or is canceled. aws cognito-idp start-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111 Figure 3: Approving the recovery Figure 4: Recovery confirmation aws cognito-idp cancel-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111 Your application integration doesn’t change Because PITR rolls back the data in your existing user pool rather than creating a new one, your application integration doesn’t need any changes. A recovery restores user data and leaves your user pool configuration in place, so configuration changes you made after the recovery point are preserved. For example, a custom attribute you added to the schema, an AWS Lambda trigger you updated, or a password policy you tightened stays as it is. The user pool ID also stays the same, and so do your app client IDs and secrets, managed login and domain, identity provider and SAML/OIDC configurations, and the provider Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) that services such as Amazon API Gateway and Application Load Balancer use to validate tokens. Recreated users keep the same sub identifiers, so downstream references to them keep working. How PITR complements multi-Region replication Multi-Region replication and PITR address different failure modes. Multi-Region replication keeps a synchronized replica of your user pool in another Region, so if the primary Region is impaired, you can fail over traffic to a replica Region with minimal downtime. PITR helps with data problems, such as erroneous bulk operations that corrupt your user pool’s state. You roll back to any point within your recovery window without changing your application integration. Security considerations A recovery changes the identity data that every sign-in and authorization decision depends on, so treat recovery permissions like any other high-impact administrative access. Separate who initiates a recovery from who approves it. Because initiating and approving are separate API actions, you can assign them to different AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Give an operator the permission InitiatePointInTimeRecovery , and give an approver the permission StartPointInTimeRecovery . Both permissions need DescribePointInTimeRecovery and ListPointInTimeRecoveries to review the preview, and CancelPointInTimeRecovery to stop a recovery. IAM keeps the two permissions on separate roles, but it doesn’t stop one person from assuming both. Assign the roles to different people or teams, and grant the approver role only for the duration of an approved change. Treat initiating a recovery as sensitive. Initiating a recovery pauses write operations on the user pool until the recovery is approved or canceled. If no action is taken within 24 hours, the preview automatically cancels and write operations are resumed. While writes are paused, users can’t sign up, reset their passwords, or update their profiles. A user pool also allows only one successful recovery per 24 hours, so an unauthorized recovery uses up a recovery you might need for a real incident. Review restored users after a recovery. A recovery recreates users who were deleted after the target time, including users you removed on purpose, such as employees who have left or compromised accounts. After a recovery completes, check the recreated users against your incident timeline. Disable any that should stay removed and revoke their sessions with AdminUserGlobalSignOut . Monitor recovery activity. Amazon Cognito records PITR API calls in AWS CloudTrail . Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that notifies your security team whenever InitiatePointInTimeRecovery or StartPointInTimeRecovery is called, so that no recovery goes unnoticed. Pricing PITR is included at no additional charge in eligible feature plans with a recovery window of up to 1 day on the Essentials feature plan and up to 14 days on the Plus feature plan. Conclusion In this post, we showed you how to recover an Amazon Cognito user pool after an erroneous bulk operation with PITR, from reviewing the changes in a preview to approving the recovery. PITR provides protection for your users’ identities, with no custom export-and-restore pipeline to build or operate. Because the recovery happens in place on the same user pool, your application integration keeps working unchanged. PITR is already enabled for eligible user pools. Before you need it, separate the initiate and approve permissions, add an alert on recovery calls, and practice the preview workflow on a test pool. To get started: Related post: Improve your application resilience with Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication Related post: Amazon Cognito unlocks advanced capabilities with next-generation infrastructure See PITR in the Amazon Cognito console . Learn more on the Amazon Cognito page . Read the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide for feature details. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post . Howie Li Howie is a Product Manager at Amazon Web Services, where he strives to make auth easy by default. Outside of work, Howie enjoys exploring cultures and food through travels and making new ice cream flavors inspired by them. Sergii Nozhka Sergii is a Senior Software Development Engineer at Amazon Web Services, where he works on Amazon Cognito, helping customers build secure and scalable identity experiences. Outside of work, Sergii enjoys cooking and traveling with family. Priyank Bhardwaj Priyank is a Software Development Manager at Amazon Web Services. He leads the User Pool Management team for Amazon Cognito, helping customers build secure and scalable identity experiences. Outside of work, Priyank enjoys running outdoors and working on DIY projects around the house.
items.summary_html:
Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, microservices, and AI agents in minutes. Many of you rely on it for some of the most critical data you operate: the identities and attributes your applications use to authenticate and authorize every request. Recently, we launched point-in-time recovery (PITR) for Amazon Cognito user pools, which lets you restore a user pool to an earlier point in time if an accidental deletion, a faulty migration, or an erroneous bulk operation changes data you need. It’s turned on automatically for user pools on the eligible feature plans.

Before this launch, protecting user pool data meant building your own solution, such as exporting user attributes and group data on a schedule. That approach was time-consuming to build and operate, versioning the exports to find a clean point in time was another challenge, and reconstructing a pool from them was complicated. Users also got new sub identifiers as part of the restore process, which might break any downstream reference to the originals. Passwords, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys might not be recovered, so every affected user had to reset.

In this post, we show you how to recover a user pool after an erroneous bulk operation, using the preview to review changes before you approve them.

How PITR works

On eligible user pools (see Prerequisites), Amazon Cognito now tracks changes so you can recover the pool to any point within the recovery window. The length of that window depends on your user pool feature plan. The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed.

One behavior to understand is what happens to passwords during a recovery. A recovery restores passwords for users it recreates. A user who still exists and changed their password after the target time keeps the same password. The recovery doesn’t revert password changes, so users who legitimately changed their credentials don’t lose them.

A recovery is preview-based and has three steps:

  1. Initiate a recovery to a target point in time (InitiatePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito pauses write operations to the user pool and generates a preview for your review before any changes are applied. Read operations and sign-in continue to work normally. The call returns a RestoreId.
  2. Review the recovery preview (DescribePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito reports how many users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys the recovery would create, update, or delete to return the pool to its state at the target time.
  3. Approve or cancel. If the preview looks right, you approve the recovery with StartPointInTimeRecovery, and Amazon Cognito restores the pool to its state at the target time. If it doesn’t look right, you cancel it with CancelPointInTimeRecovery; no changes are applied, and write operations resume.
Prerequisites

To follow along with this post, you need:

  • An AWS account with an Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus feature plan. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. The examples use a pool named anycompany-prod-user-pool in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1).
  • The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with permissions for the Amazon Cognito user pools PITR operations.

Before you run a recovery, keep these limits in mind:

  • You can run one recovery at a time per user pool, and one successful recovery per 24 hours per pool.
  • The target time must be at least 15 minutes in the past and no earlier than the pool’s creation time.
  • Recovery is initiated from the pool’s primary Region and can’t start while a multi-Region replication (MRR) operation, such as replica creation or deletion, is in progress on the pool.
Recovering a user pool after an unintentional change

AnyCompany runs its user sign-in on an Amazon Cognito user pool, anycompany-prod-user-pool.

At 15:45 PDT, an operator runs a bulk change that’s supposed to set an attribute on a subset of users. A defect in the script instead deletes and modifies users. By 15:54 PDT, support receives cases of failed sign-ins and the operator halts the script. The team needs the pool as it was at 15:39 PDT. They decide to use PITR and preview the recovery before approving it.

Step 1: Start the recovery

The team initiates a recovery with a target time of 15:39 PDT by running the command in the preceding example. Figure 1 shows the same step in the console, where the team enters the target time and starts the recovery. The response includes a RestoreId that identifies this recovery throughout the workflow, along with a RestoreStatus and the RestoreTimestamp that you targeted.

aws cognito-idp initiate-point-in-time-recovery \   
--user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \   
--restore-timestamp 2026-10-28T22:39:00Z

Figure 1: Initiating a recovery to a target point in time

Step 2: Review the recovery preview

DescribePointInTimeRecovery returns the Restoration for this RestoreId, including a RestorePreview that summarizes how many entities will be affected if the pool is returned to the target time. The team reviews the preview and confirms the number of affected users matches the scope.

aws cognito-idp describe-point-in-time-recovery \   
--user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \   
--restore-id a69b8c1e-9866-441d-EXAMPLE11111

In this case, the preview reports 16 users to create and 5 users to update, as the following sample response shows. Figure 2 shows the same preview in the console, with the create, update, and delete counts for users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys. These numbers match the scope of the bulk operation, so the team continues. If the preview had shown unexpected changes, the team could cancel the recovery with no changes applied.

 {
      "Restoration": {
          "RestoreId": "a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111",
          "RestorePreview": [
              {
                  "Entity": "Users",
                  "CreateCount": 16,
                  "DeleteCount": 0,
                  "UpdateCount": 5
              },
              {
                  "Entity": "Groups",
                  "CreateCount": 0,
                  "DeleteCount": 0,
                  "UpdateCount": 0
              },
              {
                  "Entity": "User MFAs",
                  "CreateCount": 0,
                  "DeleteCount": 0,
                  "UpdateCount": 0
              },
              {
                  "Entity": "Passkeys",
                  "CreateCount": 0,
                  "DeleteCount": 0,
                  "UpdateCount": 0
              }
          ],
          "RestoreStatus": "PREVIEW_GENERATED",
          "RestoreTimestamp": 1793227140,
          "TriggerTimestamp": 1793228700
      }
  }

Figure 2: Reviewing the recovery preview before applying

Step 3: Approve the recovery

If the preview is correct, the team approves the recovery with the command in the following example, and Amazon Cognito restores anycompany-prod-user-pool to its 15:39 PDT state. Figure 3 shows the approval step in the console, and Figure 4 shows the confirmation that appears after the recovery starts. Writes to the user pool resume automatically after the recovery completes or is canceled.

aws cognito-idp start-point-in-time-recovery \    
--user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \   
--restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Figure 3: Approving the recovery


Figure 4: Recovery confirmation

aws cognito-idp cancel-point-in-time-recovery \    
--user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \   
--restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Your application integration doesn’t change

Because PITR rolls back the data in your existing user pool rather than creating a new one, your application integration doesn’t need any changes. A recovery restores user data and leaves your user pool configuration in place, so configuration changes you made after the recovery point are preserved. For example, a custom attribute you added to the schema, an AWS Lambda trigger you updated, or a password policy you tightened stays as it is. The user pool ID also stays the same, and so do your app client IDs and secrets, managed login and domain, identity provider and SAML/OIDC configurations, and the provider Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) that services such as Amazon API Gateway and Application Load Balancer use to validate tokens. Recreated users keep the same sub identifiers, so downstream references to them keep working.

How PITR complements multi-Region replication

Multi-Region replication and PITR address different failure modes. Multi-Region replication keeps a synchronized replica of your user pool in another Region, so if the primary Region is impaired, you can fail over traffic to a replica Region with minimal downtime. PITR helps with data problems, such as erroneous bulk operations that corrupt your user pool’s state. You roll back to any point within your recovery window without changing your application integration.

Security considerations

A recovery changes the identity data that every sign-in and authorization decision depends on, so treat recovery permissions like any other high-impact administrative access.

  • Separate who initiates a recovery from who approves it. Because initiating and approving are separate API actions, you can assign them to different AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Give an operator the permission InitiatePointInTimeRecovery, and give an approver the permission StartPointInTimeRecovery. Both permissions need DescribePointInTimeRecovery and ListPointInTimeRecoveries to review the preview, and CancelPointInTimeRecovery to stop a recovery. IAM keeps the two permissions on separate roles, but it doesn’t stop one person from assuming both. Assign the roles to different people or teams, and grant the approver role only for the duration of an approved change.
  • Treat initiating a recovery as sensitive. Initiating a recovery pauses write operations on the user pool until the recovery is approved or canceled. If no action is taken within 24 hours, the preview automatically cancels and write operations are resumed. While writes are paused, users can’t sign up, reset their passwords, or update their profiles. A user pool also allows only one successful recovery per 24 hours, so an unauthorized recovery uses up a recovery you might need for a real incident.
  • Review restored users after a recovery. A recovery recreates users who were deleted after the target time, including users you removed on purpose, such as employees who have left or compromised accounts. After a recovery completes, check the recreated users against your incident timeline. Disable any that should stay removed and revoke their sessions with AdminUserGlobalSignOut.
  • Monitor recovery activity. Amazon Cognito records PITR API calls in AWS CloudTrail. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that notifies your security team whenever InitiatePointInTimeRecovery or StartPointInTimeRecovery is called, so that no recovery goes unnoticed.
Pricing

PITR is included at no additional charge in eligible feature plans with a recovery window of up to 1 day on the Essentials feature plan and up to 14 days on the Plus feature plan.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how to recover an Amazon Cognito user pool after an erroneous bulk operation with PITR, from reviewing the changes in a preview to approving the recovery. PITR provides protection for your users’ identities, with no custom export-and-restore pipeline to build or operate. Because the recovery happens in place on the same user pool, your application integration keeps working unchanged. PITR is already enabled for eligible user pools. Before you need it, separate the initiate and approve permissions, add an alert on recovery calls, and practice the preview workflow on a test pool.

To get started:

  • Related post: Improve your application resilience with Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication
  • Related post: Amazon Cognito unlocks advanced capabilities with next-generation infrastructure
  • See PITR in the Amazon Cognito console.
  • Learn more on the Amazon Cognito page.
  • Read the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide for feature details.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

items.title: KQL of the Week: Hunting Exposed Offensive AI Infrastructure with KQL Queries
items.summary: AI-powered offensive security frameworks are no longer limited to isolated research environments. Some expose web consoles and APIs directly to the public Internet. But how many of these instances are visible online and are any of our systems communicating with them? offensive.agency provides an interesting starting point. Using Internet scanning data from ONYPHE, the project tracks publicly exposed web consoles and APIs associated with autonomous offensive security agents. The tracker uses several fingerprint families to identify probable or confirmed deployments, including web pages, favicons and certificates. It also provides historical observations, domain information and infrastructure context. One important distinction: an exposed offensive AI agent is not automatically malicious infrastructure. Researchers, penetration testers, students and malicious actors may all operate these tools. The objective of this hunting exercise is to discover potentially interesting interactions that deserve further investigation. From public threat intelligence to Defender XDR The project provides several public exports: https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt https://offensive.agency/api/domains.txt https://offensive.agency/api/hosts.csv https://offensive.agency/api/hosts.json It also supports filters such as scope=all, c2=1, country, level, kind and tool. The interesting part is that Microsoft Defender XDR supports the KQL externaldata() operator. This means we can query the public feeds directly, without manually downloading IP lists or maintaining static indicators. Let’s turn that data into several hunting scenarios. Hunt 1 — Outbound interactions to exposed offensive AI infrastructure Firstly, I am identifying endpoints establishing connections to IP addresses included in the tracker. DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table let OffensiveIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") | project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess" | join kind=inner (OffensiveIPs) on $left.RemoteIP == $right.IP URLClickEvents XDR Table let OffensiveIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") | project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); UrlClickEvents | join kind=inner (OffensiveIPs) on $left.IPAddress == $right.IP This gives us visibility into which devices contacted infrastructure associated with exposed offensive AI agents. However, an IP match alone is not evidence of malicious activity. Shared hosting and cloud infrastructure can introduce false positives such as CloudFare connections. Hunt 2 — Connections to offensive AI domains IP addresses are not always reliable indicators, particularly when infrastructure is hosted behind CDNs. The tracker also provides a domain export, allowing us to search for connections using the destination hostname. DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table let OffensiveDomains = externaldata(Domain:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/domains.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(Domain) and not(Domain startswith "#") | project Domain=tolower(trim(@"\s+",Domain)); DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) | extend Host=tolower(tostring(split(tostring(split(RemoteUrl,"://")[-1]),"/")[0])) | extend Host=tostring(split(Host,":")[0]) | join kind=inner (OffensiveDomains) on $left.Host == $right.Domain URLClickEvents XDR Table let OffensiveDomains = externaldata(Domain:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/domains.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(Domain) and not(Domain startswith "#") | project Domain=tolower(trim(@"\s+",Domain)); UrlClickEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where isnotempty(Url) | extend Host=tolower(tostring(split(tostring(split(Url,"://")[-1]),"/")[0])) | extend Host=tostring(split(Host,":")[0]) | join kind=inner (OffensiveDomains) on $left.Host == $right.Domain This is particularly useful for identifying interactions with exposed web consoles where multiple unrelated services share the same public IP. It searches network destination hostnames rather than relying on DNS events being available. Hunt 3 — Inbound connections from tracked infrastructure What happens when infrastructure included in the tracker initiates connections toward our monitored endpoints? This hunting scenario looks for inbound network activity associated with the published IP addresses. DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table let OffensiveIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") | project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType startswith "Inbound" | join kind=inner (OffensiveIPs) on $left.RemoteIP == $right.IP | project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc 🚨 Interesting findings include unexpected inbound connections to administrative services, repeated connection attempts or the same external IP communicating with multiple internal servers. Hunt 4 — Infrastructure with C2 co-hosting indicators One particularly interesting feature of offensive.agency is its ability to identify infrastructure where other services, including command-and-control frameworks, have also been observed. The API provides a c2=1 filter. We can use it to prioritize infrastructure that deserves closer inspection. KQL — DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table let C2AssociatedIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt?c2=1"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") | project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | join kind=inner (C2AssociatedIPs) on $left.RemoteIP == $right.IP | summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Processes=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName,20), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,20), RemoteURLs=make_set(RemoteUrl,20), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP A match against C2-associated infrastructure deserves attention, but it does not mean that the observed connection used a C2 protocol. The same IP may host several unrelated services. Some important limitations The tracker is based on passive analysis of Internet scanning data. It does not actively interact with the identified hosts. It distinguishes active observations from historical records and warns about the limitations of shared infrastructure. The scope=all option includes historical observations, but an IP address observed in the past may now belong to another organization. For that reason, historical IP matches should be evaluated against the observation dates in the source data. Also, externaldata() retrieves the external feed at query execution time. This is useful for interactive hunting, but it means the feed can change between investigations. For reproducible investigations, preserving the feed snapshot and collection time is valuable. Final thoughts Threat intelligence becomes much more valuable when we move beyond collecting indicators and start correlating them with actual endpoint behavior. The offensive.agency project provides an interesting dataset for exploring the growing exposure of offensive AI infrastructure. With KQL, we can quickly investigate outbound connections, inbound activity, domain matches, suspicious processes and infrastructure associated with C2 services. ⚠️ Important: The goal is not to flag every listed IP as malicious. The goal is to understand why our devices are communicating with that infrastructure. References offensive.agency — Methodology and Exports ONYPHE Microsoft Defender XDR — Advanced Hunting Best Practice KQL of the Week: Hunting Exposed Offensive AI Infrastructure with KQL Queries was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
AI-powered offensive security frameworks are no longer limited to isolated research environments. Some expose web consoles and APIs directly to the public Internet. But how many of these instances are visible online and are any of our systems communicating with them? offensive.agency provides an interesting starting point.

Using Internet scanning data from ONYPHE, the project tracks publicly exposed web consoles and APIs associated with autonomous offensive security agents. The tracker uses several fingerprint families to identify probable or confirmed deployments, including web pages, favicons and certificates. It also provides historical observations, domain information and infrastructure context.

One important distinction: an exposed offensive AI agent is not automatically malicious infrastructure. Researchers, penetration testers, students and malicious actors may all operate these tools.

The objective of this hunting exercise is to discover potentially interesting interactions that deserve further investigation.

From public threat intelligence to Defender XDR

The project provides several public exports:

  • https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt
  • https://offensive.agency/api/domains.txt
  • https://offensive.agency/api/hosts.csv
  • https://offensive.agency/api/hosts.json
It also supports filters such as scope=all, c2=1, country, level, kind and tool. The interesting part is that Microsoft Defender XDR supports the KQL externaldata() operator. This means we can query the public feeds directly, without manually downloading IP lists or maintaining static indicators. Let’s turn that data into several hunting scenarios.
Hunt 1 — Outbound interactions to exposed offensive AI infrastructure

Firstly, I am identifying endpoints establishing connections to IP addresses included in the tracker.

DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table

let OffensiveIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt"] with (format="txt") 
| where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") 
| project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); DeviceNetworkEvents 
| where Timestamp > ago(7d) 
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess" | join kind=inner (OffensiveIPs) on $left.RemoteIP == $right.IP

URLClickEvents XDR Table

let OffensiveIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") | project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); 
UrlClickEvents | join kind=inner (OffensiveIPs) on $left.IPAddress == $right.IP

This gives us visibility into which devices contacted infrastructure associated with exposed offensive AI agents.

However, an IP match alone is not evidence of malicious activity. Shared hosting and cloud infrastructure can introduce false positives such as CloudFare connections.
Hunt 2 — Connections to offensive AI domains

IP addresses are not always reliable indicators, particularly when infrastructure is hosted behind CDNs. The tracker also provides a domain export, allowing us to search for connections using the destination hostname.

DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table

let OffensiveDomains = externaldata(Domain:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/domains.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(Domain) and not(Domain startswith "#") 
| project Domain=tolower(trim(@"\s+",Domain));
DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) | extend Host=tolower(tostring(split(tostring(split(RemoteUrl,"://")[-1]),"/")[0]))
| extend Host=tostring(split(Host,":")[0]) 
| join kind=inner (OffensiveDomains) on $left.Host == $right.Domain

URLClickEvents XDR Table

let OffensiveDomains = externaldata(Domain:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/domains.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(Domain) and not(Domain startswith "#") 
| project Domain=tolower(trim(@"\s+",Domain));
UrlClickEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where isnotempty(Url) | extend Host=tolower(tostring(split(tostring(split(Url,"://")[-1]),"/")[0]))
| extend Host=tostring(split(Host,":")[0]) 
| join kind=inner (OffensiveDomains) on $left.Host == $right.Domain

This is particularly useful for identifying interactions with exposed web consoles where multiple unrelated services share the same public IP. It searches network destination hostnames rather than relying on DNS events being available.

Hunt 3 — Inbound connections from tracked infrastructure

What happens when infrastructure included in the tracker initiates connections toward our monitored endpoints? This hunting scenario looks for inbound network activity associated with the published IP addresses.

DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table

let OffensiveIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt"] with (format="txt") | where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") | project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType startswith "Inbound" | join kind=inner (OffensiveIPs) on $left.RemoteIP == $right.IP | project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc
🚨 Interesting findings include unexpected inbound connections to administrative services, repeated connection attempts or the same external IP communicating with multiple internal servers.
Hunt 4 — Infrastructure with C2 co-hosting indicators

One particularly interesting feature of offensive.agency is its ability to identify infrastructure where other services, including command-and-control frameworks, have also been observed. The API provides a c2=1 filter. We can use it to prioritize infrastructure that deserves closer inspection.

KQL — DeviceNetworkEvents XDR Table

let C2AssociatedIPs = externaldata(IP:string) [@"https://offensive.agency/api/ips.txt?c2=1"] with (format="txt") 
| where isnotempty(IP) and not(IP startswith "#") | project IP=trim(@"\s+",IP); 
DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | join kind=inner (C2AssociatedIPs) on $left.RemoteIP == $right.IP 
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Processes=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName,20), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,20), RemoteURLs=make_set(RemoteUrl,20), Actions=make_set(ActionType,10)
 by DeviceName, RemoteIP

A match against C2-associated infrastructure deserves attention, but it does not mean that the observed connection used a C2 protocol. The same IP may host several unrelated services.

Some important limitations

The tracker is based on passive analysis of Internet scanning data. It does not actively interact with the identified hosts. It distinguishes active observations from historical records and warns about the limitations of shared infrastructure. The scope=all option includes historical observations, but an IP address observed in the past may now belong to another organization.

For that reason, historical IP matches should be evaluated against the observation dates in the source data. Also, externaldata() retrieves the external feed at query execution time. This is useful for interactive hunting, but it means the feed can change between investigations. For reproducible investigations, preserving the feed snapshot and collection time is valuable.

Final thoughts

Threat intelligence becomes much more valuable when we move beyond collecting indicators and start correlating them with actual endpoint behavior. The offensive.agency project provides an interesting dataset for exploring the growing exposure of offensive AI infrastructure.

With KQL, we can quickly investigate outbound connections, inbound activity, domain matches, suspicious processes and infrastructure associated with C2 services.

⚠️ Important: The goal is not to flag every listed IP as malicious. The goal is to understand why our devices are communicating with that infrastructure.

References

  • offensive.agency — Methodology and Exports
  • ONYPHE
  • Microsoft Defender XDR — Advanced Hunting Best Practice

items.title: “Gangsters Run the World”: Citizen Lab Founder Ron Deibert Warns of Unchecked Spyware Abuse
items.summary: Director Ron Deibert spoke with IRPI Media about the “pandemic” of spyware abuse happening worldwide. He warns that spyware allows governments to surveil political opponents and dissenting voices, silencing those who speak up and interfering with democratic processes. While spyware abuse is prolific, progress has been made to uncover and expose it. Technology companies were uninterested in talking about these issues ten years ago, but Apple now sends notifications to spyware victims. Deibert sees this as “something we can take some hope from.” Without oversight and consequences for those responsible for spyware abuses, however, he warns that nothing will change. “The message seems to be: do whatever you want, you’ll get away with it, because nobody cares.” Read the article

items.title: ARTEX leads to persistent ZQAgent backdoor
items.summary:
Over the last few months, NVISO has responded to an increasing amount of intrusions leveraging adversary LLM tools such as ARTEX. Several industry peers have corroborated 1 this increased activity, with LLM-driven tools excelling at exploitation and credential abuse. LLM-driven intrusions have to date maintained a relatively consistent attack-chain commonly permitting containment through the isolation of its initial-access vector and the subsequent extensive revocation of compromised and staged credentials. Amplified by the speed and noise of LLMs, these intrusions are often experienced as smash-and-grab operations, rarely resulting in long-lasting footholds beyond collected and staged credentials. However, as part of a recent incident response engagement, NVISO observed ARTEX deploying ZQAgent, a new backdoor providing its operator with a long-lasting foothold within the target environment. The usage of a persistent backdoor by LLM-driven tools deviates from their current autonomous nature and is instead believed to be the result of operator-specific instructions. The usage of LLMs is still rarely observed 2 in traditional backdoor deployment operations, we see no reason that, over the near future, the usage of LLMs would not widely spread to these historically conventional operations. ZQAgent ZQAgent, named through ARTEX artifacts, is a new stealthy backdoor providing adversaries with commonly desired capabilities such as arbitrary code execution, filesystem operations, network tunneling and more. NVISO observed ZQAgent’s deployment in Belgium, initially under /tmp/ zqa /systemd-timesyncd , with similar samples 3 , 4 reported from Taiwan. As part of our incident response activities, NVISO was able to confirm all known samples were configured to use 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com for command and control; We currently associate this infrastructure with FOG0003. ZQAgent’s decrypted configuration. Network intelligence contributed by Team Cymru further suggests that FOG0003 likely deployed ZQAgent within Asia, affecting government and human-rights organizations. Runtime Evasion To hinder detection, ZQAgent migrates itself in memory to a temporary anonymous file. This migration results in the apparent filename /memfd:a (deleted) , also observed in the earlier discussed public samples. ZQAgent’s temporary anonymous file allocation. ZQAgent’s public samples, named “memfd:a (deleted)”. Once ZQAgent copied itself to the temporary anonymous file, the backdoor restarts as a detached process impersonating the dbus-daemon utility 5 . ZQAgent’s command-line spoofing. ZQAgent’s command-line spoofing results in the following spoofed process, without being linked to the original executable. /usr/bin/dbus-daemon --session --address=systemd: --nofork --nopidfile --systemd-activation --syslog-only /usr/bin/dbus-daemon --session --address=systemd: --nofork --nopidfile --systemd-activation --syslog-only Additional runtime evasion strategies include the dynamic encryption of configuration settings, only temporarily decrypted when evaluated, as well as the usage of multiple network encryption layers (e.g., ChaCha20 variants). Operator Capabilities ZQAgent provides its operators with a wide variety of capabilities. The below operation codes constitute most of ZQAgent’s features. Codes Actions 0x04 , 0x08 Get and change the current working directory through getcwd and chdir 0x0A , 0x15 Update some of ZQAgent’s runtime configuration 0x0C Move a file, similar to the usage of cp 0x0E List a directory’s content, similar to the usage of ls 0x0F List mounted filesystem types 0x11 Remove a file or directory, similar to the usage of rm 0x12 Rename a file through rename 0x16 Get the current user context, similar to the usage of id 0x18 Read a file’s first 2048 bytes, conceptually similar to the usage of head 0x1B Create a directory through mkdir 0x1C Enable, disable or check ZQAgent’s persistence 0x25 , 0x26 , 0x27 Blocking TCP connection management (connecting, sending, closing) 0x29 Get an arbitrary process’ statistics through /proc 0x2A Terminate an arbitrary process through kill 0x2B Start a command as a managed process using /bin/sh -c 0x2E List all managed processes 0x2F Terminate a managed process 0x34 Create a memory-only (i.e., memfd ) managed process 0x3E , 0x3F , 0x40 , 0x41 , 0x42 , 0x43 , 0x45 , 0x46 Non-blocking TCP/UDP connection management (connecting, listening, sending, closing, …) 0x47 Allocate a new managed shell (i.e., /bin/bash or, if unavailable, /bin/sh ) 0x48 Write to a managed shell’s standard input ZQAgent’s operation codes and associated capabilities. Persistence ZQAgent’s persistence is twofold, leveraging both services and cron jobs while time-stomping all staged artifacts. When enabled, ZQAgent copies itself under an attacker-controlled name within any of the following paths: For root , under /usr/lib/systemd/%s For any other user, under $HOME/.local/share/%s If the HOME environment variable is not defined, under /tmp/.local/share/%s ZQAgent subsequently creates the associates service, which references the above staged binary through the ExecStart statement. The service definition is staged at any of the following paths: For root , as /etc/systemd/system/%s.service For any other user, as $HOME/.config/systemd/user/%s.service If the HOME environment variable is not defined, as /tmp/.config/systemd/user/%s.service The below snippet shows the differences between ZQAgent’s root and non- root service template. [Unit] Description=Device event journal daemon -After=multi-user.target +After=default.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=%s Restart=always RestartSec=30 StandardOutput=null StandardError=null [Install] -WantedBy=multi-user.target +WantedBy=default.target [Unit] Description=Device event journal daemon -After=multi-user.target +After=default.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=%s Restart=always RestartSec=30 StandardOutput=null StandardError=null [Install] -WantedBy=multi-user.target +WantedBy=default.target Once ZQAgent staged itself and the service definition, the backdoor enables the service through systemctl , using the --user flag if not running as root . systemctl [--user] daemon-reload systemctl [--user] enable %s.service systemctl [--user] daemon-reload systemctl [--user] enable %s.service When not running as root , ZQAgent ensures it can outlive regular user sessions by calling loginctl enable-linger 6 . Next to services, ZQAgent also deploys a cron job to achieve persistence. While root sessions deploy the following template under /etc/cron.d/%s , non-root sessions append the user’s existing cron definitions through the crontab binary 7 . SHELL=/bin/sh PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin @reboot root %s >/dev/null 2>&1 SHELL = /bin/sh PATH = /usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin @reboot root %s > /dev/null 2>&1 Conclusions Over the last few months, NVISO has responded to several LLM-driven intrusions. Compromises such as those achieved through ARTEX often exhibit relatively common attack-paths; Initial access is often gained through exploitation or compromised credentials while the rest of the attack-path consists of rapidly abusing both misconfigurations as well as lingering credentials. While LLMs do deploy custom artifacts, these are often intended at lowering the complexity of their lateral movement (e.g., internal web-shells, SSH credentials, …). The containment of these relatively-common attack-paths is often achieved by isolating the initial-access vector, providing responders with sufficient time to revoke compromised/staged credentials and cleaning-up remaining artifacts. The recently observed deployment of novel backdoors during LLM-driven intrusions however raises concerns over the evolution of these LLM attack-paths. Historically conventional cyber-operations such as ransomware or espionage would drastically benefit from this approach; We see no reason that the usage of LLMs would not spread to these operations. To date, ransomware remains a time-consuming activity for human operators, accentuated by slow initial access vectors as well as complex privilege escalation and lateral movement efforts. These time-consuming activities have often benefited mature organizations, providing them with sufficient time to contain and eradicate threats. For espionage, significant effort was historically required to identify and compromise specialized appliances. Recent trends however outline the increasing possibility that LLMs may further reduce the time-to-ransom from hours 8 to minutes, while espionage campaigns will likely be able to scope wider attack-surfaces. LLMs have over the last few months changed the balance of defensive cost imposition, and organizations have yet to react. These new cost-effective attacker capabilities will require organizations to aggressively harden their stance. Most notably, organizations will need to significantly harden their perimeters (e.g., increased segmentation, mandatory asset security telemetry, EASM, …) and drastically reduce response times. Historically frowned upon solutions such as automated asset isolation are back under consideration now that attacker speeds outpace human reaction. Indicators of Compromise Type Indicator Note IP 37.122.150[.]15 FOG0003 ZQAgent Command & Control Domain bloonspace[.]com FOG0003 ZQAgent Command & Control SHA256 c5d1358ece7dff7834507a29f59fdc35a1a2afa3045ae8d754fb497f6f999296 ZQAgent SHA256 0319739869e1aadb2d598152a0290215c057c8364257f3a84a42164cf863019f ZQAgent (Public 03197 ) SHA256 a49f43d0ae373cb35df2cb7a5542bc58234764dad15a628d28a5c67fc6834357 ZQAgent (Public a49f4 ) SHA1 f585e980a16e52b8da2d2328dc5688cb0a1dc5cd ZQAgent SHA1 7e9fd6f02d35806af0b7447038322fdf0eed4318 ZQAgent (Public 03197 ) SHA1 2cbeaed3a591219c0eca708b4cb9f4e249231b89 ZQAgent (Public a49f4 ) MD5 8211127a7bc385bc784822d22f69c426 ZQAgent MD5 e9a03f331f3d737a2dcf479a54b94fd7 ZQAgent (Public 03197 ) MD5 97669d76529bc5efd4fa6506de13fb71 ZQAgent (Public a49f4 ) YARA rule FOG0003_ZQAgent_backdoor : FOG0003 ZQAgent TA0011 T1071 T1071_001 { meta: author = "Maxime THIEBAUT (NVISO)" description = "Detects strings unique to the ZQAgent backdoor" url = "https://blog.nviso.eu/2026/11/23/artex-fog0003-zqagent-backdoor/" sha256 = "0319739869e1aadb2d598152a0290215c057c8364257f3a84a42164cf863019f" sha256 = "a49f43d0ae373cb35df2cb7a5542bc58234764dad15a628d28a5c67fc6834357" created = "2026-11-15" strings: $persist_unknown = "unknown subcommand (1=install 2=remove 3=check)" $persist_ok_root = "autostart installed (cron): %s -> %s (runs at boot, not started now)" $persist_invalid = "invalid name (allowed: [A-Za-z0-9_.@-], without .service suffix)" $persist_remove = "autostart removed: %s (unit %s, binary %s, cron %s)" $cnc_header = "%s %s HTTP/1.1

items.summary_html:
Over the last few months, NVISO has responded to an increasing amount of intrusions leveraging adversary LLM tools such as ARTEX. Several industry peers have corroborated1 this increased activity, with LLM-driven tools excelling at exploitation and credential abuse. LLM-driven intrusions have to date maintained a relatively consistent attack-chain commonly permitting containment through the isolation of its initial-access vector and the subsequent extensive revocation of compromised and staged credentials.

Amplified by the speed and noise of LLMs, these intrusions are often experienced as smash-and-grab operations, rarely resulting in long-lasting footholds beyond collected and staged credentials. However, as part of a recent incident response engagement, NVISO observed ARTEX deploying ZQAgent, a new backdoor providing its operator with a long-lasting foothold within the target environment. The usage of a persistent backdoor by LLM-driven tools deviates from their current autonomous nature and is instead believed to be the result of operator-specific instructions.

The usage of LLMs is still rarely observed2 in traditional backdoor deployment operations, we see no reason that, over the near future, the usage of LLMs would not widely spread to these historically conventional operations.

ZQAgent

ZQAgent, named through ARTEX artifacts, is a new stealthy backdoor providing adversaries with commonly desired capabilities such as arbitrary code execution, filesystem operations, network tunneling and more. NVISO observed ZQAgent’s deployment in Belgium, initially under /tmp/zqa/systemd-timesyncd, with similar samples3,4 reported from Taiwan. As part of our incident response activities, NVISO was able to confirm all known samples were configured to use 37.122.150[.]15 and bloonspace[.]com for command and control; We currently associate this infrastructure with FOG0003.

ZQAgent’s decrypted configuration.

Network intelligence contributed by Team Cymru further suggests that FOG0003 likely deployed ZQAgent within Asia, affecting government and human-rights organizations.

Runtime Evasion

To hinder detection, ZQAgent migrates itself in memory to a temporary anonymous file. This migration results in the apparent filename /memfd:a (deleted), also observed in the earlier discussed public samples.

ZQAgent’s temporary anonymous file allocation.
ZQAgent’s public samples, named “memfd:a (deleted)”.

Once ZQAgent copied itself to the temporary anonymous file, the backdoor restarts as a detached process impersonating the dbus-daemon utility5.

ZQAgent’s command-line spoofing.

ZQAgent’s command-line spoofing results in the following spoofed process, without being linked to the original executable.

/usr/bin/dbus-daemon --session --address=systemd: --nofork --nopidfile --systemd-activation --syslog-only
/usr/bin/dbus-daemon --session --address=systemd: --nofork --nopidfile --systemd-activation --syslog-only

Additional runtime evasion strategies include the dynamic encryption of configuration settings, only temporarily decrypted when evaluated, as well as the usage of multiple network encryption layers (e.g., ChaCha20 variants).

Operator Capabilities

ZQAgent provides its operators with a wide variety of capabilities. The below operation codes constitute most of ZQAgent’s features.

CodesActions0x04, 0x08Get and change the current working directory through getcwd and chdir0x0A, 0x15Update some of ZQAgent’s runtime configuration0x0CMove a file, similar to the usage of cp0x0EList a directory’s content, similar to the usage of ls0x0FList mounted filesystem types0x11Remove a file or directory, similar to the usage of rm0x12Rename a file through rename0x16Get the current user context, similar to the usage of id0x18Read a file’s first 2048 bytes, conceptually similar to the usage of head0x1BCreate a directory through mkdir0x1CEnable, disable or check ZQAgent’s persistence0x25, 0x26, 0x27Blocking TCP connection management (connecting, sending, closing)0x29Get an arbitrary process’ statistics through /proc0x2ATerminate an arbitrary process through kill0x2BStart a command as a managed process using /bin/sh -c0x2EList all managed processes0x2FTerminate a managed process0x34Create a memory-only (i.e., memfd) managed process0x3E, 0x3F, 0x40, 0x41, 0x42, 0x43, 0x45, 0x46Non-blocking TCP/UDP connection management (connecting, listening, sending, closing, …)0x47Allocate a new managed shell (i.e., /bin/bash or, if unavailable, /bin/sh)0x48Write to a managed shell’s standard inputZQAgent’s operation codes and associated capabilities. Persistence

ZQAgent’s persistence is twofold, leveraging both services and cron jobs while time-stomping all staged artifacts. When enabled, ZQAgent copies itself under an attacker-controlled name within any of the following paths:

  • For root, under /usr/lib/systemd/%s
  • For any other user, under $HOME/.local/share/%s
    • If the HOME environment variable is not defined, under /tmp/.local/share/%s

ZQAgent subsequently creates the associates service, which references the above staged binary through the ExecStart statement. The service definition is staged at any of the following paths:

  • For root, as /etc/systemd/system/%s.service
  • For any other user, as $HOME/.config/systemd/user/%s.service
    • If the HOME environment variable is not defined, as /tmp/.config/systemd/user/%s.service

The below snippet shows the differences between ZQAgent’s root and non-root service template.

 [Unit]
 Description=Device event journal daemon
-After=multi-user.target
+After=default.target

 [Service]
 Type=simple
 ExecStart=%s
 Restart=always
 RestartSec=30
 StandardOutput=null
 StandardError=null

 [Install]
-WantedBy=multi-user.target
+WantedBy=default.target

 [Unit]
 Description=Device event journal daemon
-After=multi-user.target
+After=default.target

 [Service]
 Type=simple
 ExecStart=%s
 Restart=always
 RestartSec=30
 StandardOutput=null
 StandardError=null

 [Install]
-WantedBy=multi-user.target
+WantedBy=default.target

Once ZQAgent staged itself and the service definition, the backdoor enables the service through systemctl, using the --user flag if not running as root.

systemctl [--user] daemon-reload
systemctl [--user] enable %s.service
systemctl [--user] daemon-reload
systemctl [--user] enable %s.service

When not running as root, ZQAgent ensures it can outlive regular user sessions by calling loginctl enable-linger6.

Next to services, ZQAgent also deploys a cron job to achieve persistence. While root sessions deploy the following template under /etc/cron.d/%s, non-root sessions append the user’s existing cron definitions through the crontab binary7.

SHELL=/bin/sh
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin
@reboot root %s >/dev/null 2>&1
SHELL=/bin/sh
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin
@reboot root %s >/dev/null 2>&1
Conclusions

Over the last few months, NVISO has responded to several LLM-driven intrusions. Compromises such as those achieved through ARTEX often exhibit relatively common attack-paths; Initial access is often gained through exploitation or compromised credentials while the rest of the attack-path consists of rapidly abusing both misconfigurations as well as lingering credentials. While LLMs do deploy custom artifacts, these are often intended at lowering the complexity of their lateral movement (e.g., internal web-shells, SSH credentials, …). The containment of these relatively-common attack-paths is often achieved by isolating the initial-access vector, providing responders with sufficient time to revoke compromised/staged credentials and cleaning-up remaining artifacts.

The recently observed deployment of novel backdoors during LLM-driven intrusions however raises concerns over the evolution of these LLM attack-paths. Historically conventional cyber-operations such as ransomware or espionage would drastically benefit from this approach; We see no reason that the usage of LLMs would not spread to these operations.

To date, ransomware remains a time-consuming activity for human operators, accentuated by slow initial access vectors as well as complex privilege escalation and lateral movement efforts. These time-consuming activities have often benefited mature organizations, providing them with sufficient time to contain and eradicate threats. For espionage, significant effort was historically required to identify and compromise specialized appliances. Recent trends however outline the increasing possibility that LLMs may further reduce the time-to-ransom from hours8 to minutes, while espionage campaigns will likely be able to scope wider attack-surfaces.

LLMs have over the last few months changed the balance of defensive cost imposition, and organizations have yet to react. These new cost-effective attacker capabilities will require organizations to aggressively harden their stance. Most notably, organizations will need to significantly harden their perimeters (e.g., increased segmentation, mandatory asset security telemetry, EASM, …) and drastically reduce response times. Historically frowned upon solutions such as automated asset isolation are back under consideration now that attacker speeds outpace human reaction.

items.title: ARTEX führt zu einer dauerhaften ZQAgent-Backdoor
items.summary:
In den vergangenen Monaten hat NVISO eine zunehmende Zahl von Angriffen untersucht, bei denen Angreifer LLM-gestützte Tools wie ARTEX einsetzen. Auch andere Unternehmen der Branche bestätigen diesen Anstieg 1 . Besonders beim Ausnutzen von Schwachstellen und beim Missbrauch von Zugangsdaten erweisen sich diese Tools als leistungsfähig. Bislang folgen LLM-gestützte Angriffe einer weitgehend einheitlichen Angriffskette. Anschließend nutzen die Angreifer in schneller Folge Fehlkonfigurationen und weiterhin gültige Zugangsdaten aus. Solche Angriffsketten lassen sich oft eindämmen, indem der ursprüngliche Zugangsweg isoliert wird. Dadurch gewinnen die Incident-Response-Teams genügend Zeit, um kompromittierte und für spätere Zugriffe hinterlegte Zugangsdaten zu sperren oder zurückzusetzen und verbleibende Artefakte zu entfernen. Der kürzlich beobachtete Einsatz neuartiger Backdoors bei LLM-gestützten Angriffen wirft jedoch die Frage auf, wie sich diese Angriffsketten weiterentwickeln werden. Auch bislang konventionell durchgeführte Cyberoperationen wie Ransomware-Angriffe oder Spionage könnten erheblich von diesem Ansatz profitieren. Wir sehen keinen Grund, warum sich der Einsatz von LLMs nicht auch auf diese Bereiche ausweiten sollte. Bislang sind Ransomware-Angriffe für menschliche Angreifer zeitaufwendig. Gleichzeitig dürften Spionagekampagnen künftig größere Angriffsflächen abdecken. LLMs haben in den vergangenen Monaten das Kräfteverhältnis verändert: Schutzmaßnahmen, die Angreifern bislang erheblichen Aufwand abverlangten, verlieren an Wirkung. Organisationen müssen darauf noch reagieren. Die neuen, kostengünstigen Angriffsmöglichkeiten erfordern eine konsequente Härtung der eigenen Umgebung.
