ZQAgent stellt Angreifern eine Vielzahl von Funktionen zur Verfügung. Die in der nachfolgenden Tabelle aufgeführten Operationscodes decken den Großteil des Funktionsumfangs von ZQAgent ab.

CodesAktionen0x04, 0x08Aktuelles Arbeitsverzeichnis mit getcwd abrufen bzw. mit chdir wechseln0x0A, 0x15Teile der Laufzeitkonfiguration von ZQAgent aktualisieren0x0CEine Datei verschieben, ähnlich wie mit cp*0x0EVerzeichnisinhalt auflisten, ähnlich wie mit ls0x0FTypen der eingebundenen Dateisysteme auflisten0x11Eine Datei oder ein Verzeichnis entfernen, ähnlich wie mit rm0x12Eine Datei mit rename umbenennen0x16Aktuellen Benutzerkontext abrufen, ähnlich wie mit id0x18Die ersten 2.048 Bytes einer Datei lesen, vergleichbar mit head0x1BEin Verzeichnis mit mkdir erstellen0x1CPersistenz von ZQAgent aktivieren, deaktivieren oder überprüfen0x25, 0x26, 0x27Blockierende TCP-Verbindungen verwalten (Verbindung herstellen, Daten senden, Verbindung schließen)0x29Prozessstatistiken eines beliebigen Prozesses über /proc abrufen0x2AEinen beliebigen Prozess mit kill beenden0x2BEinen Befehl mit /bin/sh -c als verwalteten Prozess starten0x2EAlle verwalteten Prozesse auflisten0x2FEinen verwalteten Prozess beenden0x34Erstellen eines ausschließlich im Arbeitsspeicher verwalteten Prozesses (mittels memfd)0x3E, 0x3F, 0x40, 0x41, 0x42, 0x43, 0x45, 0x46Nicht blockierende TCP-/UDP-Verbindungen verwalten (Verbindung herstellen, auf eingehende Verbindungen warten, Daten senden, Verbindung schließen usw.)0x47Eine neue verwaltete Shell starten (/bin/bash oder, falls nicht verfügbar, /bin/sh)0x48In die Standardeingabe einer verwalteten Shell schreibenDie Befehlscodes von ZQAgent und die damit verbundenen Funktionen. Persistenz

ZQAgent nutzt zwei Mechanismen zur Persistenz: Dienste und Cron Jobs. Dabei manipuliert die Backdoor die Zeitstempel aller abgelegten Artefakte (Timestomping). Wird die Persistenz aktiviert, kopiert sich ZQAgent unter einem vom Angreifer festgelegten Namen in eines der folgenden Verzeichnisse:

  • Bei Ausführung als root: /usr/lib/systemd/%s
  • Bei Ausführung als anderer Benutzer: $HOME/.local/share/%s
    • Falls die Umgebungsvariable HOME nicht definiert ist: /tmp/.local/share/%s

Anschließend erstellt ZQAgent den zugehörigen Dienst, dessen ExecStart-Anweisung auf die zuvor abgelegte ausführbare Datei verweist. Die Dienstdefinition wird unter einem der folgenden Pfade gespeichert:

  • Bei Ausführung als root: /etc/systemd/system/%s.service
  • Bei Ausführung als anderer Benutzer: $HOME/.config/systemd/user/%s.service
    • Falls die Umgebungsvariable HOME nicht definiert ist: /tmp/.config/systemd/user/%s.service

Der folgende Ausschnitt zeigt die Unterschiede zwischen den Dienstvorlagen für die Ausführung mit und ohne Root-Rechte.

 [Unit]
 Description=Device event journal daemon
-After=multi-user.target
+After=default.target

 [Service]
 Type=simple
 ExecStart=%s
 Restart=always
 RestartSec=30
 StandardOutput=null
 StandardError=null

 [Install]
-WantedBy=multi-user.target
+WantedBy=default.target

 [Unit]
 Description=Device event journal daemon
-After=multi-user.target
+After=default.target

 [Service]
 Type=simple
 ExecStart=%s
 Restart=always
 RestartSec=30
 StandardOutput=null
 StandardError=null

 [Install]
-WantedBy=multi-user.target
+WantedBy=default.target

Nachdem ZQAgent sich selbst und die Dienstdefinition abgelegt hat, aktiviert die Backdoor den Dienst mit systemctl. Läuft sie nicht als root, verwendet sie dabei die Option --user.

systemctl [--user] daemon-reload
systemctl [--user] enable %s.service
systemctl [--user] daemon-reload
systemctl [--user] enable %s.service

Läuft ZQAgent ohne Root-Rechte, stellt die Backdoor mit loginctl enable-linger6 sicher, dass sie auch nach dem Abmelden des Benutzers weiterlaufen kann.

Neben den Diensten richtet ZQAgent einen Cron Job zur Persistenz ein. Bei Ausführung als root wird die folgende Vorlage unter /etc/cron.d/%s abgelegt. Ohne Root-Rechte werden die bestehende cron definitionen des Benutzers mithilfe von crontab7 angefügt.

SHELL=/bin/sh
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin
@reboot root %s >/dev/null 2>&1
SHELL=/bin/sh
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin
@reboot root %s >/dev/null 2>&1
Fazit

In den vergangenen Monaten hat NVISO mehrere LLM-gestützte Angriffe untersucht. Angriffe mit Tools wie ARTEX folgen häufig ähnlichen Mustern: Der Erstzugriff (Initial access) erfolgt meist über die Ausnutzung von Schwachstellen oder kompromittierte Zugangsdaten. Anschließend nutzen die Angreifer in schneller Folge Fehlkonfigurationen und weiterhin gültige Zugangsdaten aus. Zwar setzen LLM-gestützte Tools auch eigens erstellte Artefakte ein, diese dienen jedoch häufig dazu, die laterale Bewegung zu erleichtern (etwa durch interne Webshells oder SSH-Zugangsdaten). Solche Angriffsketten lassen sich oft eindämmen, indem der ursprüngliche Zugangsweg isoliert wird. Dadurch gewinnen die Incident-Response-Teams genügend Zeit, um kompromittierte und für spätere Zugriffe hinterlegte Zugangsdaten zu sperren oder zurückzusetzen und verbleibende Artefakte zu entfernen.

Der kürzlich beobachtete Einsatz neuartiger Backdoors bei LLM-gestützten Angriffen wirft jedoch die Frage auf, wie sich diese Angriffsketten weiterentwickeln werden. Auch bislang konventionell durchgeführte Cyberoperationen wie Ransomware-Angriffe oder Spionage könnten erheblich von diesem Ansatz profitieren. Wir sehen keinen Grund, warum sich der Einsatz von LLMs nicht auch auf diese Bereiche ausweiten sollte.

Bislang sind Ransomware-Angriffe für menschliche Angreifer zeitaufwendig. Insbesondere der langsame Erstzugriff sowie die oft komplexe Ausweitung von Berechtigungen und die laterale Bewegung kosten Zeit. Organisationen mit einem hohen Sicherheitsreifegrad konnten dieses Zeitfenster häufig nutzen, um Angriffe einzudämmen und die Bedrohung vollständig zu beseitigen. Bei Spionageoperationen war bislang erheblicher Aufwand nötig, um spezialisierte Appliances zu identifizieren und zu kompromittieren. Aktuelle Entwicklungen deuten jedoch darauf hin, dass LLMs die Zeit bis zum Einsatz von Ransomware von Stunden8 auf Minuten verkürzen könnten. Gleichzeitig dürften Spionagekampagnen künftig größere Angriffsflächen abdecken.

LLMs haben in den vergangenen Monaten das Kräfteverhältnis verändert: Schutzmaßnahmen, die Angreifern bislang erheblichen Aufwand abverlangten, verlieren an Wirkung. Organisationen müssen darauf noch reagieren. Die neuen, kostengünstigen Angriffsmöglichkeiten erfordern eine konsequente Härtung der eigenen Umgebung. Besonders wichtig sind ein deutlich besserer Schutz der extern erreichbaren Systeme und ihrer Zugangswege (etwa durch stärkere Segmentierung, verpflichtende Sicherheitstelemetrie für IT-Assets und External Attack Surface Management (EASM), …) sowie wesentlich kürzere Reaktionszeiten. Auch bislang kritisch betrachtete Maßnahmen wie die automatisierte Isolation von IT-Assets rücken wieder in den Fokus, da Angreifer inzwischen schneller handeln, als Menschen reagieren können.

items.summary: .kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column492162_d006dd-b2 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Meta’s AI agent, Muse, reportedly flagged a private Signal message an employee said she hadn’t given it access to A Meta team member said built-in prompts to engage users triggered hallucinations Check your AI agent’s permissions, especially whether it can read notifications from other apps Internal posts reviewed by Reuters describe Meta’s AI agent Muse surfacing private information unprompted, and Reuters’ own tests backed up part of the story. Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal Meta posts. One employee said Muse reminded her to answer a Signal message from her sister. The employee wrote that she did “not grant it access to other apps.” Another post described a stray note quoting bank balances. ZDNET adds that Muse booked an Airbnb nobody asked for. A Meta Superintelligence team member said the hallucinations were triggered by built-in prompts meant to re-engage users between sessions. He told Fortune the prompts “bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances, security, and safety.” Meta says Muse only accesses data users have given it permission to access. It calls the examples “isolated incidents” and says many were hallucinations that have been fixed. Signal President Meredith Whittaker called deploying agents with this much device access “technologically reckless.” She wants a consistent way for apps to mark themselves off-limits to agents, and for operating systems to enforce it. Signal has also begun restricting screenshots to block agents, but experts note this doesn’t stop an AI agent from reading notifications on Android. Apple recently changed macOS to restrict accessibility tools and add agent-specific permissions. Google said it is considering changes. Meanwhile, major banks , United Airlines , and other companies are blocking or have announced they’ll block AI agents from acting on behalf of their users. The customers most affected by United’s new policy are those who use agentic AI like Meta’s Muse. Since its launch in September, Muse has been downloaded more than 10 million times , becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI. How to stay safe You can limit the exposure, mostly by checking permissions. Granting notification or accessibility access can expose other apps on your device, not just the one you had in mind. So, there are a few things you can check: Audit notification access on Android . Go to Settings > Notifications > Device & app notifications (the path may vary by phone) and switch off notification access for any AI agent. Check Mac permissions. Update macOS first, since Apple has already restricted this route. Then remove AI agents from Accessibility and Screen Recording, and review Full Disk Access. Hide message previews. Turn off notification content for sensitive apps like Signal and your banking apps. Don’t grant access during setup unless you need it. Think through what permissions that app needs. Keep the agent away from money. Don’t link payment methods or banking apps. You should be the one deciding when it’s time to pay. Uninstall AI agents that you don’t trust or that overstep your boundaries. Scammers know more about you than you think. Malwarebytes Mobile Security protects you from phishing, scam texts, malicious sites, and more. In this article
  • Meta’s AI agent, Muse, reportedly flagged a private Signal message an employee said she hadn’t given it access to
  • A Meta team member said built-in prompts to engage users triggered hallucinations
  • Check your AI agent’s permissions, especially whether it can read notifications from other apps

Internal posts reviewed by Reuters describe Meta’s AI agent Muse surfacing private information unprompted, and Reuters’ own tests backed up part of the story.

Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal Meta posts. One employee said Muse reminded her to answer a Signal message from her sister. The employee wrote that she did “not grant it access to other apps.” Another post described a stray note quoting bank balances. ZDNET adds that Muse booked an Airbnb nobody asked for.

A Meta Superintelligence team member said the hallucinations were triggered by built-in prompts meant to re-engage users between sessions. He told Fortune the prompts

“bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances, security, and safety.”

Meta says Muse only accesses data users have given it permission to access. It calls the examples “isolated incidents” and says many were hallucinations that have been fixed.

Signal President Meredith Whittaker called deploying agents with this much device access “technologically reckless.” She wants a consistent way for apps to mark themselves off-limits to agents, and for operating systems to enforce it.

Signal has also begun restricting screenshots to block agents, but experts note this doesn’t stop an AI agent from reading notifications on Android.

Apple recently changed macOS to restrict accessibility tools and add agent-specific permissions. Google said it is considering changes. Meanwhile, major banks, United Airlines, and other companies are blocking or have announced they’ll block AI agents from acting on behalf of their users.

The customers most affected by United’s new policy are those who use agentic AI like Meta’s Muse. Since its launch in September, Muse has been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI.

How to stay safe

You can limit the exposure, mostly by checking permissions. Granting notification or accessibility access can expose other apps on your device, not just the one you had in mind. So, there are a few things you can check:

  • Audit notification access on Android. Go to Settings > Notifications > Device & app notifications (the path may vary by phone) and switch off notification access for any AI agent.
  • Check Mac permissions. Update macOS first, since Apple has already restricted this route. Then remove AI agents from Accessibility and Screen Recording, and review Full Disk Access.
  • Hide message previews. Turn off notification content for sensitive apps like Signal and your banking apps.
  • Don’t grant access during setup unless you need it. Think through what permissions that app needs.
  • Keep the agent away from money. Don’t link payment methods or banking apps. You should be the one deciding when it’s time to pay.
  • Uninstall AI agents that you don’t trust or that overstep your boundaries.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

items.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 Supply Chain Attack: How to Secure AI Gateways Beyond Code Signatures
items.summary: On October 21, 2026, LiteLLM’s official release pipeline built, signed, and published version 1.107.0 from an attacker-controlled lookalike fork. The v1.107.0 source tag on GitHub was clean, and the compromised images carried a valid signature. The maintainers have since published their root cause analysis and moved to keyless signing, so security teams can now check two things: whether a compromised artifact ever ran in their environment, and whether their deployment policies would catch the next one. Which LiteLLM Artifacts Were Affected? All seven litellm==1.107.0 wheels on the Python Package Index (PyPI) were affected, along with the images behind four tags on Docker Hub and GitHub Container Registry (GHCR). Times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on October 21, 2026. Artifact Tags or files Exposure window PyPI wheels All seven litellm==1.107.0 wheels 11:39 to 13:23 GHCR images v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, main-stable for litellm, litellm-database, and litellm-non_root 11:46 to 13:51 Docker Hub images The same four tags 11:46 to 14:20 The source distribution carried a tampered build configuration but not the payload files. Mirrors, caches, and images built on an affected base can extend exposure beyond these windows, so match the digests in the LiteLLM advisory rather than tags. Would You Be Affected If You Never Imported LiteLLM? Possibly, yes. The wheels placed cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py in site-packages, outside the litellm package. Python processes these files at interpreter startup, so any Python launch in an affected environment could run the credential collector, including an unrelated pip install. A separate loader could fetch further code from an attacker-controlled server. The stolen credentials were used quickly. Public research observed Amazon Web Services (AWS) instance-role credentials taken from continuous integration (CI) runners and Kubernetes nodes being validated with sts: GetCallerIdentity and then used to list Amazon Bedrock models later that day. On hosts, LiteLLM’s advisory points to the startup files above and a detached Python process holding /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock. For the attack itself, see the maintainers’ official indicators , including the lookalike Berri-AI organization and the attacker’s Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. A missing artifact does not prove a host is clean. Why Are AI Gateways High-Value Targets? LiteLLM gives applications one interface to many model providers. A self-hosted proxy can hold upstream provider keys, a proxy master key, virtual keys, and database credentials, often alongside a cloud identity that can call managed model services. The same package on a developer laptop or CI runner exposes something different: source-control tokens, registry and deployment access, and sometimes signing material. Where the package ran determines which credentials were at risk. What Should You Do If You Installed Or Ran LiteLLM 1.107.0? Treat the environment as compromised, scope exposure from the artifact that ran, and rotate everything it could reach. Find every copy that ran. Check direct and transitive dependencies, lock files, build logs, CI runners, developer environments, private mirrors, and image caches. A moving tag may resolve to a clean image today while a cluster or downstream image still runs the compromised build. Contain and inspect safely. Isolate affected workloads and preserve filesystem, process, network, and identity evidence. Inspect them from a known-clean system, because running Python or pip inside a suspect environment can trigger the payload again. Follow the credentials. AI gateways concentrate secrets as explained above. From a clean machine, rotate everything the affected process could reach, starting with credentials that can mint tokens or change production. On gateways, that means provider keys, proxy master and virtual keys, and database passwords. For build runners, it means access to source control, the registry, deployment, and signing. Revoke sessions, then review cloud, identity, model-provider, and source-control logs for use after exposure, including GetCallerIdentity calls from workload roles. Rebuild instead of repairing. Removing the package or retagging an image does not count as recovery. Redeploy from a verified release on clean infrastructure, rebuild downstream images, and confirm the digests actually running. Keep watching the exposed identities after the workload is gone. How Did Attackers Use a Leaked Key To Reach LiteLLM’s Release Pipeline? The attackers used a leaked administrative key that was never revoked. In May, a configuration file containing a key for LiteLLM’s internal Agent Platform was committed to a public repository. On October 10, an attacker used it to obtain an organization owner’s GitHub Command-line Interface (CLI) token, then harvested additional maintainer tokens via short-lived workflows. On release day, the owner token overrode branch protection and pointed the staging build at the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm fork. A second stolen token approved production. This incident was separate from the March compromise of versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8. Why Didn’t Image Signing Stop The Attack? A signature proves who signed an artifact, not what source that signer built. The official pipeline signed 1.107.0 exactly as it would sign a legitimate release. Public analysis of the image provenance found that it named LiteLLM’s real release workflow as the builder and the lookalike fork as the source repository. A deployment policy that checked the expected source repository and revision, in addition to the signature, had the evidence it needed to reject this release. LiteLLM rotated its signing key on October 23 and adopted keyless signing from v1.111.0-dev.3 on November 15. Trust the previous key only for images published before 1.107.0. Verify releases from October 24 until keyless signing began with the rotated key, after checking its fingerprint against LiteLLM’s advisory . Verify keyless releases by the certificate identity and the OpenID Connect (OIDC) issuer, not by a key. Pin approved digests and package hashes. Give release identities short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials instead of personal CLI tokens, and require independent approval for changes to the build source. For AI gateways, map each deployment to its owner, model provider accounts, cloud identity, and secrets. Use separate identities per environment and restrict egress, so responders know what to isolate and revoke first. How Qualys TotalAI Helps You Scope AI Supply Chain Exposure Qualys TotalAI brings AI software, workloads, and containers into one inventory built on Qualys sensors and connectors. Responders can use it to move from an advisory to a list of assets that need investigation. Find where AI software runs. The AI Workloads view shows whether AI software is installed, running, or communicating on each host, with binary, arguments, last-seen time, and Qualys Query Language (QQL) search. See inside AI containers. AI Containers adds installed software, Kubernetes metadata, and linked hosts and containers. Trace code to deployment. When QScanner runs in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), Code Assets link repositories to the images built from them. Qualys then correlates those images with container, cloud, and Kubernetes inventory to show where the software is deployed. Prioritize the response. Combine TruRisk scores with what each workload can reach to decide what to isolate and which credentials to rotate first. Start Your 30-Day No-Cost Qualys TotalAI Trial Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) Which LiteLLM version should I run? Run a release other than 1.107.0 that you have verified against LiteLLM’s current signing guidance, and pin it by hash or digest. Does uninstalling LiteLLM remove the malware? No. The startup files sit outside the package directory, and stolen credentials stay valid until they are revoked. Rebuild the environment and rotate credentials. Do images built on LiteLLM need checking? Yes. Any image built on an affected base image or with an affected wheel carries the payload, whatever its own tag says. That includes builds after the exposure window that pulled from a cache or mirror. Check each image’s base digest and installed packages, not its build date. Were LiteLLM Enterprise customers affected? According to the maintainers, customers running the private enterprise release were not affected.

items.summary: TL;DR: AI runtime security in Kubernetes is proven by a prohibited operation being denied and an approved workflow still completing. An audit event showing what would have been blocked cannot establish either outcome under enforcement. Aquasec supports that distinction through local policy enforcement inside running workloads, with Drift Prevention providing a concrete execution boundary to &mldr

items.title: AMSI Memory Patching Refrain
items.summary: Much has been written about the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) over the years in the cyber security industry. From a penetration testing perspective, AMSI is viewed as an impediment that needs to be overcome during offensive operations. Putting this aside for a moment, let’s start with defining exactly what AMSI is first. What is AMSI? AMSI is Microsoft’s signature and behavioral analysis response to in-memory script object and .NET assembly execution threats. AMSI provides object scanning coverage for: PowerShell since version 5.0 VBScript since Windows 10 Jscript since Windows 10 Office 2016+ macros .NET Assemblies version 4.8 and above Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) The architecture of AMSI is divided into two parts: the AMSI client implemented in the amsi.dll file, and the AMSI provider, which is Windows defender providing the signature matching and behavioral analysis components. The AMSI client DLL has two functions that are called upon for scanning objects, AmsiScanString() and AmsiScanBuffer() . Ultimately, the string scanning function ends up just using the AmsiScanBuffer() function anyway, which means that all data flows through the AmsiScanBuffer() function in the DLL when scanning objects. There are two output indications from using this function. The first is the function return value itself, and the second is the result parameter. The buffer scanning function writes into a result parameter buffer one of three values : AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (0x00 hex) meaning no threat detected. AMSI_RESULT_NOT_DETECTED (0x01 hex) again meaning no threat. AMSI_RESULT_DETECTED (0x8000 hex) meaning malware has been detected. The function return value is either going to be S_OK , which is a zero or some HRESULT (refer to MSDN for details) error code. A notable error code that can be returned, which we will address later in this blog is E_INVALIDARG , hexadecimal 0x80070057. How do we know if AMSI is enabled on a system? The easiest test and one that I personally love is to use PowerShell and just test a known evil string in a script or statement. The screenshot below shows my favorite test. There are many possibilities to effectively bypass AMSI functionality , which include: Memory patching Script/object obfuscation PowerShell scripted reflection bypass Downgrade attacks DLL hijacking COM hijacking Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypassing Our focus in this blog is memory patching within the amsi.dll itself. Since the implementation of amsi.dll will change over time, the reader should note that this blog is based on research performed using the Windows installation as detailed in this table. Memory (Machine Code) Patching As already mentioned, the critical path with AMSI is the flow of data through the AmsiScanBuffer() function. What memory patching really represents is direct machine code patching once the amsi.dll is loaded. Using direct Win32 API calls, it is a simple recipe to: Load the amsi.dll Find the address of the AmsiScanBuffer() function Change memory protections to allow writing to some part of the function (Read/Write) Write a machine code patch Change the memory protections back to normal “Read/Execute” Wait just a second though. If we do this, won’t we get caught by defenses? The answer to this question is maybe, because it depends on what defenses are installed on that system. In the context of installed EDR, there are ways you could get caught. EDR might have installed user mode hooks on the use of ntdll.dll functions used to manipulate memory, the most common of which is: NtProtectVirtualMemory() . A very well-known EDR signature is the changing of any virtual memory page protections to Read/Write/Execute (RWX). EDR is probably using Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) provider subscriptions to capture system telemetry. Good EDRs also have a kernel driver component, which is probably subscribed to selected Windows kernel mode notifications. During process creation, it is entirely feasible that EDR defensive solutions are scanning portions of memory pages of certain common DLLs, which may include amsi.dll . There are methods to squelch telemetry feeds for EDRs, which include things like overwriting ntdll.dll hooks and patching ETW telemetry. There are also ways to perform direct or indirect system calls when leveraging ntdll.dll functions for memory protection and writing functions. For the purposes of this blog post, we are just going to focus on the in-memory AMSI patch itself in an x64 Windows architecture context. In the Intel/AMD 64-bit processor , the RAX register is used to contain the return value for any function. When a function returns, it is executing the assembly instruction of “RET”, which is hexadecimal 0xc3. The most obvious machine code patch in this case would be to search for the beginning of the AmsiScanBuffer() function and just write a single byte 0xc3 to that location. This seems very intuitive and might work, but there is one problem. When the function is called, we have no idea what the value of the RAX register is. A likely case is that RAX contains some other random value, and we just don’t know what the behavior will be of the PowerShell or other calling process that used the scan function. Why? Because some uses of amsi.dll might completely ignore the return code and purely focus on the “result” parameter (buffer) and some might take a return value other than the expected/defined codes as a real problem. The coolest thing, however, at this juncture is that we have options! If we are patching at the very beginning of the function, we are in the context of the function prologue, which is focused on setting up the stack for this function variable/memory use, and then usually validating parameters. In other words, there are a lot of machine code opcodes between the start of the function and the subsequent function call into where the real signature or behavioral matching occurs. This implies that all we need to really care about here is the RAX (return code) value itself. Here are some common HRESULT (return values) that we might consider putting into RAX before using our RET instruction. S_OK (0x00000000) : Success S_FALSE (0x00000001) : Success, but no results or data returned E_FAIL (0x80004005) : Unspecified failure E_INVALIDARG (0x80070057) : Invalid parameter or argument passed E_OUTOFMEMORY (0x8007000E) : Out of memory E_ACCESSDENIED (0x80070005) : Access denied / permissions issue E_NOTIMPL (0x80004001) : Not implemented Now we are getting into writing assembler code, albeit relatively simple assembler code. If we are moving any value that is less than 32-bits a register, we also have the option to use different opcodes based on the bit-length of the register, giving us additional variability on opcode use. As we use smaller register opcodes, the arguments become progressively smaller, meaning we reduce the size of the byte patch. The more flexible variations we have to use for a machine code patch, the more likely we will be able to evade a signature match. For example: mov rax, 0 (64-bit register use) 0x48, 0xc7, 0xc0, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00 (7 bytes) mov eax, 0 (32-bit register use) 0xb8, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00 (5 bytes) mov ax, 0 (16-bit register use) 0x66, 0xb8, 0x00, 0x00 (4 bytes) For reference below is a diagram of the x64 processor architecture reminding us of the register layout. The easiest way to launch is to use the Launch Executable option in WinDbg and navigate to the full pathname of the PowerShell exe file as shown here. After launching, you immediately must hit the Go button or type the g command into the debugger so that PowerShell is fully launched and loads all the usual DLL/modules it needs. In the case of the screenshot above, the function is located at address 0x00007ffd85b58160 . Our next job is to attempt a patch by assembling machine code live inside the debugger! Here are the steps: Click into the command box at the bottom and type the command for machine code assembly along with the memory address. And there you have it, your very first machine code patch in a running process! Oh wait, the process is still paused in a break state, let’s just continue it by hitting the Go button or using the g command. Now just test your work and see what happens! Look at the awesome hacking we are doing. PowerShell now does not see the string “invoke-mimikatz” as malicious. That’s fabulous, and thus we have just got our machine code hacker training wheels established. Although we can use quite a lot of variability in the machine opcodes we use for this patch, we are actually doing something that can be detected quite easily by defensive software. The reason is that any memory scanners built into EDR products for example will scan the initial byte sequences of many critical functions (particularly in ntdll.dll and others) to see if any tampering has occurred. The EDR products do this by subscribing to kernel event notifications on process and thread startup. A better and potentially more evasive approach is to look much deeper into the function we are patching, gain an understanding in more depth about how the function works, and create a more sophisticated, light weight, patch. Disassembling the function in WinDbg shows an interesting set of tests and conditional branches just beyond the prologue. In the screenshot below, we can see that after each TEST or CMP instruction (which is a register or memory address comparison), there is a JE instruction, which means “jump if equal to”. We can observe that the destination of the JE instruction happens to be the same memory address in all the six cases, and that there happens to be six parameters to use this function according to MSDN documentation. Looking at the destination of the JE instruction, we can see that the RAX/EAX register receives the value of 0x80070057 using a MOV instruction. You might recall from the table above that this hexadecimal value corresponds to an invalid parameter error. Thus, we can confidently conclude that the sequence of instructions above is validating the correctness of the function parameters. This analysis raises an opportunity for another bypass method. The x64 assembly JMP (short) instruction is a single byte opcode of “0xeb”; therefore, it becomes trivial to replace the JE instruction in one of six locations with a JMP instruction. The logic then becomes an unconditional JMP and the overall function will return a parameter error without writing anything into the result buffer as no actual scanning would have occurred assuming our analysis is correct. As with our prior bypass attempt, we can validate this in WinDbg by taking the very first JE instruction opcode and replacing it with JMP using a direct byte entry command. I followed this exact sequence in the screenshot below. The WinDbg command for replacing bytes in memory happens to be eb so don’t be confused that we entered the eb command with a memory address and then entered eb again to represent a JMP instruction. This just happens to be a coincidence! Repeating a disassembly command confirms that we now have an unconditional jump/branch entered correctly into the function. In order to test, we can get into our PowerShell process and repeat the write-output command with the invoke-mimikatz string. If you want to confirm that the JMP is following the correct logic path, you can use the bp command in WinDbg to set a breakpoint at the 0x00007ffd85b581b0 address, hit the Go button, then use the write-output command and watch the debugging hit the breakpoint. After the breakpoint is hit, you can step through the instructions using the t command one at a time until the function hits its normal RET instruction. If you do this, don’t be surprised when the PowerShell Window freezes as the breakpoint is hit! That’s completely normal. You can hit the Go button again to continue past a breakpoint; it is also possible that the breakpoint gets hit more than one time! For me, it was hit twice after I replaced the JE instruction with JMP and tried the PowerShell command. The screenshot below shows the before and after picture with my PowerShell test. This is a pretty good solution overall. However, there are still more opportunities further down into the AmsiScanBuffer() function that we can consider. Think about either trying to avoid having the actual in depth buffer scanning function run, or alternatively if it does run, consider modifying the results to make things appear benign. If we politely ask our favorite AI assisted search engines what amsi!guard_dispatch_icall$thunk$10345483385596137414 represents, we find out that it is an indirect function call into the Microsoft Control Flow Guard (CFG) mechanism whereby the pointer to the actual function being called is expected to be contained in the RAX register. For the purposes of this research blog, we are going to steer clear of CFG for now but make the assumption that this particular indirect function call is where the actual AMSI buffer scanning is really taking place. Our first task is to confirm this assumption. The most logical way to go about confirming this is to set a breakpoint right at the JMP instruction that follows this call and then examine the registers to see what comes back given both some benign and malicious input. We first need to make sure our earlier patch attempts are not in effect by restarting the debugging session. We can also trace execution right up to the RET instruction and/or set another breakpoint at the RET instruction to examine memory and registers right before the AmsiScanBuffer() function returns. We care about the value of RAX (the return value), and the value of RSP + 0x30 , which is the memory address where the result will be stored. How do we know that the result will be stored in RSP + 0x30 ? The reason is that the function calling conventions for function arguments in the x64 processor and the Microsoft Windows operating system are defined as follows: Argument #1 expected in register RCX Argument #2 expected in register RDX Argument #3 expected in register R8 Argument #4 expected in register R9 Any integer pointer arguments on the stack thereafter typically starting with: RSP + 0x28 RSP + 0x30 The stack is expected to be 16-byte aligned, and the function caller is always expected to provide 32 bytes (0x20 hex) of shadow space for the first four arguments. [ RSP + 00h ] Return address [ RSP + 08h ] Shadow space for RCX [ RSP + 10h ] Shadow space for RDX [ RSP + 18h ] Shadow space for R8 [ RSP + 20h ] Shadow space for R9 [ RSP + 28h ] 5th argument [ RSP + 30h ] 6th argument In the screenshot below, we set a breakpoint right at the RET statement at the end of the function. We also set up a memory view looking at the stack. I use two statements in PowerShell, one to write-output “Hello Joff”, and the other to write-output “invoke-mimikatz”. First, we trigger a malware/malicious response using our usual test string. Then we calculate the position in the stack where we expect the sixth function parameter (the “result”) parameter to be stored. In the screenshot below, the value in the stack is 0x19f3f788 . Why is this not the actual result of the AMSI scan? Because it is a variable, which means it is a pointer to parent/caller stack frame! So now we examine the stack memory of parent/caller stack frame at this address, and we see the actual result of the AMSI scan as 0x8000. This corresponds to the value AMSI_RESULT_DETECTED meaning it is malicious which is exactly what we expected. Then all we do is repeat the same exercise for the benign string of “Hello Joff”, and we get an AMSI result of 0x01, which means AMSI_RESULT_NOT_DETECTED . The stack addresses happen to be the same only because we are in the same debugging session. Looking at the RAX register in both sessions we see a function return value of 0x0 in both cases meaning the scan function itself was successfully executed and returned an S_OK HRESULT value. Wow that was fun! Now we have real questions to answer. Can we find a way between after the real CFG protected AMSI scan function runs and the RET opcode of this function to write 0x0 or 0x1 into that result stack variable in the parent/caller stack frame? Can we do it in a way that does not corrupt other machine code opcodes leaving the function to exit cleanly with proper stack management and alignment? As I was personally approaching these particular questions, I decided that the most obvious target was the JMP instruction that exists right after the CFG AMSI function dispatch call as this function serves only to leap over the MOV instruction which places the invalid function arguments value in RAX . Between these two machine opcodes, we have a total of seven usable bytes. The challenge thus becomes to write a 0x0 value into the correct parent/caller stack frame address using a maximum of seven bytes. We don’t care if we replace these two instructions because a return value of 0x80070057 (invalid function arguments) just does not matter but getting that result value written matters a lot! Let’s just set a break point right at this address of 0x00007ffd85b58205 (the JMP instruction) and then see what the stack and registers look like when we hit this break. After triggering the break point with another PowerShell write-output command, we look at the registers and stack. There are a few observations and an exciting discovery here: Our break point is hit before the stack is realigned for function exit. Stack realignment occurs using the effective address loaded from register r11, which is eventually moved to the stack pointer. The result value from the AMSI scan has already been written to the parent stack frame. The stack frame base pointer (RBP) happens to point at the exact address of the result variable memory in the parent stack frame. The conclusion is that we can write an effective bypass by just writing a zero value to the stack base pointer (RBP) address if we do this in only seven bytes. Let’s go back to our online assembler. The assembly code we need is “MOV QWORD POINTER RBP, 0x0”. Once assembled, we get a resulting byte sequence of eight bytes. Ok, we used a quad word form of the MOV instruction which is a full 64-bit unsigned integer value. However, we are only storing a zero and it does not have to be expressed as a quad word. So, let’s try “MOV DWORD PTR [rbp], 0x0”. Exactly seven bytes! We have a winner! We can move forward with WinDbg and try our proposed solution. We very carefully type in the individual hexadecimal values using the eb function, and then disassemble to confirm afterwards, as seen below. Eureka! We have patched replacing both the JMP and the MOV instruction while not corrupting the stack frame reconstruction for the function to exit properly. Of course, we have to test again with our usual fun testing string. With that achieved, we can now conclude this blog post. In the next blog of this series, I will talk about how to implement these ideas in the C programming language, followed by the same implementation in the Rust programming language.

Much has been written about the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) over the years in the cyber security industry. From a penetration testing perspective, AMSI is viewed as an impediment that needs to be overcome during offensive operations. Putting this aside for a moment, let’s start with defining exactly what AMSI is first.

What is AMSI?

AMSI is Microsoft’s signature and behavioral analysis response to in-memory script object and .NET assembly execution threats. AMSI provides object scanning coverage for:

  • PowerShell since version 5.0
  • VBScript since Windows 10
  • Jscript since Windows 10
  • Office 2016+ macros
  • .NET Assemblies version 4.8 and above
  • Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI)

The architecture of AMSI is divided into two parts: the AMSI client implemented in the amsi.dll file, and the AMSI provider, which is Windows defender providing the signature matching and behavioral analysis components.

The AMSI client DLL has two functions that are called upon for scanning objects, AmsiScanString() and AmsiScanBuffer(). Ultimately, the string scanning function ends up just using the AmsiScanBuffer() function anyway, which means that all data flows through the AmsiScanBuffer() function in the DLL when scanning objects. There are two output indications from using this function. The first is the function return value itself, and the second is the result parameter. The buffer scanning function writes into a result parameter buffer one of three values:

  • AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (0x00 hex) meaning no threat detected.
  • AMSI_RESULT_NOT_DETECTED (0x01 hex) again meaning no threat.
  • AMSI_RESULT_DETECTED (0x8000 hex) meaning malware has been detected.

The function return value is either going to be S_OK, which is a zero or some HRESULT (refer to MSDN for details) error code. A notable error code that can be returned, which we will address later in this blog is E_INVALIDARG, hexadecimal 0x80070057. How do we know if AMSI is enabled on a system? The easiest test and one that I personally love is to use PowerShell and just test a known evil string in a script or statement. The screenshot below shows my favorite test.

There are many possibilities to effectively bypass AMSI functionality, which include:

  • Memory patching
  • Script/object obfuscation
  • PowerShell scripted reflection bypass
  • Downgrade attacks
  • DLL hijacking
  • COM hijacking
  • Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypassing

Our focus in this blog is memory patching within the amsi.dll itself. Since the implementation of amsi.dll will change over time, the reader should note that this blog is based on research performed using the Windows installation as detailed in this table.

Memory (Machine Code) Patching

As already mentioned, the critical path with AMSI is the flow of data through the AmsiScanBuffer() function. What memory patching really represents is direct machine code patching once the amsi.dll is loaded. Using direct Win32 API calls, it is a simple recipe to:

  1. Load the amsi.dll
  2. Find the address of the AmsiScanBuffer() function
  3. Change memory protections to allow writing to some part of the function (Read/Write)
  4. Write a machine code patch
  5. Change the memory protections back to normal “Read/Execute”

Wait just a second though. If we do this, won’t we get caught by defenses? The answer to this question is maybe, because it depends on what defenses are installed on that system. In the context of installed EDR, there are ways you could get caught.

  • EDR might have installed user mode hooks on the use of ntdll.dll functions used to manipulate memory, the most common of which is: NtProtectVirtualMemory(). A very well-known EDR signature is the changing of any virtual memory page protections to Read/Write/Execute (RWX).
  • EDR is probably using Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) provider subscriptions to capture system telemetry.
  • Good EDRs also have a kernel driver component, which is probably subscribed to selected Windows kernel mode notifications.
  • During process creation, it is entirely feasible that EDR defensive solutions are scanning portions of memory pages of certain common DLLs, which may include amsi.dll.

There are methods to squelch telemetry feeds for EDRs, which include things like overwriting ntdll.dll hooks and patching ETW telemetry. There are also ways to perform direct or indirect system calls when leveraging ntdll.dll functions for memory protection and writing functions. For the purposes of this blog post, we are just going to focus on the in-memory AMSI patch itself in an x64 Windows architecture context.

In the Intel/AMD 64-bit processor, the RAX register is used to contain the return value for any function. When a function returns, it is executing the assembly instruction of “RET”, which is hexadecimal 0xc3.

The most obvious machine code patch in this case would be to search for the beginning of the AmsiScanBuffer() function and just write a single byte 0xc3 to that location. This seems very intuitive and might work, but there is one problem.

When the function is called, we have no idea what the value of the RAX register is. A likely case is that RAX contains some other random value, and we just don’t know what the behavior will be of the PowerShell or other calling process that used the scan function. Why? Because some uses of amsi.dll might completely ignore the return code and purely focus on the “result” parameter (buffer) and some might take a return value other than the expected/defined codes as a real problem. The coolest thing, however, at this juncture is that we have options!

If we are patching at the very beginning of the function, we are in the context of the function prologue, which is focused on setting up the stack for this function variable/memory use, and then usually validating parameters. In other words, there are a lot of machine code opcodes between the start of the function and the subsequent function call into where the real signature or behavioral matching occurs. This implies that all we need to really care about here is the RAX (return code) value itself.

Here are some common HRESULT (return values) that we might consider putting into RAX before using our RET instruction.

  • S_OK (0x00000000): Success
  • S_FALSE (0x00000001): Success, but no results or data returned
  • E_FAIL (0x80004005): Unspecified failure
  • E_INVALIDARG (0x80070057): Invalid parameter or argument passed
  • E_OUTOFMEMORY (0x8007000E): Out of memory
  • E_ACCESSDENIED (0x80070005): Access denied / permissions issue
  • E_NOTIMPL (0x80004001): Not implemented

As we use smaller register opcodes, the arguments become progressively smaller, meaning we reduce the size of the byte patch.

The more flexible variations we have to use for a machine code patch, the more likely we will be able to evade a signature match.

For example:

  • mov rax, 0         (64-bit register use)
    • 0x48, 0xc7, 0xc0, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00    (7 bytes)
  • mov eax, 0         (32-bit register use)
    • 0xb8, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00    (5 bytes)
  • mov ax, 0           (16-bit register use)
    • 0x66, 0xb8, 0x00, 0x00    (4 bytes)

For reference below is a diagram of the x64 processor architecture reminding us of the register layout.

After launching, you immediately must hit the Go button or type the g command into the debugger so that PowerShell is fully launched and loads all the usual DLL/modules it needs. After this has occurred, you can use the Break button, which looks like a pause icon to break the running execution. Our first action is to look at the function prologue of the AmsiScanBuffer() function itself. In the case of the screenshot above, the function is located at address 0x00007ffd85b58160. Our next job is to attempt a patch by assembling machine code live inside the debugger!

Here are the steps:

    a 00007ffd`85b58160

  2. When you are in assembly mode in WinDbg, you can type the assembly code one line at a time, and then just hit enter a second time to exit from assembly mode.

    Input> mov eax, 0   
    Input> ret

  2. Can we do it in a way that does not corrupt other machine code opcodes leaving the function to exit cleanly with proper stack management and alignment?

As I was personally approaching these particular questions, I decided that the most obvious target was the JMP instruction that exists right after the CFG AMSI function dispatch call as this function serves only to leap over the MOV instruction which places the invalid function arguments value in RAX. Between these two machine opcodes, we have a total of seven usable bytes.

The challenge thus becomes to write a 0x0 value into the correct parent/caller stack frame address using a maximum of seven bytes. We don’t care if we replace these two instructions because a return value of 0x80070057 (invalid function arguments) just does not matter but getting that result value written matters a lot!

Let’s just set a break point right at this address of 0x00007ffd85b58205 (the JMP instruction) and then see what the stack and registers look like when we hit this break. After triggering the break point with another PowerShell write-output command, we look at the registers and stack.

There are a few observations and an exciting discovery here:

  1. Our break point is hit before the stack is realigned for function exit.
  2. Stack realignment occurs using the effective address loaded from register r11, which is eventually moved to the stack pointer.
  3. The result value from the AMSI scan has already been written to the parent stack frame.
  4. The stack frame base pointer (RBP) happens to point at the exact address of the result variable memory in the parent stack frame.


The conclusion is that we can write an effective bypass by just writing a zero value to the stack base pointer (RBP) address if we do this in only seven bytes. Let’s go back to our online assembler.

The assembly code we need is “MOV QWORD POINTER RBP, 0x0”. Once assembled, we get a resulting byte sequence of eight bytes.

Ok, we used a quad word form of the MOV instruction which is a full 64-bit unsigned integer value. However, we are only storing a zero and it does not have to be expressed as a quad word. So, let’s try “MOV DWORD PTR [rbp], 0x0”.


Exactly seven bytes! We have a winner! We can move forward with WinDbg and try our proposed solution. We very carefully type in the individual hexadecimal values using the eb function, and then disassemble to confirm afterwards, as seen below.

Eureka! We have patched replacing both the JMP and the MOV instruction while not corrupting the stack frame reconstruction for the function to exit properly. Of course, we have to test again with our usual fun testing string.

With that achieved, we can now conclude this blog post. In the next blog of this series, I will talk about how to implement these ideas in the C programming language, followed by the same implementation in the Rust programming language.

items.title: Jensen Huang Returns as NVIDIA CEO Following Unanimous Board Vote
items.summary: NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer, and board director on November 23, 2026, after a unanimous vote. The decision took effect immediately, but an independent board inquiry into reports that a foreign intelligence effort targeted Huang remains open. In its announcement, NVIDIA said the board met with Huang several times and received input from senior U.S. government officials before deciding that his return posed no national security risk. That was the board’s judgment about reinstatement, not a finding that closed the inquiry. Harvey C. Jones will remain board chair. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO after Huang stepped down, will continue as chief financial officer. The vote reversed the board’s position from its November 17 earnings call, when Jones said it did not intend to reinstate Huang. NVIDIA said Huang supports the independent investigation and has committed to cooperating. NVIDIA Reinstates Jensen Huang As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the original NVIDIA investigation , the board announced the inquiry on November 8 after reports that Huang had been targeted. A committee made up solely of independent directors is leading the review with help from outside lawyers. At the time, the board said it had no reason to believe NVIDIA secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. The reinstatement announcement did not publish findings or give a date for completing the review. The public record does not establish that anyone obtained company information, and the board’s decision to restore Huang to his roles does not settle that question. The board inquiry is separate from a U.S. investigation involving Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that authorities are examining over possible diversion of restricted NVIDIA chips to China. NBC News reported that the Commerce Department opened its investigation in 2024 and that the Justice Department later took the lead in the criminal probe. The Associated Press also reported on a related policy concern: companies can use advanced chips remotely through overseas data centers without taking physical delivery of the hardware. That difference matters in shared AI infrastructure. Knowing where a server is installed does not necessarily tell a provider who is using its computing power. Cyber Security News’ AI data center security checklist covers a separate part of that challenge: securing GPUs, firmware, and the hardware supply chain. Those controls address risks inside the data center, while export compliance addresses who can receive or use restricted technology. NVIDIA has formed a separate National Security and Export Control Committee, staffed only by independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is bringing in lawyers with national security experience, who will retain specialist advisers. NVIDIA is also starting a search for a chief compliance officer who will oversee compliance across the company and report to the board’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA says it will continue cooperating with government investigations and inquiries. Huang’s return settles who runs the company, but the independent directors have yet to report what their review found. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. items.title: Who Does AI Listen To?
items.summary: In a video series from Radio Free Asia, Citizen Lab’s Emile Dirks and Mohamed Ahmed speak about the biases and misjudgments inherent in AI tools. Dirks notes that AI can make mistakes, and using it for predictive policing could put people at risk of being falsely accused of crimes. Ahmed discusses how training data can reinforce biases, which can cause tools to make mistakes. He says that AI tools “aren’t objective arbiters of truth,” and should be subject to fact-checking rather than being taken at face value. Watch Emile’s interview here Watch Mohamed’s interview here

items.summary: Key Takeaways AWS Zero Trust requires continuous monitoring because security risks can change even after access has been authorized. Monitoring unusual identity behavior, API requests, and resource access helps detect compromised credentials and suspicious activity. Continuous cloud posture assessment helps identify misconfigurations, vulnerabilities, excessive permissions, and configuration drift. Correlating endpoint, network, and cloud activity helps security teams investigate suspicious connections, potential lateral movement, and emerging threats. Fidelis Elevate ® and Fidelis CloudPassage Halo ® complement AWS security controls by providing broader visibility into network, endpoint, cloud, and workload security. Organizations implementing Zero Trust in AWS often rely on AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), least-privilege policies, and identity verification to control access to cloud resources. However, security risks do not disappear once access is granted. A compromised IAM role could be misused to access Amazon S3 data, an Amazon EC2 instance could develop vulnerabilities, or an authorized workload could begin communicating with suspicious destinations. This is why AWS Zero Trust requires visibility beyond initial authorization. Although the role has legitimate permissions, attackers who compromise the instance could misuse those permissions to access sensitive data. AWS CloudTrail automatically records management events, including IAM role changes, EC2 security group modifications, and console sign-ins, with 90 days of event history available by default. However, S3 object-level activities, such as GetObject and PutObject, are not logged by default and require data event logging to be explicitly configured through a CloudTrail trail or event data store. Amazon GuardDuty, once enabled, analyzes CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS activity to detect potential threats, such as unusual API calls, compromised credentials, and communication with malicious IP addresses. Additional protection features, such as S3 Protection and Runtime Monitoring, provide further threat detection capabilities when enabled. Combining AWS IAM with continuous cloud posture assessment and threat detection helps security teams identify unusual user behavior, resource configuration changes, and unexpected network activity that may indicate a potential compromise. Here, visibility is even more important as security teams must understand what is happening and what risks exist across identities, endpoints, workloads, and networks after access has been granted. For government agencies, continuous monitoring is essential for supporting federal Zero Trust initiatives, maintaining audit readiness, and identifying security risks across cloud environments. However, organizations also need continuous visibility and security monitoring across their environments. The security context of an authorized session can change when user behavior shifts, workloads or configurations change; new vulnerabilities appear, or credentials are compromised. Organizations must monitor what happens after access is granted, not just whether access was authorized. This includes correlating identity activity to cloud posture, endpoint activity, network activity, asset relationships, and ever-changing risk. AWS security controls, complemented by solutions such as Fidelis Elevate ® and Fidelis CloudPassage Halo ® , can help organizations strengthen their Zero Trust architecture through improved security visibility and contextual threat detection. One useful exercise for organizations that are assessing their current AWS Zero Trust strategy is to trace the access path through their system and identify where they lose track of the access path after the user has been authenticated. Any place where teams are not sure what happened, what the resource is doing and/or whether risks have increased is a potential “visibility gap” that must be addressed. Frequently Asked Questions Does AWS Zero Trust stop threats after access is granted? Not by itself. AWS Zero Trust controls help enforce identity-based and context-aware access decisions, but organizations also need continuous monitoring and threat detection to identify suspicious activity after authorization. How often should organizations review AWS Zero Trust security risks? Organizations should continuously monitor security events and assess cloud configurations whenever changes occur. AWS services such as CloudTrail, GuardDuty, and AWS Config can help teams track activity and identify potential threats. Periodic reviews of IAM permissions, workload vulnerabilities, and security policies can help address risks that automated monitoring may miss. Can a compromised AWS account bypass Zero Trust controls? A compromised account may continue to authenticate successfully because the attacker is using valid credentials. Monitoring identity behavior, resource access, network activity, and other context can help identify activity that differs from expected behavior. How does cloud posture affect Zero Trust? Zero Trust depends on the security condition of the resources being accessed. Misconfigurations, vulnerabilities, excessive permissions, and configuration drift can create risk even when access controls are correctly implemented. Continuous cloud posture assessment helps identify these conditions. How can organizations close visibility gaps in AWS Zero Trust? Organizations can combine identity and access controls with continuous visibility across cloud workloads, endpoints, networks, and user activity. Fidelis Elevate® and Fidelis CloudPassage Halo® can complement AWS controls by providing additional security context across these areas.

Compromised credentials can look legitimate

Attackers do not necessarily have to circumvent authentication. They can gain access to AWS resources using valid credentials. From an access-control perspective, the request may appear valid. From a threat-detection perspective, however, the subsequent activity may be abnormal.

For example, a compromised AWS identity could:

  • Assume an unfamiliar IAM role using AWS Security Token Service (STS).
  • Make unusual AWS API requests, such as creating new access keys or attaching policies that grant additional permissions.

Cloud configurations can change after authorization

AWS environments are constantly changing. Teams launch new workloads, change permissions, update applications, and add temporary resources. A workload that met security requirements at deployment may not meet them later.

Configuration drift in AWS can introduce:

  • Excessive permissions in AWS IAM policies.
  • Publicly accessible Amazon S3 buckets.
  • EC2 security groups with unnecessarily broad inbound access.
  • Vulnerable software running on EC2 instances.
  • Insecure Amazon EKS workload configurations.

A valid identity does not necessarily mean the device associated with that identity remains secure. An approved endpoint might be compromised after being authenticated. Continuous visibility in AWS requires connecting identity activity with resource configurations, workload security, and network communications. Does AWS Zero Trust stop threats after access is granted?

Not by itself. AWS Zero Trust controls help enforce identity-based and context-aware access decisions, but organizations also need continuous monitoring and threat detection to identify suspicious activity after authorization.

How often should organizations review AWS Zero Trust security risks?

Organizations should continuously monitor security events and assess cloud configurations whenever changes occur. AWS services such as CloudTrail, GuardDuty, and AWS Config can help teams track activity and identify potential threats. Periodic reviews of IAM permissions, workload vulnerabilities, and security policies can help address risks that automated monitoring may miss.

Can a compromised AWS account bypass Zero Trust controls?

A compromised account may continue to authenticate successfully because the attacker is using valid credentials. Monitoring identity behavior, resource access, network activity, and other context can help identify activity that differs from expected behavior.

How does cloud posture affect Zero Trust?

Zero Trust depends on the security condition of the resources being accessed. Misconfigurations, vulnerabilities, excessive permissions, and configuration drift can create risk even when access controls are correctly implemented. Continuous cloud posture assessment helps identify these conditions.

How can organizations close visibility gaps in AWS Zero Trust?

Organizations can combine identity and access controls with continuous visibility across cloud workloads, endpoints, networks, and user activity. Fidelis Elevate® and Fidelis CloudPassage Halo® can complement AWS controls by providing additional security context across these areas.

items.title: European Commission Disables Access to EU Academy After Cyberattack Exposes User Data
items.summary: The European Commission disabled public access to EU Academy on Monday, November 23, after confirming that a wider cyberattack exposed users’ personal data. The online learning platform hosts courses and workshops produced by EU institutions. The Commission posted a notice on the academy’s website, but it did not say how many users were affected or when they could access their courses again . Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that the academy was affected by the same cyber campaign the Commission disclosed the previous week. The exposed information includes names and email addresses, according to the Associated Press. EU Academy is the first service in the wider incident for which the Commission has publicly confirmed a leak of users’ personal data. It has not said whether passwords were exposed. EU Academy Cyberattack Data Breach At its November 19 press briefing , the Commission said it had taken several applications offline as a precaution and had restored most of them. The Commission detected the campaign on October 22 and confirmed the incident on October 26 after an initial investigation. As Cyber Security News reported in its earlier coverage of the European Commission cyberattack , the disruption affected staff tools used for timesheets and medical reimbursements. Those outages do not establish that attackers accessed the records those tools handle. The Commission confirmed that the campaign used an AI-assisted tool. It has not publicly explained how the attackers first gained access or what role the tool played in the EU Academy data breach. The distinction matters because identifying a tool used in a campaign does not establish how attackers reached a particular service. Euronews reported that officials suspect a China-backed hacking group and that the wider attack had not been fully contained by Monday. The report cited people familiar with the investigation. The Commission has not publicly named the group, so the suspected link to China is not a confirmed finding. Taking EU Academy offline also does not mean the wider incident is over. The Commission warned EU Academy users to be cautious about unexpected emails or messages and not to share personal information in response. Users who receive a message about a course, account access, or the breach should open the academy’s website directly instead of following a link in the message. A notice that knows a user’s name or email address is not proof that it came from the Commission. As Cyber Security News noted in its coverage of the Vimeo data breach , exposed email addresses can help scammers make phishing messages look more credible. In the EU Academy case, a fake message could claim that learners need to verify their accounts or sign in through a temporary page to regain access to a course. That is a risk to watch for, not a report that such messages have already been sent. The Commission has yet to disclose how many users are affected, whether the leak included other types of data, or when public access will return. For learners waiting to resume a course, the official academy website remains the place to check for updates. Until the Commission provides more detail, the confirmed exposure of names and email addresses should not be read as confirmation that login details were also taken. items.title: Hackers Hide RevStealer Malware in Fake Claude AI App to Steal Passwords and Crypto Wallets
items.summary: Hackers are distributing RevStealer, a Windows infostealer, in a fake Claude AI desktop app that promises free access. The download, branded “Claude Opus 5 Free Desktop,” comes in an archive of roughly 101 MB. Running the executable does not open a chat window. Instead, it starts malware designed to steal saved passwords, browser sessions, cryptocurrency wallet data, and other information stored on the computer. The operators distributed the package through GitHub repositories and sites themed around game cheats. Those channels give the download two ways to reach people: as a supposed shortcut to paid AI features or as another unofficial tool offered for free. A separate fake Claude download campaign used the same brand to lure users, but it was not the RevStealer operation. Cyberint researchers noted that RevStealer was first observed in September 2026 and described the campaign in an October 18 report. They did not attribute it to a named threat actor. The findings describe attackers impersonating Anthropic’s software, not a breach of Claude or evidence that Anthropic’s official installer was compromised. Hackers Hide RevStealer Malware in Fake Claude AI App The counterfeit app is built with Electron, a framework used by legitimate desktop software. On launch, its loader checks the computer’s memory, processor, hostname, and graphics hardware before unpacking an encrypted component. It places that component in a randomly named folder under Windows AppData and starts it in the background. Since the executable has no visible interface, a user could mistake the lack of a window for a failed launch. RevStealer also checks for signs that it is running inside a security researcher’s test environment and attempts to make Microsoft Defender skip scanning AppData. That change is useful evidence for responders, especially when it appears alongside a suspicious download and an unexpected process running from a user folder. A separate counterfeit Claude desktop campaign also targeted Defender, but delivered remote-access malware rather than RevStealer. The stealer collects browser databases and encryption keys, session cookies, Windows Credential Manager entries, password-manager artifacts, and data from cryptocurrency wallets. It also targets VPN and remote-access credentials, messaging and gaming apps, clipboard contents, screenshots, and selected documents. For businesses, that mix matters: a single infected workstation can expose both a user’s personal accounts and credentials used to reach company systems. For wallet holders, the risk depends on what sensitive wallet material was stored on the device. Stolen cookies pose a different problem from stolen passwords. An active session cookie can let someone reuse a login the victim has already completed without facing a fresh multifactor authentication prompt. Earlier reporting on stolen AI session tokens shows why changing a password is not always enough: some credentials may stay valid until the service revokes them. Cyberint reported that RevStealer sends stolen data in encrypted records and can obtain a replacement server address through a Polygon smart contract if needed. The malware then deletes itself rather than relying on continued execution to complete the theft. That means responders may find little left on disk even when endpoint alerts, network logs, or account activity point to a compromise. Cyberint also noted that the malware’s tasking channel can deliver additional components. If the fake app was run, isolate the computer and use a clean device to revoke active sessions and change exposed passwords. Organizations should review recent identity and VPN activity, check for unauthorized Defender exclusions, and preserve endpoint and network logs. If a wallet’s private key or recovery phrase may have been exposed, move funds to a new wallet created on a clean device. For new installations, use Anthropic’s official download page rather than a third-party archive. items.title: Vmcloudoor Malware Could Let Hackers Secretly Control Linux Cloud Servers and Steal Sensitive Files
items.summary: A newly found Linux backdoor named Vmcloudoor can quietly take over cloud servers and pull files off them. It is built to infect virtual machines on Chinese cloud platforms, mainly Alibaba Cloud. It also targets Tencent Cloud and Huawei Cloud. The malware pretends to be a normal cloud management agent, so administrators are less likely to notice it or shut it down. Linux backdoors that hide in plain sight are not new, as the Auto-Color Linux backdoor showed earlier. Vmcloudoor takes the idea further by copying the names and folders of trusted cloud tools. Researchers at Exatrack found the implant during a threat hunting session and described it as a very precise tool made to hide itself. They only recovered the “helper” module. Even so, it shows the main features of the backdoor. A second module called “Core” exists and is meant to run commands received from the attacker. Vmcloudoor Malware Could Let Hackers Secretly Control Linux Cloud Servers When Vmcloudoor starts, it checks which cloud it is running on. It looks for known folders and running processes tied to Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei agents. Based on the result, it picks a matching disguise. On Alibaba it uses the name AliyunSysAssist, on Tencent it uses YunJingSysAssist, and on Huawei it uses UniAgentSys. If it finds none of these, it hides in /dev/shm/.ov2/ and calls itself kworker/0:2H, which looks like a normal Linux kernel worker. It then renames its own process to match, so it looks like part of the cloud setup. The command channel is also unusual. Instead of calling a server run by the attacker, the malware checks an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket for tasks meant for that one machine. It builds a web address from a machine fingerprint and a five-minute time window. By default the file does not exist, so the server answers with a 404 error. When the attacker wants to act, they place a task file there and the server answers with a 200 response. Because the traffic goes to a public cloud service, it is easy to mistake for normal activity and hard to block. Similar blending tricks have been seen in BPFDoor attacks on telecom networks , where malware copied trusted server processes. Each task has a type number. Type 1 runs a command, type 2 pushes a file onto the machine, and type 3 uploads a file from the machine to an address chosen by the attacker. Type 9 collects a machine inventory, including the hostname, user name, operating system, kernel version, processor type and memory. File transfers must use a full path and stay under 100 MB. The malware also looks for security tools. It checks for products such as CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Sophos and Elkeid, and it labels the machine as clean, antivirus-protected or EDR-protected. It then suggests longer waiting times between check-ins on better-protected machines. If the storage bucket is closed, the malware fetches a new one from a Gitee repository. The malware never checks HTTPS certificates. Git Mistakes Reveal Clues About the Developer The attacker made some careless errors. The Gitee repository, named “plus”, was created by a throwaway account called test9527. Its commit history shows three different author identities. One is hpgoc2-deploy with the email deploy@hpgoc2.local, which hints at an internal project name. Another is thor8848, tied to a GitHub account created in 2020 that appears to belong to a Chinese user working in penetration testing. A later commit also records a switch from the bucket top-sec to assist-logs. Exatrack believes this was a slip in operational security, not a deliberate false trail. The researchers suspect the author may be a Chinese pentester, possibly running red team work, though they admit this is only an assumption. The commit data alone does not prove who operated the backdoor or whether it was used with permission. Reports also say it is still unclear how the malware first lands on a server or how many systems it has reached. Exatrack also found a newer version that shares 88 percent of its code with the first one. The changes mostly affect check-in cycles and timeout values, which suggests the tool is still being improved. Since the backdoor can run commands and move files, defenders should treat it like any other cloud credential threat, such as the Telnyx SDK credential theft case, and rotate keys if a host looks infected. Teams can also watch for unknown processes in /dev/shm, fake cloud agent names, and unexpected traffic to Alibaba storage endpoints. The newer BPFDoor variants with stateless C2 are a reminder that Linux backdoors keep changing how they hide. Since the backdoor can run commands and move files, defenders should treat it like any other cloud credential threat, such as the Telnyx SDK credential theft case, and rotate keys if a host looks infected.

Teams can also watch for unknown processes in /dev/shm, fake cloud agent names, and unexpected traffic to Alibaba storage endpoints. The newer BPFDoor variants with stateless C2 are a reminder that Linux backdoors keep changing how they hide.
