items.title: Probing DNS at Cloudflare
items.summary: Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken. This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed. DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production. For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back. A little background At Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected. We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS. What is Flamingo? Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service. Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments. Being delightful When we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity. One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format. For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart. TEST test-redirect SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com GET "http://$(hostname)/" ASSERT STATUS IS 301 ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/" Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world. Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action . Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome. In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner: pub enum Action { Query { method: String, url: Expression, parameters: Vec , }, DnsQuery { query_name: Expression, query_type: Expression, parameters: Vec , }, } pub enum ActionOutput { Http(http::FetchResponse), Dns(dns::QueryResponse), } pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc< dyn Fn( Action, Arc , InterpreterConfig, ) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result > + Send + Sync + 'static, >; pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc< dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction + Send + Sync + 'static, >; What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic. pub async fn query( action: Action, ctx: Arc , cfg: InterpreterConfig, ) -> Result { let Action::Query { method, url, parameters, } = action else { bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}"); }; ... } pub async fn execute_module ( ctx: Arc , cfg: &InterpreterConfig, handler_lut: F, ) -> Result where F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction), { let func = handler_lut(action); let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?; ... } Using Flamingo to probe DNS The adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS . Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures. DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover. We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked. To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver). TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62 MOD dns SET $hostname "some.probe.domain" SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com QUERY $hostname TXT TARGET $authNs ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS[0] GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90") Catching bugs (SLO and steady) To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system. By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly. Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately. Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back. The road ahead By moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet. DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch. If this kind of reliability engineering interests you, check out our careers page for open roles.

Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken.

This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed.

DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production.

For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back.

A little background

At Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected.

We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS.

What is Flamingo?

Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service.

Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments.

Being delightful

When we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity.

One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format.

For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart.

TEST test-redirect
SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com

GET "http://$(hostname)/"

ASSERT STATUS IS 301
ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/"

Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world.

Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action. Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome.

In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner:

pub enum Action {
  Query {
    method: String,
    url: Expression,
    parameters: Vec,
  },
  DnsQuery {
    query_name: Expression,
    query_type: Expression,
    parameters: Vec,
  },
}

pub enum ActionOutput {
  Http(http::FetchResponse),
  Dns(dns::QueryResponse),
}

pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc<
  dyn Fn(
      Action,
      Arc,
      InterpreterConfig,
    )
      -> BoxFuture<'static, Result>
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;

pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc<
  dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;

What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic.

pub async fn query(
  action: Action,
  ctx: Arc,
  cfg: InterpreterConfig,
) -> Result {
  let Action::Query {
    method,
    url,
    parameters,
  } = action
  else {
    bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}");
  };
  ...
}

pub async fn execute_module(
  ctx: Arc,
  cfg: &InterpreterConfig,
  handler_lut: F,
) -> Result
where
  F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction),
{
  let func = handler_lut(action);
  let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?;
  ...
}
Using Flamingo to probe DNS

The adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS. Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures.

DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover.

We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked.

To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver).

TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62
MOD dns

SET $hostname "some.probe.domain"
SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com

QUERY $hostname TXT
TARGET $authNs

ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR
ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA
ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS[0] GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90")
Catching bugs (SLO and steady)

To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system.

By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly.

Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately.

Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back.

The road ahead

By moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet.

DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch.

items.title: How we cleared our backlog with SonarQube Remediation Agent
items.summary: Every engineering team has a backlog of known issues, and most have carried it for years. Fixing it has always meant a tradeoff: time spent on old issues is time not spent on new work, and the fixes usually lose. You no longer have to accept that tradeoff, and the timing matters. AI is making it easier to find and exploit weaknesses in code, which makes a backlog of known issues a bigger risk than it used to be. Teams need a zero-tolerance approach to the issues they already know about. Guided reasoning agents make that possible, because they don’t just write fixes. They verify them. Here’s how that worked when we pointed two agents at our own backlog. In two weeks, SonarQube Remediation Agent and Gitar , Sonar’s code review agent, helped us fix 2,447 issues across three core repositories at Sonar. Every fix was verified with SonarQube analysis before a pull request (PR) was opened. Of the PRs that merged, 64% went through without human intervention, under approval rules our engineers set in advance. Before we turned on automatic merging, we tested Gitar’s judgment in one repository. Engineers merged every PR Gitar approved and closed a couple it flagged for human review. That gave the team the confidence to let low-risk fixes merge on their own. None of the auto-merged PRs has been reverted. Below, we walk through how each fix gets verified, how we built confidence in automatic merging, and how you can start with one repository. The setup: one agent writes, the other reviews Our workflow is built around SonarQube Remediation Agent and Gitar. Remediation Agent groups backlog issues by the kind of fix they need. If the same issue appears in several files, the agent can fix those occurrences together in one PR. Unrelated fixes go in separate PRs, so each PR contains one kind of change. A PR changes either test code or production code, never both. We set Remediation Agent internally to run once an hour in each repository and open at most one PR per run. Each team also sets a limit on how many agent PRs can be open at once. Once a team reaches its limit, the agent waits until an existing PR is merged or closed. That keeps teams from being flooded with PRs and gives them time to investigate if something goes wrong. Fix, verify, fix again Why not just ask a coding assistant to fix the backlog? It can write a fix. The hard part is proving the fix is right: that it clears the issue, doesn’t create new ones, keeps the build and tests passing, and holds up under review. Without that proof, an engineer still has to check every change by hand, and that’s the work that kept the backlog growing. Our workflow checks each fix at every step and sends it back for another round when it falls short. Verification starts before a PR exists. Remediation Agent applies each fix in a sandbox and verifies it with SonarQube analysis. It rejects any fix that doesn’t clear the issue or that adds new ones. That gives every fix two independent checks before it can merge: SonarQube confirms the issue is gone and no new ones were added, and Gitar judges whether the change is safe in the context of the code around it. Remediation Agent then opens a PR and starts monitoring its CI checks. If a check fails, the agent reads its output. If the code needs a change, the agent can make it and run the checks again. If the failure points to a flaky test or an infrastructure problem, it can retry the job without changing the code. The PR is ready only when the build, automated tests and all other required CI checks pass. Once the checks pass, Gitar reviews the changes. Gitar can approve the PR, ask for a revision, or leave the decision to an engineer. If Gitar asks for a revision, Remediation Agent updates the code and replies on the PR. Gitar then reviews the new version and the process repeats. No engineer has to steer that exchange, and the agent that writes the code never approves its own work. By the time a fix reaches the merge step, it has cleared SonarQube analysis, every required CI check, and an independent review. If a later commit changes the PR, the checks run again. Remediation Agent writes the fix. SonarQube verifies it, and Gitar reviews it. Even with Gitar’s approval, the PR stays open until every required check passes and every review thread is resolved. An engineer reviews medium- and high-risk changes. How we put PR approval and merge in the agents’ hands We let Gitar approve changes based on the risk of the fix, not the severity of the issue it addresses. To assess that risk, Gitar looks at how the changed code is used and whether the fix could alter behavior elsewhere. We wrote approval criteria so that only PRs opened by Remediation Agent qualify. Gitar reviews the latest version of the PR, including any revisions it requested: Low risk : Gitar can approve the PR without asking an engineer to review it. Medium or high risk : an engineer decides whether to approve it. Teams can keep merging PRs themselves after Gitar approves them. We chose to let the agents merge eligible PRs automatically. But approval alone isn't enough. Our branch protection rules still require the build, unit tests, integration tests, and every other required CI/CD check to pass, and every review thread to be resolved. The conditions are checked again on every push: if a new commit raises the risk, the earlier approval no longer counts. Our criteria also stop Gitar from approving changes to GitHub Actions workflows or build scripts, even if it rates the PR as low risk. The agents can work on the code, but they can't approve changes that weaken or bypass the checks that code has to pass. Here’s how that played out on one PR. Remediation Agent refactored three methods to fix three critical cognitive-complexity issues. Gitar rated the change low risk and merged it 35 minutes after it was opened, with no engineer involved. Remediation Agent refactored three methods to fix three critical cognitive-complexity issues. SonarQube analysis confirmed all three issues were gone, Gitar rated the change low risk and merged it 35 minutes after it was opened, with no engineer involved. Building confidence in autonomous merges Before asking engineers to allow the agents to merge on their own, we made sure the PRs were easy to review. Remediation Agent handled CI failures and addressed Gitar’s feedback before handing a PR to an engineer. By then, the checks were green and the engineer could read Gitar’s review alongside the diff. Because each PR contained one kind of change, the engineer could understand the fix once, then scan for a place where it didn’t fit. Only 4% of the agent’s PRs that reached a decision were closed without being merged. Easy reviews were only the first step. Engineers don’t hand merge decisions to an agent because someone asks them to. They do it once they’ve seen the agent make the same call they would make. So we built confidence in stages and let the results decide when to move to the next one: Engineers approve and merge. Remediation Agent fixes and SonarQube verifies. People make every decision. Gitar approves, engineers merge. Gitar approves low-risk PRs, and engineers compare its judgment with their own before they merge. Gitar approves, the PR merges automatically. Low-risk PRs merge once every required check passes. Medium- and high-risk PRs still go to an engineer. Teams can stay at any stage for as long as they need. We ran the second stage first in one repository, the same way we suggest you start. Gitar automatically approved low-risk PRs, but engineers still decided whether to merge. They compared Gitar’s judgment with their own and merged every PR it had approved. They also closed a couple of the PRs Gitar flagged for human review. Every time Gitar approved a PR, the engineers agreed. After that dry run, the team turned on automatic merging for eligible PRs. None of the PRs that merged automatically has been reverted. PRs that engineers merged stayed open for a median of about 42 hours. Almost all of that time was spent waiting for someone to pick them up. For PRs that Gitar merged, the median time from open to merge was 30 minutes. Across the three repositories, 64% of merged PRs went through automatically without human involvement, and engineers merged another 32% that Gitar had approved as low risk. Issues fixed by the agents over two weeks. What stands out is the difference in how quickly the backlog came down once automatic merging was switched on. What slowed us down Some PRs still needed an engineer’s attention. One reason was a CI failure unrelated to the fix. The agent could rerun a flaky test. It couldn’t fix an integration test that another change in the repository had broken. That code was outside its task, so the PR stayed open until an engineer could investigate. Other PRs had green CI and Gitar’s approval but still needed reviews from several teams because they touched code with different owners. We’ve since changed how the agent groups fixes: files with different code owners now go into separate PRs. Each team can review and merge fixes to its own code without waiting for another team’s approval. What’s next for us Next, we’re extending this to higher-risk changes. We’re testing how much of that work the agents can do before asking for approval, and what evidence would justify automatic merging for some of those changes. What you can try today You can set up a similar workflow today with SonarQube Remediation Agent and Gitar. You'll need a Remediation Agent subscription on SonarQube Cloud or SonarQube Server 2026.5, plus a Gitar Pro or Enterprise plan for auto-approve and auto-merge. items.summary_html:
Every engineering team has a backlog of known issues, and most have carried it for years. Fixing it has always meant a tradeoff: time spent on old issues is time not spent on new work, and the fixes usually lose.

You no longer have to accept that tradeoff, and the timing matters. AI is making it easier to find and exploit weaknesses in code, which makes a backlog of known issues a bigger risk than it used to be. Teams need a zero-tolerance approach to the issues they already know about. Guided reasoning agents make that possible, because they don’t just write fixes. They verify them.

Here’s how that worked when we pointed two agents at our own backlog.

In two weeks, SonarQube Remediation Agent and Gitar, Sonar’s code review agent, helped us fix 2,447 issues across three core repositories at Sonar. Every fix was verified with SonarQube analysis before a pull request (PR) was opened. Of the PRs that merged, 64% went through without human intervention, under approval rules our engineers set in advance. Before we turned on automatic merging, we tested Gitar’s judgment in one repository. Engineers merged every PR Gitar approved and closed a couple it flagged for human review. That gave the team the confidence to let low-risk fixes merge on their own. None of the auto-merged PRs has been reverted.

Below, we walk through how each fix gets verified, how we built confidence in automatic merging, and how you can start with one repository.

The setup: one agent writes, the other reviews

Our workflow is built around SonarQube Remediation Agent and Gitar. Remediation Agent groups backlog issues by the kind of fix they need. If the same issue appears in several files, the agent can fix those occurrences together in one PR. Unrelated fixes go in separate PRs, so each PR contains one kind of change. A PR changes either test code or production code, never both. 

We set Remediation Agent internally to run once an hour in each repository and open at most one PR per run. Each team also sets a limit on how many agent PRs can be open at once. Once a team reaches its limit, the agent waits until an existing PR is merged or closed. That keeps teams from being flooded with PRs and gives them time to investigate if something goes wrong.

Fix, verify, fix again

Why not just ask a coding assistant to fix the backlog? It can write a fix. The hard part is proving the fix is right: that it clears the issue, doesn’t create new ones, keeps the build and tests passing, and holds up under review. Without that proof, an engineer still has to check every change by hand, and that’s the work that kept the backlog growing. Our workflow checks each fix at every step and sends it back for another round when it falls short.

Verification starts before a PR exists. Remediation Agent applies each fix in a sandbox and verifies it with SonarQube analysis. It rejects any fix that doesn’t clear the issue or that adds new ones. That gives every fix two independent checks before it can merge: SonarQube confirms the issue is gone and no new ones were added, and Gitar judges whether the change is safe in the context of the code around it.

Remediation Agent then opens a PR and starts monitoring its CI checks. If a check fails, the agent reads its output. If the code needs a change, the agent can make it and run the checks again. If the failure points to a flaky test or an infrastructure problem, it can retry the job without changing the code. The PR is ready only when the build, automated tests and all other required CI checks pass.

Once the checks pass, Gitar reviews the changes. Gitar can approve the PR, ask for a revision, or leave the decision to an engineer. If Gitar asks for a revision, Remediation Agent updates the code and replies on the PR. Gitar then reviews the new version and the process repeats. No engineer has to steer that exchange, and the agent that writes the code never approves its own work.

By the time a fix reaches the merge step, it has cleared SonarQube analysis, every required CI check, and an independent review. If a later commit changes the PR, the checks run again.

Remediation Agent writes the fix. SonarQube verifies it, and Gitar reviews it. Even with Gitar’s approval, the PR stays open until every required check passes and every review thread is resolved. An engineer reviews medium- and high-risk changes.

How we put PR approval and merge in the agents’ hands

We let Gitar approve changes based on the risk of the fix, not the severity of the issue it addresses. To assess that risk, Gitar looks at how the changed code is used and whether the fix could alter behavior elsewhere. We wrote approval criteria so that only PRs opened by Remediation Agent qualify.  Gitar reviews the latest version of the PR, including any revisions it requested:

  • Low risk: Gitar can approve the PR without asking an engineer to review it.
  • Medium or high risk: an engineer decides whether to approve it.

Teams can keep merging PRs themselves after Gitar approves them. We chose to let the agents merge eligible PRs automatically. But approval alone isn't enough. Our branch protection rules still require the build, unit tests, integration tests, and every other required CI/CD check to pass, and every review thread to be resolved. The conditions are checked again on every push: if a new commit raises the risk, the earlier approval no longer counts.

Our criteria also stop Gitar from approving changes to GitHub Actions workflows or build scripts, even if it rates the PR as low risk. The agents can work on the code, but they can't approve changes that weaken or bypass the checks that code has to pass.

Here’s how that played out on one PR. Remediation Agent refactored three methods to fix three critical cognitive-complexity issues. Gitar rated the change low risk and merged it 35 minutes after it was opened, with no engineer involved.

Remediation Agent refactored three methods to fix three critical cognitive-complexity issues. SonarQube analysis confirmed all three issues were gone, Gitar rated the change low risk and merged it 35 minutes after it was opened, with no engineer involved.

Building confidence in autonomous merges

Before asking engineers to allow the agents to merge on their own, we made sure the PRs were easy to review. Remediation Agent handled CI failures and addressed Gitar’s feedback before handing a PR to an engineer. By then, the checks were green and the engineer could read Gitar’s review alongside the diff. Because each PR contained one kind of change, the engineer could understand the fix once, then scan for a place where it didn’t fit. Only 4% of the agent’s PRs that reached a decision were closed without being merged.

Easy reviews were only the first step. Engineers don’t hand merge decisions to an agent because someone asks them to. They do it once they’ve seen the agent make the same call they would make. So we built confidence in stages and let the results decide when to move to the next one:

  • Engineers approve and merge. Remediation Agent fixes and SonarQube verifies. People make every decision.
  • Gitar approves, engineers merge. Gitar approves low-risk PRs, and engineers compare its judgment with their own before they merge.
  • Gitar approves, the PR merges automatically. Low-risk PRs merge once every required check passes. Medium- and high-risk PRs still go to an engineer.

Teams can stay at any stage for as long as they need.

We ran the second stage first in one repository, the same way we suggest you start. Gitar automatically approved low-risk PRs, but engineers still decided whether to merge. They compared Gitar’s judgment with their own and merged every PR it had approved. They also closed a couple of the PRs Gitar flagged for human review. Every time Gitar approved a PR, the engineers agreed. After that dry run, the team turned on automatic merging for eligible PRs. None of the PRs that merged automatically has been reverted.

PRs that engineers merged stayed open for a median of about 42 hours. Almost all of that time was spent waiting for someone to pick them up. For PRs that Gitar merged, the median time from open to merge was 30 minutes.

Across the three repositories, 64% of merged PRs went through automatically without human involvement, and engineers merged another 32% that Gitar had approved as low risk. 

Issues fixed by the agents over two weeks. What stands out is the difference in how quickly the backlog came down once automatic merging was switched on.

What slowed us down

Some PRs still needed an engineer’s attention. One reason was a CI failure unrelated to the fix. The agent could rerun a flaky test. It couldn’t fix an integration test that another change in the repository had broken. That code was outside its task, so the PR stayed open until an engineer could investigate.

Other PRs had green CI and Gitar’s approval but still needed reviews from several teams because they touched code with different owners. We’ve since changed how the agent groups fixes: files with different code owners now go into separate PRs. Each team can review and merge fixes to its own code without waiting for another team’s approval.

What’s next for us

Next, we’re extending this to higher-risk changes. We’re testing how much of that work the agents can do before asking for approval, and what evidence would justify automatic merging for some of those changes.

What you can try today

You can set up a similar workflow today with SonarQube Remediation Agent and Gitar. You'll need a Remediation Agent subscription on SonarQube Cloud or SonarQube Server 2026.5, plus a Gitar Pro or Enterprise plan for auto-approve and auto-merge. On SonarQube Cloud, Remediation Agent also fixes CI failures and answers review comments on GitHub. Start with one repository: schedule backlog fixes in SonarQube Cloud, set a limit on open agent PRs and use Gitar to review the changes. Compare its reviews with your own before deciding which PRs you’d let merge automatically. Tell us what you learn in the Sonar Community.

items.title: Hackers Plant 13 ClickFix Traps on Compromised WordPress Site to Trick Visitors Into Running Malware
items.summary: A single hacked WordPress site was found carrying 13 separate ClickFix traps from three different malware kits. Each trap shows visitors a fake security check. It then talks them into pasting a harmful command on their own computer. The site sat in a poor state because several groups had broken into it at different times. Some of their code even fights the others for control of the page. This shows how one weak website can be used again and again by unrelated criminals. Analysts at URLScan noted the malware while testing a new feature that captures clipboard content during live browsing. They flagged a scan of the site academicpipelinedatabase[.]net that carried a ClickFix label but never wrote anything to the clipboard. The page showed a fake reCAPTCHA box over a blurred Cloudflare screen. It also held more than twenty hidden script blocks, and most of them were scrambled to hide their purpose. Hackers Plant 13 ClickFix Traps on Compromised WordPress Site ClickFix does not use a software bug. A fake page asks the visitor to prove they are human, and a click on the box silently copies a command to the clipboard. The page then tells the user to paste and run it. Because the victim runs the command, many browser and download filters never see a problem. Our earlier report on a fake CAPTCHA that hides malware in the browser cache shows how common this trick has become. Nine of the 13 traps come from a kit the researchers named LOM, after the “/lom” part found in its web addresses. Each LOM trap carries its own token and tracking link, and it sends different commands for each operating system. On Windows, the copied command uses PowerShell to download a script from the attacker’s server and run it. The command also sends a special user-agent and header, so the server only answers requests that come from a real lure. One version also carries a Mac command that pipes a downloaded script into zsh. Fake reCAPTCHA (Source – URLScan) The LOM code is delivered in five ways. Some copies sit right on the page, some are packed in base64, and some are fake plugin tags with names like “wordpress-defender”. Others use a blob loader. Two loaders use a trick called EtherHiding, which stores the next server address inside a Polygon blockchain contract. The operator can swap the server by changing the contract, so blocking one domain does not fix the problem. The same method shows up in a campaign hiding malware on Polygon that we covered earlier. Two LOM traps also try to delete rival scripts. They scan the page for code that looks like other loaders and remove it. This suggests the authors expect to share hacked sites with other criminals. LOM has grown fast. It first appeared in the week of September 21, 2026, and added over 700 new sites the next week. Rival Kits Break Each Other The second kit shows a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA and also uses EtherHiding. Three of its loaders read hidden server names from Polygon contracts. They decode the result and load a script only when they see a Windows browser. The researchers say its indicators overlap with ErrTraffic, which Sekoia and Censys have described. Only one of these loaders served a working payload. Its copied command starts a hidden PowerShell window and downloads a ZIP file. It unpacks the ZIP into a hidden folder and sets a startup registry entry named “nurture_river_mountain” so the program runs again after a reboot. The screen then prints a fake “I am not a robot” message, so the victim thinks the check passed. Another loader was added to eight theme and plugin files on disk, so cleaning the database alone would not remove it. The traps also broke each other by accident. Two copies of the same loader both used a function named decode(), each with a different key. The later one replaced the earlier one, so the first loader decoded its server list with the wrong key and failed. One malicious script had switched off another one on the same page. The third kit targets only Mac users and looks like a Google Analytics tag. The URLScan team says it overlaps with Macfinger. It shows a fake reCAPTCHA only on macOS, and its command downloads a shell script, runs it, deletes it, and wipes the shell history. This fits the wider rise in ClickFix campaigns targeting Mac users . A separate script on the page also removes any full-screen overlay except those from LOM and the second kit. So someone knew about both. Seven more loaders on the page never reached a final stage during the scan. Cleaning one injection does not make the site safe. Site owners should check theme and plugin files on disk and patch plugins. They should also look for sites that were hit by ShadowCaptcha-style WordPress compromises . Visitors should never paste a command from a web page into Run, PowerShell, or Terminal. items.title: Pluralistic: The Debt Trap (23 Nov 2026)
items.summary: Today's links The Debt Trap : Obscure causality is the downfall of us all. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : They Fight Crime; Cantenna wifi TV for Mali; Kakistocracy; Inflation or price-gouging; The long game; Fox v bloggers; Hollywood laundered money for Berlusoni; Katamari earmuffs; EMI v parody cricket songs; "Roller Girl"; Trump U was worse than you thought; London v Dieselgate; Bunnie at USC; Facebook gaslights the web; Apple bans ebooks that mention Apple; Private ambulances v babies in burning buildings; Boss preppers. Upcoming appearances : Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. The Debt Trap ( permalink ) Smoking is very stupid. I was a smoker for 17 years, from ages 13-30. I was very stupid to start smoking. That stupidity only came into sharper focus a few years ago, when I got a cancer diagnosis (don't worry, I am now cancer-free): https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail In my defense, I'll point out that I was just a kid when I started, but also, smoking belongs to a class of pernicious problems whose insidiousness is rooted in the distance between their causes and effects: https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/ I've often said that if a little tumor had sprouted immediately after I took my first puff, I never would have taken a second one. Now that I've actually had the experience of being told that I have a tumor, I can say definitively that I would not have taken that second puff. An economist would tell you that I was engaged in "hyperbolic discounting": underpricing a future cost and overvaluing a present pleasure: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting But I don't think that tells the whole story. Sure, I was engaged in hyperbolic discounting, but why was I doing that? What was it about smoking (as opposed to, say, French-kissing light-sockets) that led me to apply a hyperbolic discount to the costs of smoking? I say it was the attenuated relationship between cause and effect. It's not just that we undervalue the price of smoking: it's that we struggle to arrive at a correct price for smoking in the moment, because the intellectual knowledge of cancer statistics is in no way comparable to the visceral experience of a cancer diagnosis. Estimating the "cost" (emotional, physiological, monetary) of a cancer diagnosis is hard , especially if you're young and have had the good fortune of a life untouched by close contact with agonizing illness and death. The point I'm making is that the discount isn't just hyperbolic, it's hyperbolic because it relies so much upon guesswork, without comparable experiences to anchor your estimate. What's more, it's this same attenuated causality (in which cause is separated from effect by so much time and space) that allowed the tobacco industry to sow so much profitable doubt about the connection between smoking and cancer. Sure, some of the policymakers who let Big Tobacco off the hook were doubtlessly in their pocket, reliant on campaign contributions or beholden to a party that was in some queasy, cozy relationship with these death merchants. But the reason Big Tobacco was able ( is able) to get away with killing us for so many decades is that you don't get a tumor with each puff. I believe that most of the policymakers who reasoned their way into doubting the connection between smoking and cancer were ensnared by this attenuated causality. They might have had low morals and low intellect, but the factor that made them such easy marks for Big Tobacco's death-hustlers was this wide, long gap between cause and effect. This cuts both ways: if you're a policymaker of low intellect and morals, you can rig your policies to put their consequences a long way off in the future, which might give you time to escape to a lucrative private-sector career with the industrial interests who benefited from your chicanery. Or (if you're a Mitch McConnell-adjacent flesh-eating ghoul who plans to die only after centuries in office, chin red and slick with the heartblood of the innocent), you can put so much time and space between your fuckery and the ruin it brings that the voting public fails to connect your actions with the consequences. After all, no one ever lost money betting against the American public's object permanence. For example, Trump's Big Bill was designed to make its deepest cuts – to Medicaid, rural hospitals, the increased tax-load on workers to advantage their bosses – after the midterm elections. The cynical reasoning isn't hard to follow: We'll just tell voters that all the bad things they've been told about the coming cuts are Fake News, and then, after the cuts arrive, blame their post-midterm misery on Biden, communists, trans people, immigrants, and the phases of the moon. This cheap trick may be deplorable, but you should also save some anger for politicians who enact good policies but refuse to take account of this principle. Take Biden's 2021 plan to lower prescription drug prices. This started off as a rule that would end the longstanding, outrageous policy that bans Medicare/Medicaid from negotiating with pharma companies. Yes, you read that right: when Uncle Sucker buys drugs from Big Pharma, the government just asks the pharma companies how much public money they'd like, and then the USA writes the companies a check for whatever sum they name, no questions asked. That's why the US pays 300% more than any other advanced nation for its drugs. Thus Biden's initial proposal: let Medicare/Medicaid negotiate drug prices the same way every private insurer and every public health system does. But then, Biden's team allowed that policy to be diluted so that it would only apply to ten drugs, and only if those drugs had been on the market for at least 13 years. Finally, the piece de resistance : the plan wasn't design to kick in until 2025, after the 2024 election, which turned out to be a referendum on the cost of living (including drug prices) that saw the Dems getting their asses kicked by the stupidest, most obviously corrupt fascists in American electoral history: https://pluralistic.net/2021/11/18/bipartisan-consensus/#corruption Whether you're ignoring attenuated causality or weaponizing it, it's critical to any analysis of how we get into as much trouble as we do. It is the ruin of individuals and firms, and of political and economic systems. Take vaccinations: herd immunity requires a lot of compliance: nearly all of us have to get vaccinated before the real benefits kick in. Securing this compliance takes a lot of effort, because the system has to get people to invest their faith in the prospect that eventually we'll get to herd immunity and an end to infection. But once herd immunity is in place, noncompliance is a much smaller deal. The very fact of herd immunity means that people can opt out here or there without getting sick (because we're all up-to-date on our vaccinations). Worse, the very fact of herd immunity means that after a while, no one can really remember what the sickness was like: we think of measles as something the Little Rascals pretended to have so they could play hooky, not as a terrifyingly infectious disease that can leave you blind or brain damaged. Asking someone who's never lived through a measles epidemic to estimate the cost of measles is like asking a 13 year old to estimate what a cancer diagnosis will feel like. The same applies to antitrust enforcement. An economy of small and medium sized firms who compete with one another is an economy where workers have more bargaining leverage and regulators don't have to worry about being outspent and outlasted with decade-plus appeals when they crack down on corrupt businesses: https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/15/business/us-vsibm.html It's also an economy where companies must compete rather than collude. Look at what happened to the ad-tech industry, which is dominated by a duopoly that controls 80% of display advertising, and that duopoly has an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the market to pay publishers less and charge advertisers more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue In the post-war era, antitrust enforcers did their jobs: they blocked mergers, punished predatory pricing, and aggressively investigated sweetheart deals between retail incumbents and their suppliers that were designed to freeze out new businesses: https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities This produced an economy where companies had lower profits, because workers and consumers could force them to disgorge more of their surpluses, and because they had to invest more in improving their offerings to keep up with competitors. It was an economy where prosperity was more broadly shared and where it was easier to impose democratic accountability on the private sector. Then, starting with Jimmy Carter, America turned its back on antitrust. Year after year, presidency after presidency, enforcers waved through larger and more anticompetitive mergers and ignored more egregious predatory practices. For 50 years, the neoclassical economists who promoted this laissez-faire doctrine have smugly pointed out that even though the economy grew more consolidated thanks to their policy, we still had an economy, one that was often booming, where politicians could (sometimes) be seen to be intervening to address corporate cheating. The public, meanwhile, has historically struggled to connect the problems of oligarchy with these pro-oligarch policies. They can feel the regulatory capture, they know that labor grows weaker every year, they are furious at their sellout politicians and the system's naked corruption. But because the policy is separated from its outcomes by so much time and space, there's lots of room for the policy's architects and beneficiaries to do the economic version of denying the link between smoking and cancer; that is, denying the link between pro-monopoly policies and monopolies. Attenuated causality lets bad-faith actors sell us anti-vax, pro-monopoly, cancer denial…and, of course, climate denial. NASA's James Hansen warned Congress about climate change in 1988. It's not like the oil companies didn't know about this. As far back as the 1970s, Exxon's own scientists had warned the company about global warming, and the company took actions based on those warnings: https://insideclimatenews.org/project/exxon-the-road-not-taken/ Mobil, meanwhile, started secretly raising its drilling platforms to account for rising seas, even as it was taking out full-page ads in national daily newspapers that stated that "The science of climate change is too uncertain to mandate a plan of action": https://web.archive.org/web/20160101024248/http://graphics.latimes.com/oil-operations/ Attenuated causality was and is at the core of climate denial. If every climate-shredding gas turbine that the self-described environmental hero Elon Musk fired up at one of his AI data-centers immediately caused a flood or a wildfire or a heat-wave, we'd scrape all those data-centers down to their foundation slabs and then we'd display Musk in stocks and pelt him with rotten fruit. Musk really knows how to turn attenuated causality to his advantage. Remember when he performatively borrowed a security guard's pocket knife and started slicing through the Ethernet cables connecting Twitter's servers? https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2023-09-14/when-elon-musk-unplugged-the-twitter-servers-with-a-pocket-knife-theres-still-shit-thats-broken-because-of-it.html Or when he started shutting down whole data-centers and mass-firing Twitter's technical staff? https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/29/technology/twitter-elon-musk.html The point of this performance was to let Musk claim that Twitter's management had let itself be gulled by featherbedding engineers who grossly overbuilt Twitter's infrastructure in order to guarantee themselves perpetual employment at the expense of Twitter's shareholders. But all that spare server capacity wasn't excess: it was the cushion, the headroom, the insurance policy. Those were the servers that would pick up the slack when another server lost its power-supply or caught a bad stick of RAM. They were the servers that could shoulder the load during the next 9/11 or Arab Spring. They were the engineering staff that could execute new projects or perform emergency maintenance – and the engineering staff that could plan the next build-out in advance so that future growth wouldn't stall out when Twitter ran out of hardware. Musk's actions didn't occur in a vacuum. During the decades in which attenuated causality set the scene for an endless, incestuous orgy of mergers and acquisitions, it became normal for business leaders to hack away at their own firms' resiliency. University administrators fired tenured professors and replaced them with casualized, proletarianized adjuncts. The pedagogy – and the universities' reputations – persisted after the cuts, ebbing away slowly as the institutional memory and standards eroded bit by bit. But eventually, the universities found themselves in crisis. Campuses erupted in student revolt and spectacular scenes of violent repression: https://jayrosen.tumblr.com/post/13174138991/excerpt-from-uc-davis-2010-2012-general-catalog Universities' reputations cratered and they found themselves easy pickings for demagogues who awarded themselves a veto over faculty, curriculum and admissions: https://www.chronicle.com/article/columbia-capitulated-but-so-did-the-rest-of-higher-ed That's the thing about attenuated causality: it lets people and institutions and systems play a high-stakes game of Jenga in which every non-load-bearing block is removed and added to the top of the teetering stack. No one block causes the system to collapse…until one block does, and the whole thing falls over. It's like an avalanche. Drop one snowflake after another on the mountainside. Expose it to the midday sun and the frigid night. Sure, it creaks. Watch closely and you'll see it make minute shifts. Every now and again, a light scree of snow slides off the surface and skitters downhill, but the great mass of snow is stable. Until it isn't. Until one last snowflake alights on the mountainside and sets the whole thing rumbling and tumbling in an inexorable, unstoppable wall of snow that only halts when it can go no lower. The run-up to an avalanche is a long, long series of linear phenomena. A snowflake is minute. Add it to the pile and it will produce a minute effect. A little bit of heat causes a little bit of expansion. A little bit of wind blows a little of the loose cover around. But each one of these little strains on the system makes it less stable overall. The snowpack's stability is invisible. A snowpack that is about to cut loose is indistinguishable from one that will stay put for weeks or months. But once the snow's systemic resiliency has been exhausted, the next linear perturbation produces a wild, catastrophic, nonlinear collapse. Attenuated causality lets us build up a mountain of debt: health debt, technology debt, policy debt, credibility debt. It's impossible to know when the system's homeostatic mechanisms have been fatally weakened, such that the next compromise it is asked to bear causes it to rupture, or implode, or crumble. We can raise the level of CO2 and methane in the Earth's atmosphere year after year and see long-attenuated, linear effects: fires here, floods there, some extinctions. But one day: we overwhelm some invisible homeostatic mechanism and we lose the Gulf Stream: https://www.bbc.com/climate/impact/gulf_stream.shtml Same goes for the world's IT: we can fire IT workers, starve maintenance teams of budget and personnel, substitute indemnity for software quality, allow our "security" agencies to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities, and on average, it will all work…until it stops: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake IT might just be the most dangerously attenuated aspect of all our administrative functions. A software engineer writes a piece of code and it keeps running, even if you fire that engineer. This is one of the reasons it's so hard to unionize tech workers: when they go on strike, their scab software crosses the picket line and keeps working: https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook But software isn't an asset, it's a liability. Code runs in a system , with upstream processes that produce its inputs and downstream processes that operate on its outputs. There's adjacent processes, too: other software that also gets fed by those upstream processes and also feeds those downstream processes. Even if the code never changes, the system the code is part of changes constantly, which means that the more code you have, the more code you have to maintain. So what happens when you fire technical workers is nothing…at first. And then, bit by bit, things start to break. And break. And break. Only the people who wrote the software – and the people they trained through working alongside of them – know exactly how it works, with that deep knowledge, that Fingerspitzengefühl , that informs their intuition so they can figure out why things broke and how to fix them: https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/08/process-knowledge/#dance-monkey-dance Break that chain of knowledge and you lobotomize your institution. Reduce the full complement of experienced engineers with the wherewithal to demand higher wages and better conditions, leave behind a precarious skeleton crew of juniors you terrorize with layoff threats and AI ghost-stories, and you destroy not just your ability to spot problems before they occur, but also your capability to salvage your way out of the wreckage. And that's what Musk's Doge did to the American state: undermined its capacity to absorb shocks, to anticipate shocks and brace for them – or even to detect the shocks when they're underway. There's a reason so much variation is preserved in our genomes and species: these are the reserves of variety that can rise to meet the changing world.
