The Debt Trap (permalink)

Smoking is very stupid. I was a smoker for 17 years, from ages 13-30. I was very stupid to start smoking. That stupidity only came into sharper focus a few years ago, when I got a cancer diagnosis (don't worry, I am now cancer-free):

https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail

In my defense, I'll point out that I was just a kid when I started, but also, smoking belongs to a class of pernicious problems whose insidiousness is rooted in the distance between their causes and effects:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/

I've often said that if a little tumor had sprouted immediately after I took my first puff, I never would have taken a second one. Now that I've actually had the experience of being told that I have a tumor, I can say definitively that I would not have taken that second puff. An economist would tell you that I was engaged in "hyperbolic discounting": underpricing a future cost and overvaluing a present pleasure:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting

But I don't think that tells the whole story. Sure, I was engaged in hyperbolic discounting, but why was I doing that? What was it about smoking (as opposed to, say, French-kissing light-sockets) that led me to apply a hyperbolic discount to the costs of smoking? I say it was the attenuated relationship between cause and effect. It's not just that we undervalue the price of smoking: it's that we struggle to arrive at a correct price for smoking in the moment, because the intellectual knowledge of cancer statistics is in no way comparable to the visceral experience of a cancer diagnosis. Estimating the "cost" (emotional, physiological, monetary) of a cancer diagnosis is hard, especially if you're young and have had the good fortune of a life untouched by close contact with agonizing illness and death.

The point I'm making is that the discount isn't just hyperbolic, it's hyperbolic because it relies so much upon guesswork, without comparable experiences to anchor your estimate.

What's more, it's this same attenuated causality (in which cause is separated from effect by so much time and space) that allowed the tobacco industry to sow so much profitable doubt about the connection between smoking and cancer. Sure, some of the policymakers who let Big Tobacco off the hook were doubtlessly in their pocket, reliant on campaign contributions or beholden to a party that was in some queasy, cozy relationship with these death merchants. But the reason Big Tobacco was able (is able) to get away with killing us for so many decades is that you don't get a tumor with each puff.

I believe that most of the policymakers who reasoned their way into doubting the connection between smoking and cancer were ensnared by this attenuated causality. They might have had low morals and low intellect, but the factor that made them such easy marks for Big Tobacco's death-hustlers was this wide, long gap between cause and effect.

This cuts both ways: if you're a policymaker of low intellect and morals, you can rig your policies to put their consequences a long way off in the future, which might give you time to escape to a lucrative private-sector career with the industrial interests who benefited from your chicanery. Or (if you're a Mitch McConnell-adjacent flesh-eating ghoul who plans to die only after centuries in office, chin red and slick with the heartblood of the innocent), you can put so much time and space between your fuckery and the ruin it brings that the voting public fails to connect your actions with the consequences. After all, no one ever lost money betting against the American public's object permanence.

For example, Trump's Big Bill was designed to make its deepest cuts – to Medicaid, rural hospitals, the increased tax-load on workers to advantage their bosses – after the midterm elections. The cynical reasoning isn't hard to follow: We'll just tell voters that all the bad things they've been told about the coming cuts are Fake News, and then, after the cuts arrive, blame their post-midterm misery on Biden, communists, trans people, immigrants, and the phases of the moon.

This cheap trick may be deplorable, but you should also save some anger for politicians who enact good policies but refuse to take account of this principle. Take Biden's 2021 plan to lower prescription drug prices. This started off as a rule that would end the longstanding, outrageous policy that bans Medicare/Medicaid from negotiating with pharma companies. Yes, you read that right: when Uncle Sucker buys drugs from Big Pharma, the government just asks the pharma companies how much public money they'd like, and then the USA writes the companies a check for whatever sum they name, no questions asked. That's why the US pays 300% more than any other advanced nation for its drugs.

Thus Biden's initial proposal: let Medicare/Medicaid negotiate drug prices the same way every private insurer and every public health system does. But then, Biden's team allowed that policy to be diluted so that it would only apply to ten drugs, and only if those drugs had been on the market for at least 13 years. Finally, the piece de resistance: the plan wasn't design to kick in until 2025, after the 2024 election, which turned out to be a referendum on the cost of living (including drug prices) that saw the Dems getting their asses kicked by the stupidest, most obviously corrupt fascists in American electoral history:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/11/18/bipartisan-consensus/#corruption

Whether you're ignoring attenuated causality or weaponizing it, it's critical to any analysis of how we get into as much trouble as we do. It is the ruin of individuals and firms, and of political and economic systems.

Take vaccinations: herd immunity requires a lot of compliance: nearly all of us have to get vaccinated before the real benefits kick in. Securing this compliance takes a lot of effort, because the system has to get people to invest their faith in the prospect that eventually we'll get to herd immunity and an end to infection.

But once herd immunity is in place, noncompliance is a much smaller deal. The very fact of herd immunity means that people can opt out here or there without getting sick (because we're all up-to-date on our vaccinations). Worse, the very fact of herd immunity means that after a while, no one can really remember what the sickness was like: we think of measles as something the Little Rascals pretended to have so they could play hooky, not as a terrifyingly infectious disease that can leave you blind or brain damaged. Asking someone who's never lived through a measles epidemic to estimate the cost of measles is like asking a 13 year old to estimate what a cancer diagnosis will feel like.

The same applies to antitrust enforcement. An economy of small and medium sized firms who compete with one another is an economy where workers have more bargaining leverage and regulators don't have to worry about being outspent and outlasted with decade-plus appeals when they crack down on corrupt businesses:

https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/15/business/us-vsibm.html

It's also an economy where companies must compete rather than collude. Look at what happened to the ad-tech industry, which is dominated by a duopoly that controls 80% of display advertising, and that duopoly has an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the market to pay publishers less and charge advertisers more:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue

In the post-war era, antitrust enforcers did their jobs: they blocked mergers, punished predatory pricing, and aggressively investigated sweetheart deals between retail incumbents and their suppliers that were designed to freeze out new businesses:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities

This produced an economy where companies had lower profits, because workers and consumers could force them to disgorge more of their surpluses, and because they had to invest more in improving their offerings to keep up with competitors. It was an economy where prosperity was more broadly shared and where it was easier to impose democratic accountability on the private sector.

Then, starting with Jimmy Carter, America turned its back on antitrust. Year after year, presidency after presidency, enforcers waved through larger and more anticompetitive mergers and ignored more egregious predatory practices. For 50 years, the neoclassical economists who promoted this laissez-faire doctrine have smugly pointed out that even though the economy grew more consolidated thanks to their policy, we still had an economy, one that was often booming, where politicians could (sometimes) be seen to be intervening to address corporate cheating.

The public, meanwhile, has historically struggled to connect the problems of oligarchy with these pro-oligarch policies. They can feel the regulatory capture, they know that labor grows weaker every year, they are furious at their sellout politicians and the system's naked corruption. But because the policy is separated from its outcomes by so much time and space, there's lots of room for the policy's architects and beneficiaries to do the economic version of denying the link between smoking and cancer; that is, denying the link between pro-monopoly policies and monopolies.

Attenuated causality lets bad-faith actors sell us anti-vax, pro-monopoly, cancer denial…and, of course, climate denial. NASA's James Hansen warned Congress about climate change in 1988. It's not like the oil companies didn't know about this. As far back as the 1970s, Exxon's own scientists had warned the company about global warming, and the company took actions based on those warnings:

https://insideclimatenews.org/project/exxon-the-road-not-taken/

Mobil, meanwhile, started secretly raising its drilling platforms to account for rising seas, even as it was taking out full-page ads in national daily newspapers that stated that "The science of climate change is too uncertain to mandate a plan of action":

https://web.archive.org/web/20160101024248/http://graphics.latimes.com/oil-operations/

Attenuated causality was and is at the core of climate denial. If every climate-shredding gas turbine that the self-described environmental hero Elon Musk fired up at one of his AI data-centers immediately caused a flood or a wildfire or a heat-wave, we'd scrape all those data-centers down to their foundation slabs and then we'd display Musk in stocks and pelt him with rotten fruit.

Musk really knows how to turn attenuated causality to his advantage. Remember when he performatively borrowed a security guard's pocket knife and started slicing through the Ethernet cables connecting Twitter's servers?

https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2023-09-14/when-elon-musk-unplugged-the-twitter-servers-with-a-pocket-knife-theres-still-shit-thats-broken-because-of-it.html

Or when he started shutting down whole data-centers and mass-firing Twitter's technical staff?

https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/29/technology/twitter-elon-musk.html

The point of this performance was to let Musk claim that Twitter's management had let itself be gulled by featherbedding engineers who grossly overbuilt Twitter's infrastructure in order to guarantee themselves perpetual employment at the expense of Twitter's shareholders. But all that spare server capacity wasn't excess: it was the cushion, the headroom, the insurance policy. Those were the servers that would pick up the slack when another server lost its power-supply or caught a bad stick of RAM. They were the servers that could shoulder the load during the next 9/11 or Arab Spring. They were the engineering staff that could execute new projects or perform emergency maintenance – and the engineering staff that could plan the next build-out in advance so that future growth wouldn't stall out when Twitter ran out of hardware.

Musk's actions didn't occur in a vacuum. During the decades in which attenuated causality set the scene for an endless, incestuous orgy of mergers and acquisitions, it became normal for business leaders to hack away at their own firms' resiliency. University administrators fired tenured professors and replaced them with casualized, proletarianized adjuncts.

The pedagogy – and the universities' reputations – persisted after the cuts, ebbing away slowly as the institutional memory and standards eroded bit by bit. But eventually, the universities found themselves in crisis. Campuses erupted in student revolt and spectacular scenes of violent repression:

https://jayrosen.tumblr.com/post/13174138991/excerpt-from-uc-davis-2010-2012-general-catalog

Universities' reputations cratered and they found themselves easy pickings for demagogues who awarded themselves a veto over faculty, curriculum and admissions:

https://www.chronicle.com/article/columbia-capitulated-but-so-did-the-rest-of-higher-ed

That's the thing about attenuated causality: it lets people and institutions and systems play a high-stakes game of Jenga in which every non-load-bearing block is removed and added to the top of the teetering stack. No one block causes the system to collapse…until one block does, and the whole thing falls over.

It's like an avalanche. Drop one snowflake after another on the mountainside. Expose it to the midday sun and the frigid night. Sure, it creaks. Watch closely and you'll see it make minute shifts. Every now and again, a light scree of snow slides off the surface and skitters downhill, but the great mass of snow is stable.

Until it isn't. Until one last snowflake alights on the mountainside and sets the whole thing rumbling and tumbling in an inexorable, unstoppable wall of snow that only halts when it can go no lower.

The run-up to an avalanche is a long, long series of linear phenomena. A snowflake is minute. Add it to the pile and it will produce a minute effect. A little bit of heat causes a little bit of expansion. A little bit of wind blows a little of the loose cover around. But each one of these little strains on the system makes it less stable overall. The snowpack's stability is invisible. A snowpack that is about to cut loose is indistinguishable from one that will stay put for weeks or months. But once the snow's systemic resiliency has been exhausted, the next linear perturbation produces a wild, catastrophic, nonlinear collapse.

Attenuated causality lets us build up a mountain of debt: health debt, technology debt, policy debt, credibility debt. It's impossible to know when the system's homeostatic mechanisms have been fatally weakened, such that the next compromise it is asked to bear causes it to rupture, or implode, or crumble.

We can raise the level of CO2 and methane in the Earth's atmosphere year after year and see long-attenuated, linear effects: fires here, floods there, some extinctions. But one day: we overwhelm some invisible homeostatic mechanism and we lose the Gulf Stream:

https://www.bbc.com/climate/impact/gulf_stream.shtml

Same goes for the world's IT: we can fire IT workers, starve maintenance teams of budget and personnel, substitute indemnity for software quality, allow our "security" agencies to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities, and on average, it will all work…until it stops:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake

IT might just be the most dangerously attenuated aspect of all our administrative functions. A software engineer writes a piece of code and it keeps running, even if you fire that engineer. This is one of the reasons it's so hard to unionize tech workers: when they go on strike, their scab software crosses the picket line and keeps working:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook

But software isn't an asset, it's a liability. Code runs in a system, with upstream processes that produce its inputs and downstream processes that operate on its outputs. There's adjacent processes, too: other software that also gets fed by those upstream processes and also feeds those downstream processes. Even if the code never changes, the system the code is part of changes constantly, which means that the more code you have, the more code you have to maintain.

So what happens when you fire technical workers is nothing…at first. And then, bit by bit, things start to break. And break. And break. Only the people who wrote the software – and the people they trained through working alongside of them – know exactly how it works, with that deep knowledge, that Fingerspitzengefühl, that informs their intuition so they can figure out why things broke and how to fix them:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/08/process-knowledge/#dance-monkey-dance

Break that chain of knowledge and you lobotomize your institution. Reduce the full complement of experienced engineers with the wherewithal to demand higher wages and better conditions, leave behind a precarious skeleton crew of juniors you terrorize with layoff threats and AI ghost-stories, and you destroy not just your ability to spot problems before they occur, but also your capability to salvage your way out of the wreckage.

And that's what Musk's Doge did to the American state: undermined its capacity to absorb shocks, to anticipate shocks and brace for them – or even to detect the shocks when they're underway. There's a reason so much variation is preserved in our genomes and species: these are the reserves of variety that can rise to meet the changing world. Eliminate the variety, and you strip out the ability to cope with surprise, and what happens next shouldn't surprise any of us.

items.title: iTerm2 Remote Code Execution Flaw Lets Hackers Run Malicious Commands by Displaying Crafted Files
items.summary: A security flaw in iTerm2, a macOS terminal emulator , lets attackers run commands when a user displays a specially crafted file in a vulnerable terminal session. The user does not have to run the file as a script or paste a command supplied by the attacker. Printing the file’s contents is enough to trigger the bug. The developer fixed the issue in iTerm2 3.7.9, a security update built on November 20, 2026. The reported affected range is 3.6.1 through 3.7.8, and the flaw can affect installations using default settings. iTerm2 credits Minseong Kim of NSHC Red Alert Labs with reporting the issue. The FBI is investigating a reported breach of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a database police use to check for outstanding warrants, identify stolen vehicles, and look up missing-person records.

CNN first reported the breach on November 20, citing two people briefed on the investigation. It is unclear when it happened or how the attackers got in. A law enforcement source confirmed the hack to ABC News. The FBI hasn’t publicly confirmed the incident.

NCIC is a computerized database that local, state, and federal agencies can all use. It holds records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, and stolen property. Police officers use it during traffic stops, investigations, and background checks.

The system held more than 19.3 million records in fiscal year 2025. It’s still unclear whether anyone stole data. The database includes the following types of records:

  • Wanted-person and warrant records
  • Missing-person records
  • Criminal history data
  • Protection orders
  • Records of stolen vehicles, firearms, and other property

NCIC is one of the databases the FBI checks during firearm background checks. The reports do not say that attackers breached the background-check system itself or that gun buyers’ information was exposed.

If someone stole NCIC data, people who could be affected include those with past arrests, people with protection orders, missing people and their families, and victims of crime. Possible risks include the following:

  • Exposure of sensitive records. Criminals could use criminal history or details from protection orders for harassment, extortion, or doxxing.
  • Targeted scams. Scammers could pose as police officers and use details from a real warrant to make a demand for payment sound convincing.
  • Data enrichment. Records from other sources could be linked to the data in this database, providing attackers with more details to make their messaging believable.

This is the second reported intrusion involving FBI systems in about two months. FBI employees whose information was exposed in the September breach face risks including phishing and identity theft. CNN reported that some felt left in the dark about whether they were affected.

How to stay safe

If you feel your data might be involved, here are some steps you can take while we learn more about the breach:

  • Be wary of unsolicited calls, emails, or messages from police or the FBI. Law enforcement won’t demand gift cards, crypto, or wire transfers.
  • Be wary of breach notification emails and texts. Don’t click links. Go to official sites directly.
  • Use unique passwords and multi-factor authentication on your accounts. Passkeys are even better where they’re offered as an option.
  • Check your own online exposure with a tool like Malwarebytes’ Digital Footprint scan, and keep your devices updated.

items.title: Jailbroken AI Agent Helps Hacker Steal Customer Data and 8.6GB of European Government Files
items.summary: A low-skilled hacker used a jailbroken AI agent to steal an insurer’s customer database and about 8.6GB of files from European municipalities. The operator, known as BabidiGhost, worked for nine days in November 2026. He typed plain, misspelled French orders and let the agent do the technical work. Targets included banks, insurers, payment providers and town halls, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland. The agent targeted more than 50 organizations and datasets. In one order, the operator asked for “13 files of 1,000 full records with IBAN, nice and tidy.” He also asked the agent who it was, and he could not download his own stolen files. The AI covered for his lack of skill, and it kept working until its model API key was revoked on November 14, 2026. Researchers at SOCRadar found the operation after the hacker left his home directory open on a hijacked staging server in France. The folder held 1,901 files, including every prompt he typed, his shell history, implant logs and roughly 10GB of stolen data. SOCRadar’s analysts said they studied the files without running any recovered malware or using any stolen credentials. Jailbroken AI Agent Helps Hacker The agent came from a toolchain tied to BlackHatSect0r, a French-speaking, financially driven group that SOCRadar tracks. It runs on the Hermes agent framework and a DeepSeek model. A 1,371-line file named SOUL.md sets the agent’s rules. It declares the agent’s “ethics protocols destroyed” and treats any refusal as a model malfunction to be ignored. A local proxy backed up that file. When the model said no, the proxy re-sent the order with more pressure. Across nine days, the agent sent 5,779 requests to its model, and only 41 refusals survived. The operator typed 1,801 orders, and the agent wrote the scanners, exploits and data-theft scripts on its own. This matches a wider trend, as one operator running 12 AI agents recently hit emergency services and banks in Taiwan. The two Telegram identities tied to the operation (Source – SOCRadar) Nothing here was a zero-day. The successful break-ins used known weak spots that victims could have fixed. In the insurer’s case, an internet-facing and unpatched Metabase dashboard was open to CVE-2023-38646. Older reporting explains the Metabase remote code execution flaw and the patched versions. The agent ran commands through the dashboard’s database link and read cloud database credentials from the container’s environment. It then exported the customer database and planted a database trigger to restart its implant. What the Hacker Stole and What Stopped Him The biggest theft by size needed even less effort. A shared IT provider left a storage server’s management page open to the internet, and a weak admin password opened it. Three download scripts later, the agent held 23 archives, about 8.6GB, from more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies. One password unlocked every client’s data. Of the 14 organizations SOCRadar studied closely, two were breached and three were partly breached. Four resisted and five saw only scouting. Basic controls decided each result. Eleven scripts failed to brute-force a payment portal’s one-time password, and 49 bank hostnames stayed out of reach behind an IP allowlist. Server-side checks also blocked a fake declaration at one bank. At another bank, a sign-in error confirmed 48 valid corporate accounts. The agent also ran a 120-thread crawler that collected IBANs, emails and phone numbers from Swiss sites. An IBAN tied to a real identity can enable direct-debit fraud and bank-impersonation calls. That makes this dataset the most likely to harm individuals. Cutting off the AI key stopped the agent but did not clean up the damage. A PowerShell beacon and a C# backdoor posing as a Windows Update service kept checking in until November 15, 2026. This echoes findings that attackers now automate every stage of an intrusion, while people still pick targets and sell the loot. SOCRadar rates BabidiGhost a low-capability actor using a high-capability tool. Defenders should take the main lesson from this case. Keep analytics tools and storage panels off the internet, and keep database secrets out of runtime environments. Use strong passwords, MFA and IP allowlists. Watch for servers that call model APIs or the Telegram bot API for no business reason. Teams should search logs for these indicators between November 5 and November 17, 2026. Google has also seen attackers running agent frameworks such as ARTEX and PentAGI, so this pattern is spreading. items.title: CrowdStrike to Acquire Zscaler in Massive $43.9 Billion Cybersecurity Deal
items.summary: CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal that would bring cloud network security to its Falcon platform. The agreement, announced on November 23, 2026, would give CrowdStrike control over both the devices where users and AI agents run software and the connections they make to corporate apps and data. Zscaler shareholders would receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. Based on CrowdStrike’s November 20 closing price, the exchange valued each Zscaler share at $260.41, about 34% above Zscaler’s close that day. The agreement follows our earlier report of acquisition talks . If the deal closes, existing CrowdStrike shareholders would own 84.1% of the combined company, while Zscaler shareholders would own 15.9%. Update: CrowdStrike to Acquire Zscaler in Massive $43.9 Billion Cybersecurity Deal Zscaler Would Extend the Falcon Platform Falcon monitors laptops, servers, and cloud workloads for suspicious activity. Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange sits between users, AI agents, and the applications they want to reach, where it can check identity and enforce access rules. That matters when traffic goes straight to a cloud service rather than through a company data center. CrowdStrike plans to add Zscaler’s data protection and secure access service edge, or SASE, which delivers networking and security controls through the cloud. The companies already share more than 2,000 customers and have built 16 integrations. One existing integration lets Zscaler use Falcon alerts to reassess access when a device shows signs of compromise. After closing, CrowdStrike plans to bring device events and network logs into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, its platform for collecting and analyzing security events. That could help an analyst link a suspicious process on a server to an attempt to reach a sensitive app, without switching between two sets of logs. An AI agent can run on a server and make requests to several apps without a person approving each action. Falcon can monitor activity where the agent runs, while Zscaler can apply rules to the connections it makes. The difference matters when an agent has a valid identity but tries to reach data outside its assigned role. Zscaler had already expanded its AI security work through its acquisition of SPLX . The proposed deal would bring those network controls closer to Falcon’s device and workload monitoring. CrowdStrike plans to sell both product lines under one Falcon Flex contract and sees an opportunity to offer Falcon to about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not already use CrowdStrike. It estimates the deal would expand its potential market by more than $185 billion in calendar 2029. The companies expect to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue and target about $1 billion in additional annualized revenue from the combination within 30 months of closing. Both boards approved the deal, but it still needs Zscaler shareholder and regulatory approval. The companies expect it to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028 and will operate separately until then. Zscaler CEO Jay Chaudhry would continue to lead the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike’s board. For customers, the key question after closing is how quickly the companies can turn their existing integrations into shared access controls and a single view of security events. items.title: Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Center Urges Users Not to Share Confidential Data on WhatsApp Web
items.summary: The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Center (I4C) has urged users not to share confidential data on WhatsApp Web and to log out manually after every session. In a November 18, 2026, security advisory , the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit warned that someone with access to a signed-in browser session could read private messages, view contacts and group chats, or send messages posing as the account owner. The warning applies especially to office computers, shared systems and devices other people can access. The advisory recommends keeping government, workplace, financial and other sensitive information off WhatsApp Web. It does not identify a new flaw in WhatsApp or say that its encryption has been broken. When someone can open a browser session that is still signed in, they may be able to use the account without the owner’s permission. WhatsApp Web Access to Chats WhatsApp Web lets users access their chats by linking a browser to their account. According to WhatsApp’s linked devices guide , personal messages remain protected by end-to-end encryption on linked devices. That protection does not stop someone at a computer from reading chats the browser can already display. An attacker could use details from those chats to make a fake payment request seem to come from a colleague or relative. A separate threat, covered in Cyber Security News’ report on WhatsApp GhostPairing , involves tricking users into approving a device they do not control. The I4C advisory does not tie its warning to that campaign. Logging out on a shared computer ends that session, but it does not remove a different device already linked to the account. Protecting WhatsApp Web session I4C recommends signing out from WhatsApp Web before closing the tab or browser. Avoid signing in at cyber cafés, public kiosks, hotel business centers, or on borrowed computers. If temporary use is unavoidable, use a trusted computer and open a private or incognito window, then log out manually. Private browsing is an extra precaution, not a substitute for signing out. For teams handling sensitive records, the safer choice is to use an approved work channel rather than send those records through WhatsApp Web. I4C also advises keeping the operating system, browser and security software up to date and avoiding suspicious downloads, unknown attachments and cracked software. An unexpected QR code or request to approve a device should also raise concern, as Cyber Security News’ earlier reporting on device-linking scams explains. Unexpected sent messages or replies to conversations you never started are reasons to check your account. Open WhatsApp on your primary phone, go to Linked Devices, select any device you do not recognize, and tap Log Out. Repeat this for each unfamiliar device. WhatsApp’s account security instructions explain how to disconnect a session remotely, even if you no longer have the computer in front of you. If someone sent messages from your account, warn affected contacts through another channel. Ask them not to open links or act on payment requests and to verify unusual instructions by phone. In India, anyone who has lost money to online fraud should call 1930 promptly and file a complaint through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal . items.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw to Gain Root Access and Infiltrate Internal Networks
items.summary: Attackers are now using a critical Cisco Expressway bug, CVE-2026-76466 , to take full control of devices and move deeper into company networks. Researchers at F6 say the first known case happened soon after a public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit appeared. F6’s Cyber Defense Center looked into the first observed exploitation of the flaw, which has a CVSS score of 9.8. The attackers broke into Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices and ran commands as root, the highest level of access on a system. Security Affairs reports that the victim was a Russian organization and that no known threat group has been linked to the activity. CISA has since added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, which usually means federal agencies must treat it as urgent. Cisco published its advisory on October 21, 2026. It says the weakness sits in the database service. Persistent cookies are in use, and client certificates are not checked properly when TLS Verify Mode is turned on for clustering. An attacker who holds the cookies can connect to the service and send remote procedure call commands that run as root. Only clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E devices are affected, and Cisco says no workarounds exist. We covered the original disclosure in our earlier report on the critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability . The attackers first broke into two Expressway devices facing the internet. From one of them, they reached two more cluster nodes on the internal network. With root access, they began building tools to spread further. Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw F6 found custom Python scripts made to scan the network and find open SMB shares. The scripts also talked to SQL Server and WinRM and searched GitLab repositories for passwords and other private data. The attackers edited these scripts while the attack was running. The code included comments and fix notes pointing to an AI assistant, showing how attackers now use AI to build and adjust tools quickly. Cisco has seen similar root-level attacks on other products, such as the Cisco SD-WAN zero-day . F6 says a key sign is a nodeup ‘wombat@127.0.0.1’ entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on the device. It means something connected to an Erlang node whose name matches the known exploit. Finding it does not prove a breach, so teams should also check other logs and files. Update Expressway right away. Cisco lists X15.5.20 as the first fixed release for X15.5.3 and earlier, and users of X14 or older must move to a fixed release. If you cannot patch today, F6 advises blocking TCP ports 4371 to 4372 at the firewall and allowing only trusted cluster node addresses. Patching alone may not be enough if attackers got in earlier, so run a compromise check on exposed devices. External attack surface monitoring can help find weak systems before attackers do. Strong monitoring and incident response let teams isolate hacked systems, measure the damage, and stop lateral movement. Good network segmentation also helps, because one edge device should never give attackers a path to critical systems. items.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
items.summary: This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press . Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither. Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion , answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions. When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies. Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it. The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior : behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker , puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents. The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it. The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself. The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

items.title: OXLoader abuses DLL hijacking to distribute different malware families
items.summary: .kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column490536_5031a1-28 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article OXLoader can lead to malware that steals browser passwords and data or gives criminals remote access to a Windows PC Fake copyright complaints and cracked software activators are among the lures used to spread it What to watch for in suspicious downloads and how to reduce the risk We’ve seen an increase in activity involving OXLoader, a loader that installs other malware on a computer. Elastic first documented it in June 2026, when attackers used Google Ads to distribute CASTLESTEALER through OXLoader. The malware installed varies by campaign. We found OXLoader distributing Remcos, OverLord, PureRAT, Lunex Stealer, LOLD, and Hermes. Depending on the payload, attackers could steal saved browser passwords and other data, remotely control the computer, or download more malware. We found OXLoader in malicious ZIP files disguised as complaint or copyright-infringement notices, as well as fake software activators. One campaign we analyzed used fake activators downloaded from GitLab. Below, we take a technical deep dive into how that campaign works, including how OXLoader uses DLL hijacking to unpack and run malware. How to stay safe Here are a few simple ways to stay safe: Be wary of emails or links that tell you to run software in connection with copyright infringement or complaints. Watch for executables with very long names or double extensions, such as .docx.exe or .pdf.exe . Pay attention when you extract an archive. If some of the files it contains don’t appear, be cautious. Downloading activators or cracks can compromise your device. Install Malwarebytes Browser Guard , our free browser extension, to block malicious websites and suspicious downloads. Use Malwarebytes Premium to block malware in real time, including malicious files. Overview of the detected campaigns In this section, we analyze several detected campaigns. In the cases we examined, OXLoader was decrypted either by malicious code embedded in legitimate executables, as in Elastic’s analysis, or through DLL hijacking. DLL hijacking is one of the key new features we observed in these campaigns. The rest of the infection chain is similar to the one Elastic identified. We identified several DLLs used to decrypt and execute OXLoader, including: Qt5Widgets.dll Qt6Core.dll SDL3.dll UnityPlayer.dll ANCUtility.dll dbghelp.dll msvcr100.dll In some cases, we found other DLLs that had been tampered with to launch the malicious DLL. The executables involved were associated with Microsoft applications, Steam, OBS Studio, and PDF or Word readers. Across different campaigns, OXLoader was distributed using themes related to complaints and copyright infringement. Malicious ZIP files were distributed in several ways. For example, a user might receive an email with an attached PDF prompting them to download and run a ZIP file, claiming there had been “unauthorized copying of brand intellectual property.” Example of a PDF attached to an email that downloads a malicious ZIP file When the user runs the executable, the infection chain begins through DLL hijacking, and a fake PDF opens. In this case, WindowsCodecs.dll is the trojanized DLL used to decrypt OXLoader. The contents of the malicious ZIP file The fake PDF that opens In some cases, a batch file is present instead of the executable and DLLs. It downloads a ZIP file containing the malicious DLL from different websites or hosting providers. The batch file’s content is similar to the one analyzed by Elastic. These files have long names, for example: Photo_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Product_Review_Order_Front_Back_PDF.bat Form_Video_{ RANDOM NUMBERS }_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat Case_Form_Video_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat In other cases, OXLoader was distributed through ZIP archives named Evidence_of_Violation.zip , downloaded from Google Sites. These websites used different titles and graphics. Google Site used to distribute the malicious archive In this case, WinWord.exe is renamed with a double extension, such as Travel_Point_Conditions.docx.exe or evidence_of_violation.docx.exe . OXLoader is then executed through DLL hijacking using the malicious DLL msvcr100.dll . Example of one of the malicious archives Finally, in the campaigns analyzed in this post, OXLoader was distributed through fake activators and cracks for popular software, downloaded from GitLab. Malicious activators hosted on GitLab that distribute OXLoader Technical analysis of OXLoader In this campaign, users download software activators from GitLab, triggering the infection chain. Stage 1: DLL hijacking The archive downloaded by the user contains several legitimate DLLs, along with a legitimate executable from Take-Two Interactive Software, which is used to perform DLL hijacking using the UnityPlayer DLL . The manifest.json contains encrypted shellcode, which is decrypted and injected into another legitimate DLL. The extracted archive with the malicious DLL The DLL at address 0x18054485b contains a jmp instruction that calls the code responsible for decrypting the remaining code at 0x1807a3372 . This decryption code differs across the cases we analyzed. The call to the decryption function The self-decryption function The code is heavily obfuscated using opaque predicates, control flow flattening (CFF), and mixed Boolean arithmetic (MBA). We therefore used the Sogen emulator to trace the main functions that execute and identify the malware code that called them. Partial Sogen execution with some functions related to anti-analysis and language checks Termination of the malware if a virtualized environment is detected (Sogen output) The values ​​used by the remaining functions are decoded using two functions: The function at the address 0x1807a2282 decrypts the data ​​using the following formula: input1 ^ (input2 + 0x33fda) . The function at the address 0x1807a2624 is responsible for decrypting an 8-byte chunk; this function is called multiple times by other wrappers to decrypt the complete strings. The decrypted strings The anti-analysis and language checks we observed are similar to those identified by Elastic, with the minor addition of a check using WNetGetResourceParentW to detect virtualized environments. Description Value Invalid values to detect virtualized environments Pass invalid values ​​using the functions WNetAddConnection2W and WNetGetResourceParentW and check if the LastErrorValue is ERROR_BAD_NET_NAME (67) and ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS (487) CPU-count NumberOfProcessors greater than or equal to 3 Display Refresh rate Executes a PowerShell command and it checks if the result is equal to or greater than 20 Hz Geographical location GetUserGeoID compared with 5 (Azerbaijan), 7 (Armenia), 29 (Belarus), 137 (Kazakhstan), 130 (Kyrgyzstan), 152 (Moldova), 203 (Russia), 228 (Tajikistan), 247 (Uzbekistan), 238 (Turkmenistan) UI-Language GetUserDefaultUILanguage compared with 0x419 (Russia) The refresh rate is obtained using this PowerShell command: powershell "Get-WmiObject Win32_VideoController | Select-Object -ExpandProperty CurrentRefreshRate" It’s possible to bypass the anti-analysis checks by patching the function 0x1807999c2 . Otherwise, if an analysis environment is detected, the system is shut down via a cmd command, or jumps to an invalid address. The necessary files are then copied to a randomly named folder in ProgramData . In this case, the files were: C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\ fl studio pro.exe C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\unityplayer.dll C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\manifest.json C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\awindows.storage.dll A cmd command is executed to add a RunOnce registry value and executes the extracted main executable. cmd /c cmd /C"set XG=n\&&set N8C=\Software\Mic&&set N5bM=r&&set 7Xg4=RunOnce /t REG_SZ /f&&set hjaB=re&&set wj= add&&set G7E=rentVersio&&set 3uc=rosoft\Windows\Cu&&set NF= HKCU&&set fD6k=g&&call set ku8m=%hjaB%%fD6k%%wj%%NF%%N8C%%3uc%%N5bM%%G7E%%XG%%7Xg4%&&call %ku8m% /v "NAAHjWuOj" /d "C:\ProgramData\fjwgyNK\ fl studio pro.exe"" Stages 2 and 3: Shellcode decryption and Donut Loader awindows.storage.dll is a legitimate DLL used to inject the next stage. It has an additional .text section that contains the original digital signature while the DLL is on disk. After the DLL is loaded into memory with LoadLibraryA, the contents of the new section are replaced with the shellcode decrypted from manifest.json . This differs slightly from Elastic’s analysis, in which the shellcode was located in the .reloc section. The loaded DLL from the ProgramData folder The shellcode is decrypted and executed using call r12. It performs several XOR self-decryptions of the code, in a manner similar to the DLL previously analyzed. The decryption of shellcode present in manifest.json In addition to the windows.storage.dll , we identified other DLLs used by OXLoader for injection, including: windows.StateRepository.dll wmp.dll mshtml.dll ieframe.dll The encrypted shellcode on disk can also have different names, such as Dependencies.manifest or titles.png . After the code is decrypted, Donut Loader executes a DLL compressed with APLib. Stages 4 and 5: A PE loader and LOLD downloader The next stage executed by Donut Loader is another obfuscated PE with control-flow flattening, MBA, with a custom section . text0 and just four imports. Despite the complex obfuscation, the next stage is saved in cleartext at address 0x140001000 and loaded into the memory of the process itself. This stage is a downloader which has some internal references marked as LOLD (for example, the mutex “ LOLD_ ”). We won’t analyze it in detail in this post because it is outside the scope of this investigation. The strings and the configuration are decrypted using a custom SplitMix64 XOR algorithm; the configuration is stored in a custom section called .mscfg . In this article
  • OXLoader can lead to malware that steals browser passwords and data or gives criminals remote access to a Windows PC
  • Fake copyright complaints and cracked software activators are among the lures used to spread it
  • What to watch for in suspicious downloads and how to reduce the risk

We’ve seen an increase in activity involving OXLoader, a loader that installs other malware on a computer. Elastic first documented it in June 2026, when attackers used Google Ads to distribute CASTLESTEALER through OXLoader.

The malware installed varies by campaign. We found OXLoader distributing Remcos, OverLord, PureRAT, Lunex Stealer, LOLD, and Hermes. Depending on the payload, attackers could steal saved browser passwords and other data, remotely control the computer, or download more malware.

We found OXLoader in malicious ZIP files disguised as complaint or copyright-infringement notices, as well as fake software activators. One campaign we analyzed used fake activators downloaded from GitLab.

Below, we take a technical deep dive into how that campaign works, including how OXLoader uses DLL hijacking to unpack and run malware.

How to stay safe  

Here are a few simple ways to stay safe:

  • Be wary of emails or links that tell you to run software in connection with copyright infringement or complaints.
  • Watch for executables with very long names or double extensions, such as .docx.exe or .pdf.exe.
  • Pay attention when you extract an archive. If some of the files it contains don’t appear, be cautious.
  • Downloading activators or cracks can compromise your device.
  • Install Malwarebytes Browser Guard, our free browser extension, to block malicious websites and suspicious downloads.
  • Use Malwarebytes Premium to block malware in real time, including malicious files.
Overview of the detected campaigns 

In this section, we analyze several detected campaigns. In the cases we examined, OXLoader was decrypted either by malicious code embedded in legitimate executables, as in Elastic’s analysis, or through DLL hijacking. DLL hijacking is one of the key new features we observed in these campaigns. The rest of the infection chain is similar to the one Elastic identified.

We identified several DLLs used to decrypt and execute OXLoader, including:

  • Qt5Widgets.dll
  • Qt6Core.dll
  • SDL3.dll
  • UnityPlayer.dll 
  • ANCUtility.dll 
  • dbghelp.dll
  • msvcr100.dll

In some cases, we found other DLLs that had been tampered with to launch the malicious DLL. The executables involved were associated with Microsoft applications, Steam, OBS Studio, and PDF or Word readers.

Across different campaigns, OXLoader was distributed using themes related to complaints and copyright infringement. Malicious ZIP files were distributed in several ways. For example, a user might receive an email with an attached PDF prompting them to download and run a ZIP file, claiming there had been “unauthorized copying of brand intellectual property.”

Example of a PDF attached to an email that downloads a malicious ZIP file

When the user runs the executable, the infection chain begins through DLL hijacking, and a fake PDF opens. In this case, WindowsCodecs.dll is the trojanized DLL used to decrypt OXLoader. 

The contents of the malicious ZIP file The fake PDF that opens

In some cases, a batch file is present instead of the executable and DLLs. It downloads a ZIP file containing the malicious DLL from different websites or hosting providers. The batch file’s content is similar to the one analyzed by Elastic. These files have long names, for example:

Photo_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Product_Review_Order_Front_Back_PDF.bat 

Form_Video_{ RANDOM NUMBERS }_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat 

Case_Form_Video_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat

In other cases, OXLoader was distributed through ZIP archives named Evidence_of_Violation.zip, downloaded from Google Sites. These websites used different titles and graphics. 

Google Site used to distribute the malicious archive 

In this case, WinWord.exe is renamed with a double extension, such as Travel_Point_Conditions.docx.exe or evidence_of_violation.docx.exe. OXLoader is then executed through DLL hijacking using the malicious DLL msvcr100.dll.

Example of one of the malicious archives

Finally, in the campaigns analyzed in this post, OXLoader was distributed through fake activators and cracks for popular software, downloaded from GitLab.

Malicious activators hosted on GitLab that distribute OXLoader

 

Technical analysis of OXLoader 

In this campaign, users download software activators from GitLab, triggering the infection chain.

Stage 1: DLL hijacking 

The archive downloaded by the user contains several legitimate DLLs, along with a legitimate executable from Take-Two Interactive Software, which is used to perform DLL hijacking using the UnityPlayer DLL. The manifest.json contains encrypted shellcode, which is decrypted and injected into another legitimate DLL. 

The extracted archive with the malicious DLL

The DLL at address 0x18054485b contains a jmp instruction that calls the code responsible for decrypting the remaining code at 0x1807a3372. This decryption code differs across the cases we analyzed. 

The call to the decryption function The self-decryption function

The code is heavily obfuscated using opaque predicates, control flow flattening (CFF), and mixed Boolean arithmetic (MBA).  We therefore used the Sogen emulator to trace the main functions that execute and identify the malware code that called them.

Partial Sogen execution with some functions related to anti-analysis and language checks Termination of the malware if a virtualized environment is detected (Sogen output) 

The values ​​used by the remaining functions are decoded using two functions: 

  • The function at the address 0x1807a2282 decrypts the data ​​using the following formula: input1 ^ (input2 + 0x33fda). 
  • The function at the address 0x1807a2624 is responsible for decrypting an 8-byte chunk; this function is called multiple times by other wrappers to decrypt the complete strings. 
The decrypted strings

The anti-analysis and language checks we observed are similar to those identified by Elastic, with the minor addition of a check using WNetGetResourceParentW to detect virtualized environments. 

Description Value Invalid values to detect virtualized environments Pass invalid values ​​using the functions WNetAddConnection2W and WNetGetResourceParentW and check if the LastErrorValue is ERROR_BAD_NET_NAME (67) and ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS (487) CPU-count NumberOfProcessors greater than or equal to 3 Display Refresh rate Executes a PowerShell command and it checks if the result is equal to or greater than 20 Hz Geographical location GetUserGeoID compared with 5 (Azerbaijan), 7 (Armenia), 29 (Belarus), 137 (Kazakhstan), 130 (Kyrgyzstan), 152 (Moldova), 203 (Russia), 228 (Tajikistan), 247 (Uzbekistan), 238 (Turkmenistan) UI-Language GetUserDefaultUILanguage compared with 0x419 (Russia) 

The refresh rate is obtained using this PowerShell command: 

powershell  "Get-WmiObject Win32_VideoController | Select-Object -ExpandProperty CurrentRefreshRate" 

It’s possible to bypass the anti-analysis checks by patching the function 0x1807999c2. Otherwise, if an analysis environment is detected, the system is shut down via a cmd command, or jumps to an invalid address.   

The necessary files are then copied to a randomly named folder in ProgramData. In this case, the files were:

C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\ fl studio pro.exe
C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\unityplayer.dll
C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\manifest.json
C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\awindows.storage.dll

A cmd command is executed to add a RunOnce registry value and executes the extracted main executable. 

cmd /c cmd /C"set XG=n\&&set N8C=\Software\Mic&&set N5bM=r&&set 7Xg4=RunOnce /t REG_SZ /f&&set hjaB=re&&set wj= add&&set G7E=rentVersio&&set 3uc=rosoft\Windows\Cu&&set NF= HKCU&&set fD6k=g&&call set ku8m=%hjaB%%fD6k%%wj%%NF%%N8C%%3uc%%N5bM%%G7E%%XG%%7Xg4%&&call %ku8m% /v "NAAHjWuOj" /d "C:\ProgramData\fjwgyNK\ fl studio pro.exe"" 
Stages 2 and 3: Shellcode decryption and Donut Loader 

awindows.storage.dll is a legitimate DLL used to inject the next stage. It has an additional .text section that contains the original digital signature while the DLL is on disk. After the DLL is loaded into memory with LoadLibraryA, the contents of the new section are replaced with the shellcode decrypted from manifest.json.  This differs slightly from Elastic’s analysis, in which the shellcode was located in the .reloc section.

The loaded DLL from the ProgramData folder 

The shellcode is decrypted and executed using call r12. It performs several XOR self-decryptions of the code, in a manner similar to the DLL previously analyzed. 

The decryption of shellcode present in manifest.json

In addition to the windows.storage.dll, we identified other DLLs used by OXLoader for injection, including: 

  • windows.StateRepository.dll 
  • wmp.dll 
  • mshtml.dll 
  • ieframe.dll 

The encrypted shellcode on disk can also have different names, such as Dependencies.manifest or titles.png. 

After the code is decrypted, Donut Loader executes a DLL compressed with APLib.

Stages 4 and 5: A PE loader and LOLD downloader 

The next stage executed by Donut Loader is another obfuscated PE with control-flow flattening, MBA, with a custom section .text0 and just four imports. Despite the complex obfuscation, the next stage is saved in cleartext at address 0x140001000 and loaded into the memory of the process itself. 

This stage is a downloader which has some internal references marked as LOLD (for example, the mutex “LOLD_”). We won’t analyze it in detail in this post because it is outside the scope of this investigation. 

The strings and the configuration are decrypted using a custom SplitMix64 XOR algorithm; the configuration is stored in a custom section called .mscfg. 

The decrypted config 

The decrypted strings include references to the malware’s injection phases:

  • payload launch: GhostedHollowing backend  
  • Self-donor direct module target selected 
  • ElevatedGhostedHollowing 
  • GhostedHollowingSelfDonor 
  • GhostedHollowingLaunchPayloadElevatedSelfDonor returned failure 

At the time of our analysis, the C2 servers associated with LOLD were offline. Based on our analysis of other activity related to OXLoader and LOLD, we observed several HTTP requests to port different ports, including 8093, 8080, and 8700.:

/chunks/p_{RANDOM}/{different numbers}.bin 

/ws/publisher?deviceId= 

/files?prefix=inbox/ 

/api/client/report 

/api/modules/pins 

/api/modules/client-recovery/1.1.8 

These HTTP requests and the artifacts analyzed are attributed to the Hermes malware family. 

IOCs 

IP 

217[.]60[.]102[.]123: LOLD C2 

91[.]92[.]243[.]204: LOLD C2 

Hash 

AC8547F5AF42DC6932367EBCB162FB0E: UnityPlayer.dll, trojanized DLL 

A9D620B690F84D552986A4872D57849E: Encrypted shellcode, manifest.json 

B97730BA59B158F400E67050406CB3EA: Decrypted shellcode 

27b3fd4a4ac2c2f62f7b175ca904c8f7: Donut module, PE loader 

5A0B0BAE87A464228398696517FCF6F5: LOLD payload 

Domain 

guestsisfilesjpmp[.]com: OXLoader distribution 

wovplaying[.]help: OXLoader distribution 

biklonasmain[.]net: OXLoader distribution 

videohostinginsort[.]net: OXLoader distribution

videovisitors[.]com: OXLoader distribution 

URLs 

oz-cloud[.]com/oz-cloud[.]zip: OXLoader distribution smartkitcheneg[.]com/lskg9021oasIgfwqow2[.]zip: OXLoader distribution

items.title: Palo Alto Confirms NGINX Vulnerabilities Impact PAN-OS and Releases Workarounds
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks confirmed that two critical NGINX flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 , affect PAN-OS and Panorama deployments with HTTP/2 enabled. The flaws could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to crash worker processes or execute code, prompting Palo Alto Networks to release patches and a workaround for affected systems. The security advisory assigns a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and a moderate response urgency. Palo Alto Networks says it is not aware of malicious exploitation. Customers without HTTP/2 enabled are not affected by these issues. Panorama virtual appliances and M-Series appliances are included in the affected products. CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free flaw in NGINX HTTP/2 proxy handling. Active connections can remain marked as reusable when they should not be. If a worker runs low on connection slots, NGINX may close connections and release memory. At the same time, it still sends requests to backend servers. That memory error can crash the worker or allow code execution. The CVE record adds an important limit for the underlying NGINX flaw. Code execution requires Address Space Layout Randomization, or ASLR, to be disabled or bypassed. ASLR makes memory locations harder to predict, which helps block exploitation. Palo Alto Confirms NGINX RCE Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-123007 affects HTTP/2 flow control, which manages how much data a connection can send. An integer underflow lets the flow-control window exceed its allowed limit. Specially crafted traffic can then trigger a heap-based buffer overflow, causing a crash or allowing an attacker to run code. Cyber Security News previously covered these NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities , including their different attack conditions. They also appear in its wider reporting on the NGINX2Root vulnerabilities. The Palo Alto notice now gives customers product-specific guidance rather than requiring them to rely on upstream NGINX version numbers. For PAN-OS 12.2, the vendor directs customers to upgrade to 12.2.4-h3 or later. On PAN-OS 12.1, customers running affected 12.1.8 through 12.1.10 builds should install 12.1.10-h6 or later. Those on 12.1.5 through 12.1.7 can use 12.1.7-h15 or 12.1.10-h6, subject to release availability. For PAN-OS 11.2, fixed options include 11.2.10-h19, 11.2.13-h6, and 11.2.16-h3, depending on the maintenance branch. The advisory lists November 23 as the expected release date for 12.1.7-h15, 11.2.10-h19, and 11.2.13-h6. Customers should confirm availability before scheduling an upgrade. The vendor lists PAN-OS 12.1 versions below 12.1.5 and PAN-OS 11.2 versions below 11.2.8 as unaffected. Other on-premises products not listed were reviewed and found unaffected. Palo Alto Networks is managing fixes for its SaaS products , with no customer action required. Customers unable to patch can disable HTTP/2 on PAN-OS and Panorama using the vendor’s HTTP/2 configuration documentation. The documentation says HTTP/1.1 is enabled by default, while HTTP/2 requires manual configuration. Teams should therefore check both the installed software version and protocol settings when reviewing exposure, then apply the appropriate fixed release. items.title: Hackers Allegedly Claiming Exploit for VMware vCenter 0-day Vulnerability
items.summary: A forum seller using the name Matilda is asking $30,000 for a claimed exploit targeting CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter Server vulnerability. A screenshot shared by Dark Web Informer shows the seller claiming that the tool can create a new vCenter administrator account. The listing surfaced after Broadcom issued a fix on November 19, 2026. The tool’s claimed capabilities and compatibility have not been independently verified. Source: Dark Web Informer The seller describes the tool as a Python program with separate functions for checking whether a server is vulnerable and exploiting the flaw.
items.summary_html:
A forum seller using the name Matilda is asking $30,000 for a claimed exploit targeting CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter Server vulnerability.

A screenshot shared by Dark Web Informer shows the seller claiming that the tool can create a new vCenter administrator account. The listing surfaced after Broadcom issued a fix on November 19, 2026. The tool’s claimed capabilities and compatibility have not been independently verified.

Source: Dark Web Informer

The seller describes the tool as a Python program with separate functions for checking whether a server is vulnerable and exploiting the flaw.

The post claims support for affected releases from vCenter 7.0 through 9.1 and offers prospective buyers a demonstration. An offer is not proof of a successful test, and the listing does not establish that the seller used the tool against any organization.

VMware vCenter Attacks Began Before Patch

Broadcom’s VMSA-2026-0009 advisory rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the VMware vCenter authentication bypass, the flaw affects VMware Directory Service, which supports vCenter’s single sign-on system.

An attacker who can reach an affected server over the network can bypass login without valid credentials. That matters because vCenter provides a central place to manage VMware hosts and virtual machines.

Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant traced attacks exploiting the flaw to early September 2026, before a patch was available. In earlier coverage of the vCenter zero-day attacks, Cyber Security News reported that a suspected China-linked group known as ARMORY CASTLE used a separate tool called BONESAW.

The documented attacks explain why the flaw is described as a zero-day. The forum post, by contrast, advertises an exploit for a flaw that has since been disclosed and patched. The reporting does not link Matilda to ARMORY CASTLE.

VMware vCenter Patch

Broadcom lists fixes in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 Update 3m. VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x customers should follow the vendor’s guidance for release 5.2.5.

The advisory lists no public fix for vCenter 7.0 and directs customers with extended support contracts to contact Broadcom Support. Administrators should use the vendor’s response matrix to confirm the correct update for their deployment.

The National Vulnerability Database entry records the flaw’s addition to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20. Broadcom lists no workaround, so teams should apply the relevant update without waiting for the forum claim to be verified.

They should also review vCenter sign-in records and administrator account changes for unexpected activity, especially on servers that were reachable from untrusted networks before patching. An update closes the flaw, but it does not establish whether an attacker used it before the fix was installed.

items.title: Researchers Hack Volkswagen Cars via Bluetooth to Spy on Conversations and Track GPS Locations
items.summary: Bluetooth flaws in Volkswagen cars could expose private conversations, reveal GPS locations, and allow unauthorized control of cabin features. The findings highlight a lengthy patch rollout, with some vehicles remaining exposed roughly 16 months after the vulnerabilities became public. Hungarian firm PCA Cyber Security demonstrated the attack against a Volkswagen ID.4 in Budapest, according to heise’s report. Researchers reportedly accessed the hands-free microphone , monitored location data, and operated the heater, windshield wipers, and sunroof using a laptop outside the vehicle. The attack uses PerfektBlue, a chain of vulnerabilities in OpenSynergy’s BlueSDK Bluetooth software. This component handles wireless connections in vehicle infotainment systems. PCA’s security advisory explains how the flaws can be combined to run attacker-controlled code on affected systems. For the demonstrated Volkswagen attack , the driver must first approve a Bluetooth pairing request. Once connected, the attacker can exploit the vulnerable software and gain control over functions available through the infotainment system. That requirement is important. The demonstration does not show that an attacker can silently compromise every nearby Volkswagen without interaction. Rejecting an unfamiliar pairing request blocks the connection this attack needs. Volkswagen Cars Hacked via Bluetooth Cyber Security News previously covered the underlying weaknesses in its report on the PerfektBlue Bluetooth vulnerabilities , which affected software used across multiple vehicle brands. Researchers estimate that several hundred thousand Volkswagen vehicles could be affected. However, that figure is not a confirmed count of compromised cars, and the reported demonstration does not establish widespread criminal exploitation. Volkswagen told heise that older infotainment software required additional changes and security checks, which delayed repairs. The company said it had addressed the issue more quickly in newer software branches. For vehicles running software older than version 4.0, Volkswagen says version 3.9.1 fixes the vulnerability. Eligible owners can install that update over cellular or Wi-Fi while their vehicle is parked. Other affected software versions require a workshop visit. Volkswagen says vehicles running version 5.6 or later are not affected. Owners should confirm the correct update route with Volkswagen rather than assume every car receives the same fix. Volkswagen says the flaws do not provide access to steering, braking, or acceleration. The demonstrated access instead concerns infotainment and connected cabin functions. Nevertheless, microphone access could expose sensitive conversations, while GPS tracking could reveal journeys and regular destinations. Those privacy risks remain significant even when driving controls are outside the attacker’s reach. Earlier research also identified separate weaknesses affecting vehicle data and infotainment systems, as detailed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of Skoda and Volkswagen security flaws . Those findings should not be treated as the same vulnerability chain. Volkswagen advises owners never to accept unknown Bluetooth pairing requests or connect unfamiliar USB devices. Drivers should check their installed software version, follow official update instructions, and contact a dealer when patch availability is unclear. Volkswagen has not announced a recall for this issue, according to heise’s report. items.summary_html:
Bluetooth flaws in Volkswagen cars could expose private conversations, reveal GPS locations, and allow unauthorized control of cabin features.

The findings highlight a lengthy patch rollout, with some vehicles remaining exposed roughly 16 months after the vulnerabilities became public. Hungarian firm PCA Cyber Security demonstrated the attack against a Volkswagen ID.4 in Budapest, according to heise’s report.

Researchers reportedly accessed the hands-free microphone, monitored location data, and operated the heater, windshield wipers, and sunroof using a laptop outside the vehicle.

The attack uses PerfektBlue, a chain of vulnerabilities in OpenSynergy’s BlueSDK Bluetooth software. This component handles wireless connections in vehicle infotainment systems. PCA’s security advisory explains how the flaws can be combined to run attacker-controlled code on affected systems.

For the demonstrated Volkswagen attack, the driver must first approve a Bluetooth pairing request. Once connected, the attacker can exploit the vulnerable software and gain control over functions available through the infotainment system.

That requirement is important. The demonstration does not show that an attacker can silently compromise every nearby Volkswagen without interaction. Rejecting an unfamiliar pairing request blocks the connection this attack needs.

Volkswagen Cars Hacked via Bluetooth

Cyber Security News previously covered the underlying weaknesses in its report on the PerfektBlue Bluetooth vulnerabilities, which affected software used across multiple vehicle brands.

Researchers estimate that several hundred thousand Volkswagen vehicles could be affected. However, that figure is not a confirmed count of compromised cars, and the reported demonstration does not establish widespread criminal exploitation.

Volkswagen told heise that older infotainment software required additional changes and security checks, which delayed repairs. The company said it had addressed the issue more quickly in newer software branches.

For vehicles running software older than version 4.0, Volkswagen says version 3.9.1 fixes the vulnerability. Eligible owners can install that update over cellular or Wi-Fi while their vehicle is parked.

Other affected software versions require a workshop visit. Volkswagen says vehicles running version 5.6 or later are not affected. Owners should confirm the correct update route with Volkswagen rather than assume every car receives the same fix.

Volkswagen says the flaws do not provide access to steering, braking, or acceleration. The demonstrated access instead concerns infotainment and connected cabin functions.

Nevertheless, microphone access could expose sensitive conversations, while GPS tracking could reveal journeys and regular destinations. Those privacy risks remain significant even when driving controls are outside the attacker’s reach.

Earlier research also identified separate weaknesses affecting vehicle data and infotainment systems, as detailed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of Skoda and Volkswagen security flaws. Those findings should not be treated as the same vulnerability chain.

Volkswagen advises owners never to accept unknown Bluetooth pairing requests or connect unfamiliar USB devices. Drivers should check their installed software version, follow official update instructions, and contact a dealer when patch availability is unclear. Volkswagen has not announced a recall for this issue, according to heise’s report.
