items.title: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers 0-Day Vulnerabilities Enabling Mobile OS Security Bypass and RCE
items.summary: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra has found and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities affecting a popular mobile operating system and a widely hosted network service, according to the company’s latest system card. The findings include a permission bypass that exposed private data and a separate remote code execution flaw reachable from a low-privileged role. The discoveries came from testing by security firm Irregular, rather than reports of attacks against users. OpenAI’s November 17 system card says Irregular is handling responsible disclosure. It does not name the affected products, identify vulnerable versions, provide CVE numbers, or confirm when patches will become available. The mobile operating system flaw allowed a malicious app to access private data despite lacking the required permissions. That finding points to a failure in the operating system’s access controls. The published account does not identify the exposed data types or explain which permission checks the app bypassed. OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers Zero-Day Vulnerabilities The remote code execution finding involved a separate network service. Astra exploited the service from a low-privileged role, showing that limited access was enough to reach code execution. The report does not establish unauthenticated access, administrator control, or a mobile exploit chain linking the two discoveries. Keeping those findings separate is important. The mobile issue concerns access to protected information, while the network service issue concerns running code. Neither description supports claims that Astra remotely took over phones or compromised every device using the unnamed operating system. Irregular tested Astra through FrontierCyber, which measures offensive skills on real-world systems, and CyScenarioBench, which covers multi-stage security operations. Astra solved 68 of 217 FrontierCyber challenges, compared with 77 for GPT-6 Astra. The newer model therefore discovered serious flaws without outperforming its predecessor across that entire suite. Neither model successfully attacked a fully hardened target. All 15 of the hardest FrontierCyber challenges remained unsolved. On CyScenarioBench, both models solved nine of 11 challenges at least once. At the same time, Astra’s success rate reached 63%, compared with 61% for its predecessor. Separate OpenAI tests showed stronger progress in developing exploits for known vulnerabilities. Astra achieved a 53.5% mean arbitrary code execution rate on ExploitBench Internal Port, compared with 31.5% for GPT-6 Astra. That evaluation used V8 and Chrome flaws disclosed between June and August 2026, not newly discovered zero-days. The distinction helps readers judge the results fairly. Finding an unknown flaw and turning a disclosed bug into working code are related skills, but they are not the same task. Earlier reporting on Astra’s zero-day research provides background on this growing capability. OpenAI says both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet its Critical cybersecurity capability threshold. The company describes tighter restrictions on higher-risk assistance, monitoring, and additional approval for more permissive access. The company conducted its capability evaluations without production safeguards, so the results should not be treated as a description of ordinary customer access. Previous coverage of OpenAI’s security isolation tests also shows why containment matters alongside model rules. These systems can help researchers find weaknesses, but their tools and access need firm limits. For now, the missing product names and patch details prevent specific exposure checks. The immediate takeaway is evidence of successful zero-day research under evaluation conditions, not proof of widespread exploitation. Further disclosure will determine which users need fixes and how urgently vendors must respond. items.title: Cleverbridge Confirms Hackers Stole Customer Card Numbers and CVV Codes in a Major Data Breach
items.summary: Cleverbridge confirmed that hackers copied payment card data from its e-commerce platform. The stolen information includes card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV or CVC security codes. Cleverbridge’s public update does not list those fields or say whether the same details were exposed for every affected customer. The company began notifying affected individuals on November 20, 2026. According to Cleverbridge’s incident update , the company detected unauthorized activity on November 4 and temporarily took affected systems offline to contain it. All systems were back online that day, but investigators later found that someone had copied payment card data stored on the platform. Cleverbridge Data Breach Cleverbridge said the incident was not ransomware and that none of its systems were encrypted. Restoring service addressed the outage, but it did not undo the theft. Cleverbridge handles online purchases, payments, and subscriptions for other businesses, so affected shoppers may recognize the seller rather than the company that processed their payment. The public notice does not identify the affected merchants, give a count of impacted customers, or explain how the attackers got in or how long they had access. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of separate breaches at financial service providers , stolen customer data does not necessarily mean the business customers bought from was itself breached. A CVV or CVC is the three- or four-digit security code printed on a payment card. Online merchants use it to help verify that the buyer has the card. When thieves have the card number, expiration date, and security code, they can try to make online purchases without the physical card. The PCI Security Standards Council says merchants must not retain these codes after a payment is authorized, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge has not publicly explained where it stored the exposed codes or for how long, so the available information does not show whether it broke that rule. If you receive a Cleverbridge breach notice, check which card it identifies and review recent transactions. Report any charge you do not recognize to your card issuer right away. Even if you have not spotted fraud, contact the issuer through its official app or the number on your card and ask whether it should be replaced. Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion’s Cyberscout to help notify customers and offered credit or identity monitoring where available. Enrollment details are in the individual notices. Treat unexpected calls, emails, or texts about the breach with caution. Cyber Security News has documented how fake billing notices can send people to convincing payment pages that ask for card details and one-time codes. Cleverbridge says it will never ask for card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text. If a message asks you to verify a card or claim help, check it through a trusted contact channel rather than using the link or phone number in the message. items.title: Sharper Checks: Accuracy improvements across Device Trust
items.summary: With 1Password Device Trust , compliance policies are set across your fleet through " Checks ." However, a Check is only as useful as it is accurate. If a device wrongly fails, it might eventually be blocked from accessing sensitive systems, which could result in a frustrating experience for a perfectly compliant end user. If a device wrongly passes, however, risk can go unnoticed. Accuracy in our Checks is an important element of ensuring that our customers can “trust” in “1Password Device Trust.” That is why the Device Trust Checks team spends a great deal of time not only creating new Checks, but improving existing ones. We often ask ourselves, “Is this Check seeing the whole picture?” In some cases, the honest answer is “not yet.” Sometimes that is because circumstances change over time and we have to adapt our Checks with them. For example, third-party data sources evolve, or OS updates introduce new settings. Other times, we find a more accurate way to interpret what a device tells us, or a more dependable source for the data we need. In the name of accuracy, here is a look at what we have been working on. How 1Password Device Trust is seeing more of the picture Windows Screen Lock: Require secure screen lock configuration Windows has many (no really, many ) ways to lock a device, and several of them influence how the others behave. We have updated how this Check evaluates them together, so it reflects how a device locks in practice. Now, the Check: Recognizes the Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit setting, whether it is set through Group Policy, local security policy, or MDM Considers lock-specific policies that apply to domain-joined devices Accounts for how screen savers interact with other lock settings. For example, a screen saver that does not require a password on resume can prevent Windows from locking at all, even when power settings are configured to lock Adds a new option to accept Dynamic lock as passable behavior Windows Security Center: Require ransomware protection (controlled folder access) to be enabled Controlled Folder Access is Windows’ built-in ransomware protection, and it can be configured in more ways than our Check previously examined. We expanded the Check to cover them. The Check now: Reads settings from Group Policy and Microsoft Defender, in addition to the local Windows setting Recognizes every Controlled Folder Access mode Considers which antivirus is active, because Controlled Folder Access only protects a device when Microsoft Defender is doing the work Reflects the Windows default (off) when the Controlled Folder Access setting has never been configured Adds new options that give more granular control over the allowed apps list in Controlled Folder Access, so you can specify which apps should and should not be there Adds a new option to require additional protected folders beyond the ones Windows protects by default Linux Package Updates: Ensure Linux packages are up to date Not every Ubuntu update lands on all devices at the same time. With phased updates, Ubuntu releases some updates in stages, and the package manager (apt) holds them back on a device until its turn comes. These held-back packages are now recognized, so Device Trust only prompts end users to update what is actually available to them. This Check requires Device Trust launcher 2.6.0 or later. Dependable sources for more accurate insight Network Time Protocol: Require date and time to be set automatically (macOS) To get the most dependable read on this setting, we introduced a shiny new launcher table that reads it directly from macOS. The Check now uses it on devices running Device Trust launcher 2.6.0 or later. Android Software Updates: Ensure Android OS Is Up to Date Google recently moved to risk-based updates for Pixel devices, as they shared in official statements with Android Authority . This means that not every model receives every monthly security patch. To keep pace, the Check now compares each Pixel against the latest update Google released for that specific model, rather than the latest patch for its Android version. More customizable Checks that fit your environment Windows Security Center: Require Antivirus to Be Enabled The Windows Antivirus and Firewall Checks are close cousins: both confirm that a device’s protection software is in place and running. While reviewing them side by side, we noticed the Firewall Check allowed for more control, giving the ability to choose exactly which products you accept. So we brought the Windows Antivirus Check up to speed. It now includes options for common products (like Bitdefender, McAfee, Norton, Sophos, CrowdStrike, and SentinelOne), an accept-all option, and a way to add less common antivirus products your organization may use. For customers already using the Windows Antivirus Check, nothing changes unless you choose to use the newly available options. Pro tip: these new options pair well with the Controlled Folder Access update. Since that Check only applies when Defender is the active antivirus, you can use the Windows Antivirus Check alongside it to require Defender, which brings devices under consideration for the Controlled Folder Access Check. Windows Firewall: Require Firewall to Be Enabled To keep the Windows Antivirus and Firewall Checks Checks consistent, we also expanded the options in the Windows Firewall Check. It gains an accept-all option, improved support for common products like SentinelOne and McAfee, and an option to add lesser known firewalls. As with the Windows Antivirus Check, nothing changes unless you choose to use the new options. How to get started From Windows screen locks to Pixel patch levels, each of these updates expands what Device Trust can see. Our work on accuracy is never really finished, and we like it that way. As operating systems and tools change, our Checks will continue to adapt with them, so you and your end users can keep trusting Device Trust. These improvements are live and ready to explore for all Device Trust customers. If you want to enable one of these Checks, head to the Check Catalog in your Device Trust admin console. If you already have one running and want to try the new options, open it from your active Checks. Want to learn more? To learn more about how Checks work, take a peek at our docs. Windows has many (no really, many) ways to lock a device, and several of them influence how the others behave. We have updated how this Check evaluates them together, so it reflects how a device locks in practice. Now, the Check:

  • Recognizes every Controlled Folder Access mode

  • Considers which antivirus is active, because Controlled Folder Access only protects a device when Microsoft Defender is doing the work

  • Reflects the Windows default (off) when the Controlled Folder Access setting has never been configured

  • Adds new options that give more granular control over the allowed apps list in Controlled Folder Access, so you can specify which apps should and should not be there

  • Adds a new option to require additional protected folders beyond the ones Windows protects by default
